After two early failures, the indigenous Cryogenic Upper Stage (CUS) flew successfully on GSLV‑D5 (5 January 2014), marking India’s entry into the cryogenic club. The Mk II series (GSLV‑F05 onward) standardised the CUS and increased the payload to 2,500 kg to Geostationary Transfer Orbit (GTO). The Mk III, redesignated LVM3 (Launch Vehicle Mark‑3), debuted on 5 June 2017 with the GSAT‑19 mission. LVM3 uses two S200 solid strap‑ons, a L110 liquid core stage (two Vikas engines) and a C25 cryogenic stage (CE‑20 engine) delivering 4,000 kg to GTO and 8,000 kg to Low Earth Orbit (LEO). The LVM3‑M3 mission (26 March 2023) placed 36 OneWeb satellites (total 5,800 kg) into a 450 km circular orbit, demonstrating commercial heavy‑lift capability.

Parallel to the heavy‑lift line, the Small Satellite Launch Vehicle (SSLV) was conceived for rapid, low‑cost access to LEO for satellites up to 500 kg. After a partial failure on SSLV‑D1 (7 August 2022), the SSLV‑D2 flight (10 February 2023) successfully injected the EOS‑07, Janus‑1 and AzaadiSAT‑2 payloads into a 356 km orbit, validating the three‑stage solid‑propulsion architecture with a liquid‑propellant Velocity Trimming Module (VTM).

Looking ahead, ISRO’s Heavy‑Lift Launch Vehicle (HLV) concept targets 30–40 tonnes to LEO and 10–15 tonnes to GTO by the early 2030s. The design leverages a cluster of S200‑class boosters, a new semi‑cryogenic SCE‑200 core stage (LOX/kerosene, 2 MN thrust) under development at the Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre (LPSC), and an upgraded C32 cryogenic upper stage. The HLV is intended to support the Gaganyaan human‑spaceflight programme, lunar sample‑return missions and the proposed Indian Space Station. Funding for the SCE‑200 was approved in the 2022‑23 budget (₹1,800 crore) and the first hot‑fire test of the semi‑cryogenic engine is scheduled for 2025 at the ISRO Propulsion Complex, Mahendragiri.

Ground‑Based Quantum Key Distribution Network: Trusted‑Node Architecture and the Delhi‑Mumbai Link

India’s National Quantum Mission (NQM), approved by the Union Cabinet in April 2023 with an outlay of ₹6,003 crore for 2023‑2031, earmarked a dedicated work‑package for a fibre‑based Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) backbone linking major metropolitan centres. The first operational segment, a 800 km trusted‑node chain between New Delhi and Mumbai, was commissioned in March 2024 after a series of field trials conducted jointly by the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), the Centre for Development of Telematics (C‑DOT) and the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Delhi.

The architecture follows the ETSI GS QKD 014 trusted‑node model: quantum signals propagate over standard single‑mode fibre (ITU‑T G.652.D) at 1550 nm, while classical synchronisation and error‑correction traffic share a parallel wavelength via dense wavelength‑division multiplexing (DWDM). Intermediate trusted nodes are located at Bhopal, Indore and Surat, each housed in a hardened telecom shelter with tamper‑evident key‑management servers certified to Common Criteria EAL 4+. At each node, the incoming quantum key is measured, regenerated and forwarded, ensuring end‑to‑end secrecy provided the node itself remains uncompromised — a risk mitigated by physical security, continuous intrusion detection and periodic key‑freshness audits.

Performance metrics from the 2023‑24 trial phase show a sustained secret‑key rate of 1.2 kbps over the full 800 km distance with a quantum bit error rate (QBER) below 2.5 %, meeting the threshold for one‑time‑pad encryption of tactical voice and data links. The network integrates with the satellite‑based QKD demonstrator (QKD‑Sat) slated for launch on an LVM3 mission in 2025, enabling a hybrid space‑ground key‑exchange fabric. The ground segment also supports the “Quantum‑Safe VPN” pilot for the Ministry of Defence, where IPsec tunnels are re‑keyed every 60 seconds using QKD‑derived keys, demonstrating forward secrecy against future quantum‑computer attacks.

Regulatory alignment is being pursued through the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) draft “Quantum Communication Security Framework” (released July 2024), which mandates minimum key‑rate, maximum trusted‑node hop count (≤ 5) and auditability standards for any licenced QKD service provider. The framework also references the International Telecommunication Union (ITU‑T) X.1710 security architecture, ensuring interoperability with allied nations’ quantum networks.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: "Which of the following statements about India's ground‑based QKD network is correct? (a) It uses a single‑photon source at 1310 nm; (b) Trusted nodes are placed at every 50 km; (c) The Delhi‑Mumbai link operates at a secret‑key rate of 1.2 kbps with QBER < 2.5 %; (d) The network is fully device‑independent."
Correct answer: (c). The deployed Delhi‑Mumbai trusted‑node chain uses 1550 nm wavelength, not 1310 nm. Trusted nodes are spaced roughly 150–200 km apart (Bhopal, Indore, Surat), not every 50 km. The network is trusted‑node based, not device‑independent; device‑independent QKD remains experimental. The reported secret‑key rate of 1.2 kbps and QBER below 2.5 % are documented in the 2024 NQM progress report.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mixes quantum‑communication parameters (wavelength, key‑rate, node spacing), first eliminate options that violate the standard telecom window (1550 nm for low‑loss fibre). Then recall the specific performance figures released in the latest National Quantum Mission update — these are frequently quoted verbatim in UPSC‑style questions.

High‑Power Microwave Weapon Development for Counter‑UAV and Electronic Attack

The Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) has pursued High‑Power Microwave (HPM) weapons since the early 2000s under the KALI (Kilo Ampere Linear Injector) series at the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) and the Defence Electronics Research Laboratory (DLRL), Hyderabad. KALI‑5000, commissioned in 2011, generates 40 GW peak power in the S‑band (3 GHz) with a pulse width of 100 ns, serving as a testbed for component hardening and effect‑assessment on electronic targets.

Building on KALI data, the DURGA (Directed Energy Weapon for Unmanned Aerial Vehicle Neutralisation) programme was sanctioned in 2017. DURGA‑I, a ground‑based HPM system, employs a 10 GW, 3 GHz magnetron‑driven source coupled to a phased‑array antenna capable of electronic beam steering over ±60° in azimuth and elevation. The first open‑air trial at the Integrated Test Range (ITR), Chandipur, on 12 October 2022, successfully disrupted the flight control electronics of a swarm of five commercial quad‑copters at a range of 1.2 km, achieving a 90 % kill probability within a 3‑second engagement window.

A shipborne variant, DURGA‑II, integrates a compact 5 GW solid‑state HPM module (GaN‑based amplifiers) into the existing AKASH weapon system’s fire‑control radar, providing a non‑kinetic layer against low‑cost drone threats. Sea trials aboard INS Kochi in March 2023 demonstrated neutralisation of a target drone at 800 m while the ship manoeuvred at 15 knots. The system’s average power consumption is 120 kW, drawn from the ship’s integrated electric propulsion bus, and the duty cycle permits 30 seconds of continuous emission followed by a 90‑second cool‑down.

Parallel to DURGA, the “Surya” HPM programme at DLRL focuses on wideband (1–18 GHz) sources for stand‑off electronic attack on communication and radar nodes. A 2024 laboratory demonstration achieved 2 GW peak power across a 2 GHz instantaneous bandwidth using a relativistic backward‑wave oscillator, with a measured far‑field power density of 10 kW/m² at 5 km — sufficient to upset unhardened commercial receivers. The programme roadmap targets a mobile platform‑mounted prototype by 2027, aligned with the Indian Army’s “Future Electronic Warfare” capability matrix.

Nuclear Reactor Decommissioning Strategy: Experience from Tarapur and Future PHWR Fleet Planning

India’s first commercial nuclear power station, Tarapur Atomic Power Station (TAPS) Units 1 and 2 (160 MWe each, boiling water reactors supplied by General Electric), entered commercial operation in 1969. Following a 2018 safety review by the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB), a decommissioning licence was granted in January 2020 under the Atomic Energy Act, 1962. Defuelling of both units was completed by December 2022, with 1,200 spent‑fuel assemblies transferred to the on‑site Away‑From‑Reactor (AFR) wet storage facility. The current phase, “Safe Enclosure”, involves maintaining the reactor buildings under controlled ventilation and radiation monitoring for a 30‑year dormancy period, after which dismantling of the reactor pressure vessels and internals will commence, targeting site release by 2055.

For the Pressurised Heavy Water Reactor (PHWR) fleet, the Rajasthan Atomic Power Station (RAPS) Units 1 and 2 (100 MWe each) have undergone life‑extension assessments. In 2021, AERB approved a 10‑year licence renewal (to 2035) contingent on replacement of the calandria tubes, feeder pipes and the installation of a post‑accident containment filtered venting system. A decommissioning fund, financed through a levy of ₹0.05 per kWh generated, has accumulated ₹1,200 crore as of March 2024, earmarked for future PHWR dismantling. The Nuclear Waste Management Organisation (NWMO), established in 2022 under the Department of Atomic Energy, is tasked with developing a Deep Geological Repository (DGR) for high‑level waste; site characterisation studies are underway in the granitic terrain of the Kadapa basin.

International guidance from the IAEA’s “Decommissioning of Nuclear Power Plants” (WS‑G‑2.1) and the OECD‑NEA “Cost Estimation for Decommissioning” framework have been adopted in the Indian cost‑benchmarking exercise. The 2023 cost estimate for a 220 MWe PHWR decommissioning (including waste packaging, transport and DGR disposal) stands at ₹2,800 crore, with a projected schedule of 15 years from final shutdown to site release. The experience gained at Tarapur is being codified into a “Standard Decommissioning Plan” template for all operating PHWRs, to be submitted to AERB by 2026.

Ballistic Missile Defence Phase‑II: Exo‑Atmospheric Interceptor Testing and System Integration

India’s Ballistic Missile Defence (BMD) programme is structured in two phases. Phase‑I, declared operational in 2019, comprises the Prithvi Air Defence (PAD) exo‑atmospheric interceptor (max altitude 80 km) and the Advanced Air Defence (AAD) endo‑atmospheric interceptor (max altitude 30 km), cued by the Swordfish Long‑Range Tracking Radar (LRTR) and the Multi‑Function Fire Control Radar (MFCR). Phase‑II aims to raise the interception envelope to 150 km and engage multiple simultaneous threats.

The Phase‑II exo‑atmospheric interceptor, designated PDV‑Mk‑II, is a two‑stage solid‑propellant vehicle with a kinetic kill vehicle (KKV) employing an imaging infrared (IIR) seeker and a divert‑and‑attitude‑control system (DACS) based on cold‑gas thrusters. The first successful flight test, “Mission Divyastra”, was conducted on 27 April 2022 from the Abdul Kalam Island launch complex. The target, a modified Prithvi‑II missile simulating a 1,500 km‑class ballistic trajectory, was intercepted at 120 km altitude with a miss distance of < 0.5 m, confirming hit‑to‑kill capability.

A subsequent multi‑target test on 15 September 2023 launched two PDV‑Mk‑II interceptors against two incoming targets separated by 30 seconds. Both interceptors achieved kill, demonstrating the battle‑management software’s ability to maintain separate track files and allocate interceptors in real time. The test also validated the upgraded Swordfish‑II radar, which provides 360° azimuth coverage and a range of 1,500 km for target acquisition.

Integration with the Integrated Air Command and Control System (IACCS) was demonstrated in a joint exercise “Exercise Vajra Prahar” (March 2024), where BMD cues were fused with Akash‑NG and QRSAM engagement zones to create a layered shield over the northern border sector. The Phase‑II deployment timeline targets initial operational capability (IOC) by 2027, with four interceptor squadrons (two exo, two endo) and a dedicated BMD command post at the Air Force Station, Srinagar. The programme budget, revised in the 2023‑24 Defence Budget, stands at ₹12,500 crore, covering interceptor production, radar upgrades and the hardened command‑and‑control network.

  • Confusing the PSLV’s payload capacity to GTO (≈ 1,200 kg) with its SSPO capacity (≈ 1,750 kg).
  • Assuming the Delhi‑Mumbai QKD link uses device‑independent protocols; it relies on trusted nodes.
  • Attributing the DURGA HPM system’s 10 GW output to a solid‑state source; it is magnetron‑driven.
  • Stating that Tarapur Units 1 & 2 have been fully dismantled; they are in safe‑enclosure dormancy until 2055.
  • Believing the PDV‑Mk‑II interceptor uses a blast‑fragmentation warhead; it is a pure kinetic kill vehicle.
  • Mixing the Phase‑I PAD altitude ceiling (80 km) with Phase‑II’s 150 km envelope.
  • Overlooking that the National Quantum Mission’s ₹6,003 crore outlay covers both ground and space QKD, not only the fibre network.

These sections provide the depth and specificity required for advanced examination preparation.

Indigenous Development of the Ghatak Unmanned Combat Aerial Vehicle: Design, Stealth Features and Integration with Network‑Centric Warfare

The Ghatak programme, managed by the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) under the Aeronautical Development Establishment (ADE), represents India’s first dedicated effort to field a low‑observable, autonomous unmanned combat aerial vehicle (UCAV). The platform adopts a flying‑wing configuration with blended body‑wing geometry to minimise radar cross‑section (RCS) across X‑band and Ku‑band frequencies. Composite‑rich airframe structures, radar‑absorbent material (RAM) coatings on leading edges, and an internal weapons bay capable of carrying up to 1,000 kg of precision‑guided munitions constitute the core stealth envelope. The propulsion system uses a single after‑burning turbofan derived from the Kaveri‑derivative engine, providing a thrust‑to‑weight ratio sufficient for supersonic dash (Mach 1.2) while maintaining subsonic loiter endurance of 6–8 hours at 30,000 ft.

Autonomy is achieved through a hierarchical control architecture: a high‑level mission planner on the ground station communicates via a secure, jam‑resistant data link (S‑band/L‑band dual‑frequency) to an on‑board autonomous mission computer. The computer executes real‑time sensor fusion from an electro‑optical/infrared (EO/IR) turret, a synthetic aperture radar (SAR) pod, and an electronic support measures (ESM) suite, enabling autonomous target detection, classification, and engagement without continuous human‑in‑the‑loop input. The system complies with the Defence AI Ethics Framework’s “human‑on‑the‑loop” mandate for weapon release, requiring a positive command from a designated operator before kinetic action.

Network‑centric integration is realised through the Integrated Air Command and Control System (IACCS) and the Defence Space Agency’s Joint Space Operations Centre (JSpOC). Ghatak can receive beyond‑line‑of‑sight (BLOS) targeting cues from space‑based SAR constellations (RISAT series) and from ground‑based long‑range radars (Swordfish‑II). Its data link supports the Link‑16 compatible waveform, allowing seamless interoperability with Su‑30MKI, Rafale, and Tejas platforms for cooperative engagement and manned‑unmanned teaming (MUM‑T) missions.

Flight‑test milestones include the sub‑scale technology demonstrator SWiFT (Stealth Wing Flying Testbed) which completed its maiden autonomous flight in July 2022, validating aerodynamic stability, control law robustness, and low‑RCS signatures. The full‑scale Ghatak prototype is slated for first flight in 2025, with weapon‑release trials planned for 2026‑27. The induction timeline targets initial operational capability (IOC) by 2030, with an initial squadron of 12‑15 airframes allocated to the Indian Air Force’s strategic strike role.

Strategic implications are significant: Ghatak provides a survivable, persistent strike asset for contested environments such as the northern borders and the Indian Ocean Region, reducing reliance on manned platforms for high‑risk penetration missions. Its development also accelerates indigenous mastery of stealth airframe design, autonomous decision‑making algorithms, and secure data‑link technologies that have spill‑over benefits for future fifth‑generation fighter programmes (AMCA) and loyal‑wingman concepts.

Budgetary allocation for the Ghatak programme, as per the 2023‑24 Defence Budget, stands at ₹4,800 crore, covering airframe development, engine integration, avionics, and test infrastructure. The programme leverages the Defence Industrial Corridor in Tamil Nadu for composite manufacturing and the Uttar Pradesh corridor for avionics assembly, reinforcing the indigenisation ecosystem.

Thorium‑Based Advanced Heavy Water Reactor Programme: Fuel Cycle, Safety Features and Deployment Timeline

India’s Advanced Heavy Water Reactor (AHWR) is a 300 MWe pressure‑tube type reactor designed to demonstrate the commercial viability of the thorium‑uranium‑233 fuel cycle. The core concept uses a heterogeneous lattice: (Th‑U‑233)O₂ fuel pins in the central region surrounded by (Th‑Pu)O₂ pins, enabling in‑situ breeding of U‑233 from Th‑232 while burning plutonium from reprocessed spent fuel. This configuration achieves a conversion ratio of ~1.0, moving the country toward a near‑breeder thorium cycle without requiring fast‑neutron spectrum reactors.

Safety philosophy follows the “defence‑in‑depth” approach with passive systems as the primary mitigation layer. The reactor employs a large gravity‑driven water pool (the “passive decay heat removal system”) capable of removing 100 % of decay heat for 72 hours without operator action or external power. A double‑containment structure, a core‑catcher for severe accident mitigation, and a passive hydrogen mitigation system (catalytic recombiners) further enhance robustness. The design meets the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) safety goals for Generation‑III+ reactors, including a core damage frequency target of <10⁻⁵ per reactor‑year.

Fuel cycle closure is integral: spent AHWR fuel will be reprocessed in the upcoming Integrated Nuclear Recycle Plant (INRP) at Tarapur, where U‑233 is separated and refabricated into fresh AHWR fuel. The thorium fuel fabrication line at the Nuclear Fuel Complex (NFC), Hyderabad, has been qualified for (Th‑U‑233)O₂ pellet production using powder‑metallurgy routes. The closed cycle reduces high‑level waste volume by ~30 % relative to conventional PHWR once‑through cycles and lowers long‑term radiotoxicity due to the absence of minor actinides in the thorium matrix.

Site selection has narrowed to two coastal locations — Kudankulam (Tamil Nadu) and Jaitapur (Maharashtra) — both offering seawater for ultimate heat sink and proximity to existing nuclear infrastructure. The pre‑project activities, including detailed site evaluation, environmental impact assessment, and public consultation, were completed in 2023. The Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) targets first‑pour‑concrete (FPC) by 2026, with commercial operation expected by 2032, contingent on timely licensing by AERB and availability of U‑233 inventory from the Fast Breeder Test Reactor (FBTR) and PFBR reprocessing streams.

Economic analysis by the Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL) indicates a levelised cost of electricity (LCOE) of ₹4.2–4.5 per kWh (2024 prices), competitive with imported coal‑based generation when carbon pricing is factored. The programme also aligns with India’s commitment under the Paris Agreement to expand low‑carbon baseload capacity, leveraging the country’s vast thorium reserves (≈ 846,000 t of ThO₂) for energy security.

International collaboration includes technical exchanges with the IAEA’s Thorium Fuel Cycle Technology Working Group and bilateral agreements with France (CEA) on fuel fabrication qualification. The AHWR design has been submitted for the IAEA’s Generic Reactor Safety Review, facilitating potential export to countries pursuing thorium‑based nuclear programmes.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “Which of the following statements about the AHWR is correct? (a) It uses a fast‑neutron spectrum to breed U‑233 from Th‑232. (b) It employs a passive decay heat removal system based on a gravity‑driven water pool. (c) Its fuel cycle requires enrichment of uranium to 20 % U‑235. (d) It is a boiling water reactor design.”
Correct answer: (b). The AHWR is a heavy‑water moderated, pressure‑tube reactor operating in the thermal spectrum; it breeds U‑233 from Th‑232 using thermal neutrons, not fast neutrons. It does not require enriched uranium — its driver fuel is (Th‑Pu)O₂ and (Th‑U‑233)O₂. The reactor is not a BWR; it uses heavy water as both coolant and moderator. The passive decay heat removal system relies on a large gravity‑driven water pool, a hallmark of its Generation‑III+ safety design.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mixes reactor type, spectrum, and safety features, first identify the moderator and coolant (heavy water → thermal spectrum). Then match passive safety features to the specific design (gravity‑driven pool for AHWR, core‑catcher for PFBR). Eliminate options that mention enrichment or fast spectrum for thorium thermal breeders.

Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System Augmentation: GAGAN‑II, SBAS Interoperability and Civil‑Military Applications

The GPS Aided GEO Augmented Navigation (GAGAN) system, India’s Satellite Based Augmentation System (SBAS), entered operational service in 2013, providing integrity‑monitored corrections for GPS L1 C/A signals over the Indian Flight Information Region (FIR). GAGAN‑II, the second‑generation upgrade, expands coverage to the entire Indian Ocean Region (IOR) and adds support for dual‑frequency (L1/L5) GPS, Galileo E1/E5a, and NavIC L5/S‑band signals. The upgrade replaces the existing three GEO satellites (GSAT‑8, GSAT‑10, GSAT‑15) with two new high‑power GEO platforms (GSAT‑7C and GSAT‑7D) equipped with L‑band transponders capable of broadcasting SBAS messages at 250 bps per channel, meeting ICAO Annex 10 SARPs for APV‑II and Category‑I precision approach.

Interoperability is achieved through the Multi‑Constellation SBAS (MC‑SBAS) architecture, where the Ground Master Stations (GMS) at Bangalore, Delhi, and Kolkata process observations from a network of 30+ Reference Stations (RS) spanning the subcontinent and the IOR. The GMS computes ionospheric, tropospheric, and satellite orbit/clock corrections for each supported constellation, packaging them into a unified SBAS message format (DFMC‑SBAS) compliant with RTCA DO‑229E. This enables a single avionics receiver to consume corrections from GPS, Galileo, and NavIC simultaneously, improving availability from 99.5 % (single‑constellation) to >99.9 % for en‑route and terminal operations.

Civil aviation benefits include reduced reliance on ground‑based ILS, lower minima for regional airports (e.g., Leh, Port Blair), and fuel savings through continuous descent operations. The Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) mandated GAGAN‑II compliance for all new aircraft registrations from 2025, and the Airports Authority of India (AAI) has certified 45 airports for LPV‑200 approaches using GAGAN‑II corrections.

Military applications leverage the same integrity‑monitored corrections for precision‑guided munitions (PGMs), unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) navigation, and maritime domain awareness. The Defence Space Agency (DSA) integrates GAGAN‑II data into the Joint Space Operations Centre (JSpOC) to provide assured Positioning, Navigation, and Timing (PNT) for the Integrated Air Command and Control System (IACCS) and the Naval Integrated Fire Control System (NIFCS). The system’s anti‑spoofing and anti‑jamming features — authenticated SBAS messages via the NavIC‑based authentication layer — enhance resilience in contested electromagnetic environments.

Funding for GAGAN‑II, approved in the 2022‑23 Union Budget, totals ₹1,200 crore, covering satellite procurement, ground segment upgrades, and certification activities. The programme is executed by ISRO’s Satellite Navigation Programme Office in coordination with the Airport Authority of India and the Ministry of Defence, exemplifying a dual‑use infrastructure model.

Solid Rocket Motor Evolution for PSLV, GSLV and the Next‑Generation Launch Vehicle: S200, S139, HS200 and the Unified Motor Strategy

India’s launch vehicle fleet has relied on a family of solid rocket motors (SRMs) that share common design heritage, enabling cost‑effective production and rapid integration. The Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV) first stage uses the S139 motor (139 t propellant, 4.8 MN average thrust), while the Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle Mk II (GSLV‑Mk II) employs the same S139 as its core stage. The GSLV Mk III (LVM3) introduces the S200 strap‑on boosters (200 t propellant each, 5.15 MN thrust) and the HS200 core motor (200 t propellant, 3.6 MN thrust) — the latter being a high‑performance, high‑pressure (≈ 70 bar) motor with a carbon‑composite case and a 12‑segment grain geometry optimised for a 130‑second burn.

The S200 and HS200 share a common 3.2 m diameter, allowing a unified manufacturing line at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC) Solid Propellant Plant. The propellant formulation — HTPB‑based composite with 18 % aluminium, 68 % ammonium perchlorate, and 14 % binder — is qualified for both motors, reducing qualification cycles. The nozzle design uses a carbon‑phenolic throat insert and a silica‑phenolic exit cone, providing a 1.5 % specific impulse (Isp) improvement over the earlier S139 nozzle.

The Next‑Generation Launch Vehicle (NGLV), currently in the conceptual design phase under the Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre (VSSC), proposes a “Unified Motor Strategy” where a single 3.5 m diameter, 250 t class motor (designated S250) serves as both core and strap‑on, configurable in 2‑, 3‑, or 4‑booster clusters to cover payload classes from 5 t to 20 t to GTO. The S250 targets a chamber pressure of 100 bar, a 12‑segment star‑grain, and a 150‑second burn, leveraging additive‑manufactured nozzle extensions for weight reduction. Development milestones include a sub‑scale demonstrator (S250‑SD) static test scheduled for 2025, followed by a full‑scale qualification motor (S250‑QM) in 2027.

Cost analysis indicates that standardising on a single motor diameter and propellant batch reduces recurring production cost by ~22 % compared to maintaining separate S139, S200, and HS200 lines. The unified approach also simplifies logistics: a single transport container, a common integration fixture at the launch pad, and a shared checkout software suite. The strategy aligns with the Department of Space’s “Atmanirbhar Launch Vehicle” roadmap, which aims to achieve a launch cost of <$5,000/kg to LEO by 2030.

Environmental considerations have driven the adoption of a low‑smoke, low‑hydrogen‑chloride propellant variant (HTPB‑LS) for the S250, reducing ground‑level HCl emissions by 40 % during launch. The motor case uses a filament‑wound carbon‑epoxy composite, enabling a 15 % mass saving over steel cases used in S139. These advances position India’s solid propulsion capability competitively for both domestic missions and commercial launch services.

Electro‑Optical Intelligence Satellites: Cartosat‑3 Series, High‑Resolution Imaging and Tactical Data Dissemination

The Cartosat‑3 series, launched beginning with Cartosat‑3 on PSLV‑C47 in November 2019, represents a leap in India’s space‑based electro‑optical (EO) reconnaissance capability. Each satellite carries a panchromatic camera with a ground sampling distance (GSD) of 0.25 m at nadir, a multispectral imager (4 bands) at 1 m GSD, and a high‑resolution video payload capable of 30 fps at 0.5 m GSD. The platform’s agile attitude control system (reaction wheels + magnetic torquers) enables ±45° off‑nadir slew within 30 seconds, supporting stereo pair acquisition and rapid revisit of high‑value targets.

Data handling employs a 2.5 Gbps solid‑state recorder (SSR) with on‑board lossless compression (CCSDS 122.0‑B‑1) and a dual‑frequency X‑band downlink (8.2 GHz/8.4 GHz) providing 300 Mbps per channel. The ground segment includes the Indian Space Science Data Centre (ISSDC) at Byalalu and the National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC) at Hyderabad, linked via a 10 Gbps fibre backbone. Near‑real‑time (NRT) dissemination to strategic users is achieved through the Defence Space Agency’s (DSA) secure data relay, which routes imagery to the Joint Space Operations Centre (JSpOC) within 15 minutes of acquisition.

Operational use‑cases span topographic mapping, infrastructure monitoring, border surveillance, and disaster damage assessment. During the 2021 Ladakh standoff, Cartosat‑3 imagery provided 0.3 m resolution coverage of forward positions, enabling precise terrain analysis for operational planning. The video payload has been employed for maritime traffic monitoring in the Strait of Malacca, delivering persistent wide‑area surveillance without the revisit constraints of SAR.

Future upgrades include Cartosat‑3A (planned 2025) with an additional short‑wave infrared (SWIR) band for night‑time and camouflage detection, and Cartosat‑3B (2027) featuring an on‑board AI processor for automatic target recognition (ATR) and change detection, reducing downlink bandwidth by pre‑filtering irrelevant frames. The series will eventually be complemented by a constellation of 6‑8 microsatellites (Cartosat‑3M) in a 500 km sun‑synchronous orbit, providing daily revisit over the Indian subcontinent.

Budget allocation for the Cartosat‑3 series, including ground segment enhancements, stands at ₹2,300 crore (2023‑24). The programme leverages the Indian Industry’s capability in lightweight optics (L&T, Godrej Aerospace) and high‑speed electronics (BEL), reinforcing the domestic space industrial base.

  • Confusing the Ghatak UCAV’s first flight date with the SWiFT demonstrator’s 2022 flight; the full‑scale prototype flies later.
  • Assuming the AHWR uses fast neutrons for thorium breeding; it operates in the thermal spectrum with heavy‑water moderation.
  • Believing GAGAN‑II only augments GPS; it provides multi‑constellation SBAS corrections for Galileo and NavIC as well.
  • Mixing the S200 strap‑on motor thrust (5.15 MN) with the HS200 core motor thrust (3.6 MN) when comparing GSLV Mk III stages.
  • Thinking Cartosat‑3’s video payload operates at the same resolution as its panchromatic camera; video GSD is 0.5 m versus 0.25 m for still imagery.
  • Overlooking that the Unified Motor Strategy’s S250 motor targets 100 bar chamber pressure, a significant jump from the 70 bar of HS200.
  • Assuming the AHWR’s passive decay heat removal system requires active pumps; it is entirely gravity‑driven.

Space Traffic Management: Conjunction Assessment, Automated Collision Avoidance and International Data Sharing

India’s growing satellite fleet — spanning remote‑sensing, navigation, communication and strategic payloads — operates in an increasingly congested low‑Earth orbit (LEO) environment. The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) established the Space Situational Awareness (SSA) Control Centre at Bengaluru in 2020 to centralise conjunction data processing. The centre ingests orbital elements from the U.S. Space Surveillance Network (SSN), the Russian Space Monitoring System and the European Space Agency’s (ESA) Space Debris Office, fusing them with indigenous radar and optical observations from the Multi‑Object Tracking Radar (MOTR) at Sriharikota and the Optical Telescope at Mount Abu.

Conjunction assessment follows the standard probability‑of‑collision (Pc) threshold of 1 × 10⁻⁴ for routine operations and 1 × 10⁻⁵ for high‑value assets such as the NavIC constellation and the RISAT SAR satellites. When a conjunction exceeds the threshold, the SSA centre generates a Collision Avoidance Manoeuvre (CAM) plan, which is uploaded to the spacecraft’s on‑board propulsion system via the Indian Deep Space Network (IDSN). Since 2021, ISRO has executed over 30 CAMs, including a notable 2022 manoeuvre for Cartosat‑3 that altered its semi‑major axis by 150 m to avoid a defunct Russian Kosmos satellite.

Automation is being introduced through the “Auto‑CAM” software module, which evaluates conjunction geometry, computes the minimum Δv solution respecting fuel margins, and schedules the burn without ground‑in‑the‑loop approval for low‑risk events. The module has been validated on the GSAT‑30 and GSAT‑31 communication satellites, reducing response time from 12 hours to under 30 minutes. International data sharing is governed by the 2021 ISRO‑NASA Space Situational Awareness Arrangement, which provides real‑time Two‑Line Element (TLE) exchange and a joint working group for long‑term debris mitigation standards. India also participates in the Inter‑Agency Space Debris Coordination Committee (IADC) and contributes to the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS) guidelines on sustainable space operations.

Post‑Fukushima Safety Upgrades for Indian PHWR Fleet: Passive Systems, Hydrogen Mitigation and Severe Accident Management

The Fukushima Dai‑ichi accident in March 2011 prompted a comprehensive safety review of India’s Pressurised Heavy Water Reactor (PHWR) fleet by the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) and the Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL). The review identified three priority areas: enhancement of passive decay‑heat removal, hydrogen mitigation inside containment, and formalisation of Severe Accident Management Guidelines (SAMG).

All operating 220 MWe and 540 MWe PHWRs have been retrofitted with a Passive Decay Heat Removal System (PDHRS) that uses natural circulation of heavy‑water moderator to the external heat‑exchanger pool, eliminating reliance on active pumps. The system was first commissioned at Kakrapar Unit‑3 in 2015 and subsequently installed at Rajasthan Units‑5 & 6, Kudankulam Units‑1 & 2 (which are VVERs but adopted the same philosophy) and the under‑construction Gorakhpur Haryana Anu Vidyut Pariyojana (GHAVP) units.

Hydrogen mitigation employs Passive Autocatalytic Recombiners (PARs) distributed throughout the containment dome and the annulus. Each 540 MWe unit now hosts 12 PAR modules, each capable of recombining up to 0.5 kg h⁻¹ of hydrogen at 2 % concentration. In addition, a filtered containment venting system (FCVS) with a high‑efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filter and a molecular iodine trap has been qualified for the 700 MWe PHWR design, providing a controlled release path that limits off‑site dose to below 1 mSv under design‑basis severe accident scenarios.

The SAMG, issued by AERB in 2017, defines a three‑tier command structure: Shift‑Supervisor (on‑site), Site‑Director (plant‑level) and Emergency‑Response‑Director (off‑site). The guidelines incorporate instrumented severe‑accident monitoring (core‑exit thermocouples, hydrogen analyzers, containment pressure transducers) and prescribe decision points for initiating FCVS, PAR activation, and off‑site protective actions. Periodic tabletop exercises involving the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) and the Crisis Management Group (CMG) validate the guidelines every 18 months.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: "Which of the following safety upgrades was NOT mandated for Indian PHWRs after the Fukushima review?" Options: (a) Passive Decay Heat Removal System, (b) Active Hydrogen Recombiners requiring external power, (c) Filtered Containment Venting System, (d) Severe Accident Management Guidelines.
The correct answer is (b). Indian PHWRs installed Passive Autocatalytic Recombiners (PARs) that operate without external power; active recombiners were not mandated. The other three items — PDHRS, FCVS and SAMG — were all introduced as direct outcomes of the post‑Fukushima safety review.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question lists multiple post‑Fukushima upgrades, first eliminate any option that mentions “active” or “powered” hydrogen mitigation — Indian designs rely on passive autocatalytic recombiners. Remember the three‑tier SAMG command chain (Shift‑Supervisor → Site‑Director → Emergency‑Response‑Director) as it frequently appears in descriptive answers.

High‑Power Microwave Counter‑UAS Systems: DRDO DEW Programme, Power Scaling and Platform Integration

The Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) has pursued high‑power microwave (HPM) directed‑energy weapons (DEW) since the early 2000s under the KALI (Kilo‑Ampere Linear Injector) series. KALI‑5000, commissioned in 2012, delivers a single‑pulse microwave output of 40 GW at 3 GHz with a pulse width of 60 ns, sufficient to disrupt the avionics of small unmanned aerial systems (UAS) at ranges up to 1 km in line‑of‑sight conditions. Subsequent development focused on repetitive‑pulse operation to engage swarms.

The “Sahastra” programme, initiated in 2018, aims to produce a 10 GW‑class, 10 Hz repetitive‑pulse HPM source using a relativistic magnetron driven by a solid‑state Marx generator. Laboratory tests at the Centre for High Energy Systems and Sciences (CHESS), Hyderabad, have demonstrated 5 GW peak power at 5 Hz with a duty cycle of 0.1 %. The system’s antenna array — a phased‑array of 16 horn elements — provides electronic beam steering over a ±30° cone, enabling rapid target handoff without mechanical gimbal movement.

Platform integration trials have been conducted on a modified 6 × 6 tactical truck (Tatra 815) and on the naval offshore patrol vessel (OPV) INS Saryu. The truck‑mounted configuration includes a compact prime‑power unit (diesel‑electric generator set rated at 500 kW) and a ruggedised thermal management loop using liquid‑cooled cold plates. The naval variant draws power from the ship’s integrated electric propulsion bus, with a dedicated 1 MVA power‑conditioning module to meet the HPM’s peak‑power demand.

Operational doctrine envisions a layered counter‑UAS architecture: long‑range detection by the 3D‑CAR radar, mid‑range engagement by the HPM “soft‑kill” system, and terminal hard‑kill by the DRDO‑developed 30 mm close‑in weapon system (CIWS). The HPM’s non‑kinetic nature reduces collateral damage and allows engagement over populated areas, a key requirement for border‑security deployments along the Line of Actual Control (LAC).

Autonomous Swarm Drone Architecture for Tactical ISR: Distributed Control, AI‑Enabled Target Hand‑Off and Communication Resilience

DRDO’s “SWARM” (Smart War‑fighting Autonomous Robotic Modules) programme, launched in 2019, targets the development of a heterogeneous swarm of 10‑20 fixed‑wing and quad‑rotor micro‑UAVs for tactical intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) in contested electromagnetic environments. Each node weighs 1.2‑2.5 kg, carries a 20 MP electro‑optical payload and a software‑defined radio (SDR) operating in the L‑band (1.5 GHz) and S‑band (2.4 GHz) with frequency‑hopping spread spectrum (FHSS) to resist jamming.

The control architecture is fully distributed: no single ground control station (GCS) commands the swarm. Instead, a “leader‑follower” consensus algorithm runs on each UAV’s onboard NVIDIA Jetson AGX Xavier module, allowing dynamic role assignment based on battery state, sensor coverage and link quality. Target detection uses a lightweight YOLOv5‑tiny model quantised to INT8, achieving 30 fps inference at 15 W. When a node detects a high‑value target, it broadcasts a compressed feature vector (≈2 kb) over the mesh; neighbouring nodes validate the detection and the swarm collectively decides on a hand‑off to a dedicated “tracker” UAV that loiters at 500 m altitude.

Communication resilience is reinforced by a store‑and‑forward delay‑tolerant networking (DTN) layer. If the mesh fragments due to terrain masking, each UAV caches sensor data and forwards it when a link re‑establishes. Field trials at the Pokhran Test Range in 2023 demonstrated sustained swarm operation for 45 minutes with 85 % packet delivery ratio under simulated broadband jamming of 30 dB above thermal noise.

Integration with the Army’s Tactical Communication System (TCS) and the Air Force’s Integrated Air Command and Control System (IACCS) is achieved through a standardised MAVLink‑2.0 over UDP gateway, enabling real‑time situational awareness feeds to the Battalion‑level Common Operational Picture (COP). The programme’s next phase, “SWARM‑2”, plans to incorporate a collaborative electronic‑attack payload (miniature noise jammer) and to qualify the swarm for high‑altitude operations up to 5 km MSL.

Nuclear Reactor Decommissioning Roadmap: Cost Modelling, Waste Classification and Regulatory Licensing for Indian PHWRs

India’s first commercial PHWR, Rajasthan Atomic Power Station (RAPS) Unit‑1 (100 MWe), entered commercial operation in 1973 and is slated for permanent shutdown after 50 years of service. The Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) requires a Decommissioning Plan (DP) to be submitted at least five years before the intended final shutdown, followed by a Decommissioning Licence (DL) after safety review. The DP must address three phases: transition (fuel removal and primary system decontamination), dismantling (segmentation of reactor vessel, steam generators and containment structures), and site restoration (soil remediation and licence termination).

Cost modelling follows the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) “Cost Estimation for Decommissioning” (CED) methodology, adapted to Indian labour rates and waste disposal tariffs. For a 220 MWe PHWR, the estimated decommissioning cost ranges between 12 % and 15 % of the original capital cost, translating to approximately ₹1,200‑₹1,500 crore (2023 prices). The major cost drivers are remote‑handling equipment for reactor‑vessel segmentation, packaging of activated metal waste in shielded casks, and long‑term institutional control of the near‑surface disposal facility (NSDF) at the site.

Waste classification adheres to AERB’s “Radioactive Waste Management” (RWM) guidelines: activated structural steel and reactor internals fall under Intermediate‑Level Waste (ILW) requiring cementation in 200‑L drums; spent‑fuel cladding and control‑rod components are High‑Level Waste (HLW) destined for the future Deep Geological Repository (DGR) at Bhandari, Madhya Pradesh. Low‑Level Waste (LLW) such as contaminated concrete rubble is compacted and disposed in the on‑site NSDF, which operates under a 300‑year institutional control period.

The licensing pathway involves a Public Hearing conducted by the State Pollution Control Board, an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) clearance from the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC), and a final safety assessment by the AERB’s Decommissioning Safety Review Committee (DSRC). Upon satisfactory completion of dismantling, the AERB issues a “Licence Termination” order, releasing the site for unrestricted use. The first full‑cycle decommissioning of a PHWR is expected to conclude by 2035 for RAPS‑1, providing a benchmark for subsequent units at Madras, Narora and Kakrapar.

  • Confusing the passive autocatalytic recombiners (PARs) with active hydrogen recombiners that require external power.
  • Assuming the Auto‑CAM module operates on all ISRO satellites; it is currently qualified only on GSAT‑30/31 and newer platforms.
  • Mixing the KALI‑5000 single‑pulse output (40 GW) with the Sahastra repetitive‑pulse target (10 GW at 10 Hz) when quoting HPM capability.
  • Believing the SWARM programme uses a centralised ground control station; it employs a fully distributed consensus algorithm.
  • Thinking the decommissioning cost for a 220 MWe PHWR is a fixed figure; it is expressed as a percentage range (12‑15 % of capital cost) and varies with site‑specific factors.
  • Overlooking that the filtered containment venting system (FCVS) is qualified only for the 700 MWe PHWR design, not for the older 220 MWe units.
  • Assuming the near‑surface disposal facility (NSDF) operates indefinitely; it is licensed for a 300‑year institutional control period after which the site may be released.

Gaganyaan Human Spaceflight Programme: Crew Module, Environmental Control and Life Support System, and Abort Demonstration

India’s first crewed orbital mission, Gaganyaan, is being executed by the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) under the Human Spaceflight Programme (HSP) approved by the Union Cabinet in December 2018. The programme targets a three‑member crew to low‑Earth orbit (LEO) at 400 km altitude for a mission duration of up to seven days. The Crew Module (CM) is a 3.7‑tonne, 3.5‑metre diameter capsule derived from the earlier Crew Module Atmospheric Re‑entry Experiment (CARE) flown on the GSLV‑Mk III‑D1 in December 2014. The CM incorporates a carbon‑phenolic ablative heat shield rated for 1,650 °C peak stagnation temperature, a parachute system comprising two drogue chutes (2.5 m) and three main chutes (35 m each) for a splashdown velocity below 8 m/s, and a redundant avionics suite based on the Vikram processor with dual‑string fault tolerance.

The Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS) is a closed‑loop design that manages atmosphere revitalisation, temperature and humidity control, water recovery, and waste management. Oxygen is generated by a solid‑state electrolyser (O₂‑Gen) delivering 0.84 kg/day per crew, while CO₂ removal uses a molecular‑sieve based Carbon Dioxide Removal Assembly (CDRA) operating on a 12‑hour regeneration cycle. Water is reclaimed from humidity condensate and urine via a Vapor Compression Distillation (VCD) unit achieving 85 % recovery. The thermal control subsystem employs a pumped fluid loop with radiators mounted on the service module, maintaining cabin temperature at 22 ± 2 °C. All ECLSS hardware has been qualified through ground‑based integrated tests at the Human Spaceflight Centre (HSFC) in Bengaluru and the ISRO Propulsion Complex (IPRC) at Mahendragiri.

Abort capability is demonstrated through two distinct tests. The Pad Abort Test (PAT) conducted on 5 July 2018 at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC) validated the Crew Escape System (CES) – a set of seven solid‑propellant motors delivering a combined thrust of 1,200 kN for 20 seconds, pulling the CM to an altitude of 2.7 km and a range of 2.9 km before parachute deployment. The In‑Flight Abort Test (IFAT), scheduled for 2024 on a GSLV‑Mk III launch vehicle, will verify separation at Mach 1.2 and 15 km altitude, exercising the same CES under aerodynamic loads. Both tests feed data into the Crew Module’s autonomous abort logic, which monitors launch vehicle health parameters (acceleration, pressure, engine status) at 100 Hz and initiates escape within 200 ms of a fault detection.

The mission architecture uses the GSLV‑Mk III (LVM‑3) with an upgraded C25 cryogenic upper stage (SCE‑200) and a dedicated Human‑Rated Launch Vehicle (HRLV) configuration that includes a crew access arm, emergency egress slide, and a launch pad abort monitoring network linked to the Mission Control Centre (MCC) at ISTRAC. The first uncrewed orbital flight (G1) is planned for late 2024, followed by a second uncrewed flight (G2) with a humanoid payload (Vyommitra) to validate ECLSS performance in microgravity. The crewed mission (H1) is targeted for 2025, contingent on successful completion of G1, G2, and IFAT. The programme also establishes a cadre of Indian astronauts (Gaganyatris) selected through a joint ISRO‑IAF process, with basic training at the Yuri Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Centre (Star City) and advanced mission‑specific training at HSFC.

Thorium‑Based Advanced Heavy Water Reactor: Fuel Cycle, Safety Features and Deployment Timeline

The Advanced Heavy Water Reactor (AHWR‑300 LEU) is a 300 MWe pressure‑tube type reactor designed by the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) to demonstrate the commercial viability of the thorium‑uranium‑233 fuel cycle. The core uses a mixed oxide (MOX) fuel comprising (Th‑U‑233)O₂ pins arranged in 36‑pin clusters, with a low‑enriched uranium (LEU) driver fraction of 19.75 % U‑235 to sustain initial criticality. The reactor operates with heavy water (D₂O) as both moderator and coolant at 285 °C outlet temperature, enabling a high conversion ratio of 1.3 and a net breeding gain of 0.05 kg U‑233 per GWd. The fuel cycle envisages reprocessing of spent AHWR fuel at the Integrated Nuclear Recycle Plant (INRP) at Tarapur to recover U‑233, which is then refabricated into fresh AHWR fuel, closing the thorium loop.

Safety is anchored on passive systems: a large gravity‑driven water pool (GDWP) of 7,000 m³ provides 72 hours of core cooling without operator action; a passive containment cooling system (PCCS) uses natural circulation of air over the containment shell; and a diverse set of shutdown systems includes two independent fast‑acting shutdown rods (cadmium‑based) and a liquid poison injection system (borated water). The reactor building is designed to withstand a design‑basis earthquake of 0.3 g and a design‑basis flood level of 10 m above grade. The containment is a double‑walled steel‑concrete structure with a filtered venting system (FCVS) qualified for the 700 MWe PHWR design, but the AHWR adopts a dedicated passive filtered venting path to limit radioactive release to < 10⁻⁴ Sv/h at the site boundary under severe accident conditions.

The deployment roadmap, as outlined in the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) “Vision 2030” document, targets the first AHWR‑300 LEU to achieve first criticality by 2028 at the proposed site in Gorakhpur, Uttar Pradesh, following site‑specific environmental clearance from the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) and a construction licence from the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB). A pre‑project activity phase (2022‑2024) includes detailed design verification, procurement of long‑lead items (pressure tubes, calandria tubes, and the GDWP liner), and the establishment of a dedicated fuel fabrication line at the Nuclear Fuel Complex (NFC), Hyderabad, for (Th‑U‑233)O₂ pellets. The project cost is estimated at ₹12,500 crore (2023 prices), with 60 % funded through the DAE budget and the remainder through a public‑private partnership model involving the Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL) and select Indian engineering firms.

Strategically, the AHWR positions India to exploit its vast thorium reserves (≈ 846,000 tonnes of monazite) and reduces dependence on imported uranium. The reactor’s high conversion ratio also supports the long‑term goal of a self‑sustaining thorium fleet, complementing the fast‑breeder programme (PFBR, CFR‑600) and the pressurised heavy water reactor (PHWR) fleet. International collaboration includes a memorandum of understanding with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) for the “Thorium Fuel Cycle Technology” coordinated research project, facilitating benchmarking of fuel performance codes and safety analysis methodologies.

Examiner's Trap
A question states: "The AHWR‑300 LEU uses natural uranium as its driver fuel and relies on active pumped cooling for decay heat removal." Identify the two factual errors and correct them.
The AHWR‑300 LEU uses low‑enriched uranium (LEU) at 19.75 % U‑235 as the driver fuel, not natural uranium. Its decay‑heat removal is provided by a passive gravity‑driven water pool (GDWP) capable of 72 hours of cooling without any active pumps, not by active pumped cooling.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question mixes reactor type, fuel enrichment, and safety system descriptors, isolate each attribute: (1) reactor family (PHWR, AHWR, FBR), (2) fuel composition (natural U, LEU, MOX, Th‑U‑233), (3) cooling mode (active vs passive). The AHWR is the only Indian design that combines a thorium‑based MOX core with a fully passive GDWP; memorising this unique combination eliminates the most common distractor options.

Indigenous Electric Propulsion for Satellites: Hall Thruster Development, On‑Orbit Demonstration and Scaling to GEO Platforms

ISRO’s Electric Propulsion System (EPS) programme, initiated under the Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre (LPSC) in the early 2000s, aims to replace conventional chemical station‑keeping thrusters on geostationary (GEO) satellites with high‑specific‑impulse Hall Effect Thrusters (HETs). The first flight‑qualified unit, a 1.5 kW class HET (designated HET‑1.5), was integrated on the GSAT‑29 communication satellite launched on GSLV‑Mk III‑D2 in November 2018. The thruster uses xenon propellant, delivers a thrust of 85 mN at a specific impulse of 1,650 s, and is powered by a 1.5 kW solar array segment. On‑orbit telemetry confirmed continuous operation for 2,200 hours, achieving a total Δv of 120 m/s for north‑south station‑keeping, validating the thruster’s lifetime model of 8,000 hours.

Subsequent development produced a 4.5 kW class HET (HET‑4.5) with a thrust of 250 mN and Isp of 1,800 s, intended for the I‑6K bus (6,000 kg class) that will host the next generation of high‑throughput satellites (HTS) such as GSAT‑30/31 follow‑ons. The HET‑4.5 incorporates a magnetically shielded discharge channel to reduce erosion, a hollow cathode with a lanthanum hexaboride (LaB₆) emitter for longer life, and a digital power processing unit (PPU) with 96 % efficiency. Ground qualification at the LPSC’s Electric Propulsion Test Facility (EPTF) in Mahendragiri included 10,000 hour endurance testing, thermal‑vacuum cycling, and vibration qualification to GSLV‑Mk III launch loads.

The EPS architecture on the I‑6K platform comprises four HET‑4.5 thrusters mounted on a deployable boom, two for north‑south and two for east‑west station‑keeping, with a shared xenon tank of 250 kg capacity. The system reduces the chemical propellant mass by approximately 400 kg, translating into an additional 1.5 transponders or 2 years of mission life extension. ISRO has also demonstrated a 0.5 kW class HET on the Technology Demonstration Satellite (TDS‑01) launched in 2022, providing a low‑cost option for small‑satellite constellations in LEO.

Strategically, indigenous EPS reduces dependence on imported xenon thrusters (previously sourced from Russia’s Fakel and the USA’s Busek) and positions India to offer electric propulsion as a commercial service through NewSpace India Limited (NSIL). The roadmap includes a 10 kW class HET for future lunar cargo missions and a dual‑mode thruster capable of both chemical and electric operation for rapid orbit raising followed by efficient station‑keeping. The programme is supported by the “Electric Propulsion Development Roadmap 2025‑2035” released by the Department of Space, which earmarks ₹1,200 crore for facility upgrades, cathode material research, and in‑orbit demonstration of a 20 kW clustered HET array on a dedicated technology demonstrator slated for 2029.

AI‑Enabled Integrated Battlefield Management System: Sensor Fusion, Decision Support and Network‑Centric Operations for the Indian Army

The Indian Army’s Integrated Battlefield Management System (IBMS), branded under Project SAKSHAM, is a network‑centric command‑and‑control (C2) platform that fuses data from heterogeneous sensors – ground‑based radars (Weapon Locating Radar Swathi, Battlefield Surveillance Radar BFSR‑SR), unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) such as the Heron‑TP and the indigenous Rustom‑2, electro‑optical payloads, and space‑based assets (RISAT‑2BR1, Cartosat‑3) – into a unified Common Operational Picture (COP) at battalion, brigade and corps levels. The system architecture follows a micro‑services based middleware (the Tactical Data Link‑India, TDL‑I) compliant with NATO STANAG 4586 and the Indian Defence Information Assurance (DIA) standards, enabling real‑time exchange of track data, imagery, and electronic‑order‑of‑battle (EOB) updates over the Army’s Tactical Communication System (TCS) and the upcoming Software Defined Radio (SDR) backbone.

Artificial intelligence modules are embedded at three layers. At the sensor layer, edge‑deployed convolutional neural networks (CNNs) on the UAV’s onboard processor perform automatic target recognition (ATR) for armoured vehicles and artillery positions with a reported 92 % classification accuracy at 30 km range. At the fusion layer, a probabilistic multi‑hypothesis tracker (PMHT) running on the brigade‑level server correlates tracks from disparate sensors, resolves identity conflicts using a Bayesian belief network, and outputs a prioritized target list with confidence scores. At the decision‑support layer, a reinforcement‑learning based Course‑of‑Action (CoA) generator evaluates fire‑support plans, maneuver options, and logistics constraints, presenting the commander with three ranked CoAs within 8 seconds of a trigger event. The AI models are trained on a synthetic dataset of 1.2 million simulated engagements generated by the Army’s War Gaming Centre (WGC) and validated during the “Exercise Him Vijay” (2023) and “Exercise Vajra Prahar” (2024) field trials.

Cyber resilience is addressed through a zero‑trust architecture: each micro‑service authenticates via a hardware‑rooted Trusted Platform Module (TPM 2.0) and communicates over mutually authenticated TLS 1.3 channels. The system incorporates a continuous red‑team/blue‑team exercise framework managed by the Defence Cyber Agency (DCA), with quarterly penetration testing and automated patch deployment through a secure over‑the‑air (OTA) update mechanism. The IBMS also integrates with the Air Force’s Integrated Air Command and Control System (IACCS) and the Navy’s Maritime Domain Awareness (MDA) grid via the Joint Operations Centre (JOC) at the Integrated Defence Staff (IDS), enabling cross‑domain fire‑support coordination.

Deployment follows a spiral model: Spiral‑1 (2022‑2024) fielded the COP and basic sensor fusion at 12 infantry divisions; Spiral‑2 (2025‑2027) adds AI‑driven CoA generation and integrates the indigenous Light Combat Helicopter (LCH) data link; Spiral‑3 (2028‑2030) envisions full autonomous swarm‑UAV tasking and integration with the future “Future Infantry Combat Vehicle” (FICV) sensor suite. The programme budget is ₹9,800 crore (2023‑2030), with 65 % allocated to software development, AI model training, and test infrastructure, and the remainder to hardware procurement (ruggedised servers, SDR nodes, and edge‑AI accelerators). The project is monitored by the Defence Acquisition Council (DAC) under the “Make‑II” category, ensuring indigenous intellectual property rights (IPR) retention and export‑control compliance under the SCOMET list.

Space‑Based Laser Communication Terminals: Inter‑Satellite Links, Ground Segment and Strategic Bandwidth Augmentation

ISRO’s Laser Communication Terminal (LCT) programme, managed by the Space Applications Centre (SAC) in collaboration with the Laboratory for Electro‑Optics Systems (LEOS), aims to establish high‑rate optical links between Indian satellites and between satellites and ground stations, complementing the existing RF‑based Indian Deep Space Network (IDSN) and the Indian Data Relay Satellite System (IDRSS) under development. The first flight‑qualified LCT, a 1.5 Gbps bidirectional terminal operating at 1,550 nm wavelength, was hosted on the GSAT‑29 satellite (launched November 2018) and demonstrated a 40,000 km inter‑satellite link (ISL) with the co‑located GSAT‑30 platform in a controlled experiment in 2020. The terminal uses a 15 cm aperture telescope, a coarse‑pointing assembly (CPA) with 5 µrad resolution, and a fine‑pointing assembly (FPA) based on a fast‑steering mirror (FSM) achieving 0.2 µrad jitter performance.

The ground segment comprises two Optical Ground Stations (OGS) – one at the Indian Space Science Data Centre (ISSDC), Byalalu, Karnataka, and the other at the Spacecraft Control Centre (SCC), Hassan. Each OGS houses a 1 m adaptive‑optics telescope, a high‑power erbium‑doped fiber amplifier (EDFA) for uplink (2 W), and a superconducting nanowire single‑photon detector (SNSPD) array for downlink photon counting, enabling a link budget that supports 10 Gbps downlink under clear‑sky conditions. Cloud‑mitigation is addressed through a site‑diversity protocol that automatically hands over the optical link to the alternate OGS or falls back to the Ka‑band RF feeder link on the same satellite, ensuring 99.9 % availability for mission‑critical telemetry.

The IDRSS constellation, planned as a trio of satellites in GEO (IDRSS‑1A, 1B, 1C) with LCT payloads, will provide continuous relay coverage for LEO remote‑sensing satellites (Cartosat‑3 series, RISAT‑2BR series) and the Gaganyaan crewed module. Each IDRSS satellite carries two LCTs: one for inter‑satellite cross‑links (forming a mesh) and one for LEO‑to‑GEO uplinks. The network architecture supports store‑and‑forward Delay‑Tolerant Networking (DTN) bundles, allowing data offload from LEO platforms during brief visibility windows and subsequent high‑rate dump to ground via the GEO‑to‑ground optical link. The first IDRSS satellite is slated for launch on GSLV‑Mk III in 2026, with the full constellation operational by 2029.

Strategically, optical links offer low probability of intercept (LPI) and low probability of detection (LPD) characteristics essential for secure military communications. The Defence Space Agency (DSA) has earmarked a dedicated LCT payload on the upcoming GSAT‑7C (a military communication satellite) to provide jam‑resistant connectivity for the Navy’s carrier battle groups and the Air Force’s airborne early‑warning platforms. The programme also aligns with the “National Space Communication Policy 2023”, which encourages private sector participation in ground‑station operations and the development of indigenous photonic integrated circuits (PICs) for next‑generation 100 Gbps coherent optical terminals. Funding of ₹2,300 crore has been allocated for the 2024‑2030 phase, covering flight hardware, OGS upgrades, and a technology demonstrator for quantum‑key‑distribution (QKD) over the same optical channel, leveraging the LCT’s narrow beam divergence.

  • Confusing the AHWR’s passive GDWP with the active emergency core cooling system (ECCS) of PHWRs; the AHWR relies solely on gravity‑driven water for 72 hours.
  • Assuming the Gaganyaan Crew Escape System uses liquid propellant; it is a solid‑motor based system with seven motors.
  • Believing the 1.5 kW Hall thruster on GSAT‑29 is the final EPS configuration for GEO; the I‑6K bus will employ 4.5 kW thrusters.
  • Thinking the IBMS AI decision‑support layer operates without human‑in‑the‑loop; the system presents ranked CoAs for commander approval.
  • Mixing the LCT’s 1.5 Gbps demonstration rate with the 10 Gbps operational target for the IDRSS ground stations.
  • Overlooking that the AHWR fuel fabrication line at NFC Hyderabad is dedicated to (Th‑U‑233)O₂ MOX, not to standard PHWR UO₂ pellets.
  • Assuming the Gaganyaan uncrewed flights will carry a full ECLSS; G1 flies a simplified thermal‑control mock‑up, while G2 carries the humanoid Vyommitra with partial ECLSS.

The advanced sections above provide the mechanistic depth, programme timelines, and examiner‑focused nuances required for high‑scoring answers in the science and technology segment.

Space‑Based Infrared Early‑Warning System: Sensor Architecture, Data Fusion and Strategic Role

India’s ballistic missile defence (BMD) architecture presently relies on ground‑based phased‑array radars such as the Swordfish Long‑Range Tracking Radar and the Multi‑Function Radar (MFR) network. To close the coverage gap over the Indian Ocean and to provide launch‑point detection for missiles with depressed trajectories, the Defence Space Agency (DSA) in coordination with ISRO has initiated a Space‑Based Infrared Early‑Warning (SBIR‑EW) programme. The concept envisions a mixed constellation of three geostationary (GEO) platforms carrying staring‑array infrared payloads and a complement of low‑earth‑orbit (LEO) satellites equipped with scanning sensors for higher spatial resolution.

The GEO payloads are designed around a 1.2 m aperture telescope feeding a 256 × 256 pixel mercury‑cadmium‑telluride (MCT) focal‑plane array cooled to 80 K by a split‑Stirling cryocooler. Each sensor operates in the 3–5 µm and 8–12 µm bands, delivering a noise‑equivalent temperature difference (NETD) of ≤ 0.02 K, sufficient to detect the plume of a solid‑propellant booster at ranges exceeding 5 000 km. The LEO segment uses a 0.5 m aperture with a 1024 × 1024 InSb array, providing a ground‑sample distance of ~200 m at nadir and a revisit time of 30 minutes over the region of interest.

Data from both tiers are fused at the Joint Space Operations Centre (JSpOC) in Bengaluru. The fusion engine employs a Kalman‑filter based track‑initiation module that correlates infrared detections with radar tracks from the Swordfish and MFR assets, reducing false‑alarm rates to < 10⁻⁴ per hour. The fused track is then handed over to the BMD command‑and‑control (C2) system for intercept‑trajectory computation. Latency from photon detection to C2 hand‑over is targeted at ≤ 8 seconds, a figure validated during the 2023 “Exercise Shakti‑Star” tabletop simulation.

Strategically, the SBIR‑EW constellation provides a survivable, non‑line‑of‑sight cueing layer that cannot be degraded by terrain masking or electronic attack on ground radars. It also supports space‑domain awareness by detecting uncatalogued objects with thermal signatures, feeding the National Space Situational Awareness Centre (NSSAC). The first technology demonstrator, designated “IR‑Sat‑1”, is slated for launch on a GSLV‑Mk III in 2026, with the full three‑satellite GEO ring operational by 2030.

Accelerator‑Driven Subcritical System for Nuclear Waste Transmutation: Indian R&D Status and Deployment Timeline

The Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) has pursued an Accelerator‑Driven Subcritical System (ADS) since the early 2000s as a pathway to transmute long‑lived minor actinides (neptunium‑237, americium‑241, curium‑244) and selected fission products (technetium‑99, iodine‑129) from the closed fuel cycle. The reference design, termed the Indian ADS (IADS), couples a 1 GeV, 10 mA continuous‑wave (CW) superconducting proton linac to a lead‑bismuth eutectic (LBE) cooled subcritical core (k_eff ≈ 0.95) loaded with (Th‑U‑233)O₂‑MOX fuel pins.

Key milestones achieved to date include: (i) completion of the conceptual design report (CDR) in 2018, validated by the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB); (ii) commissioning of a 20 MeV, 5 mA injector linac at the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) in 2021 for beam‑dynamics studies; (iii) successful operation of a 100 kW LBE loop (the “LBE‑Test Facility”) demonstrating corrosion‑compatible structural steels (HT9, 316LN) at 550 °C for 10 000 h; and (iv) fabrication of 30 MOX fuel pins with 5 wt % minor actinide loading at the Nuclear Fuel Complex, Hyderabad, for irradiation testing in the Fast Breeder Test Reactor (FBTR).

The next phase (2024‑2028) targets the construction of a 100 MeV, 1 mA superconducting spoke‑cavity linac module (the “IADS‑Linac‑100”) at the Raja Ramanna Centre for Advanced Technology (RRCAT). Parallel work on a 5 MWth subcritical assembly (the “IADS‑Core‑5”) will commence at the Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR), using the same LBE coolant and a hexagonal lattice of 169 fuel pins. The integrated system demonstration, aiming at a transmutation rate of 0.5 kg yr⁻¹ of americium‑241, is projected for 2032‑2034, contingent on funding clearance from the Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL) and the Planning Commission.

Economic analyses in the 2022 “ADS Techno‑Economic Assessment” report indicate a levelised cost of transmutation of ≈ US $1 200 kg⁻¹ of minor actinide, competitive with deep geological repository expenses when the avoided repository volume is accounted for. The programme also aligns with India’s commitment under the Joint Convention on the Safety of Spent Fuel Management to reduce the radiotoxicity inventory of high‑level waste by a factor of 10 within 1 000 years.

Examiner’s Technique: Comparative Programme Mapping
A question asks: “Compare the Indian ADS programme with the European MYRRHA project in terms of accelerator energy, target coolant, and projected transmutation throughput.”
Both programmes employ a high‑power proton linac driving a subcritical core cooled by lead‑bismuth eutectic. MYRRHA targets a 600 MeV, 4 mA linac (2.4 MW beam power) and a 100 MWth core, aiming for ~1 kg yr⁻¹ of minor actinide transmutation. IADS specifies a 1 GeV, 10 mA linac (10 MW beam power) and a 5 MWth demonstration core, with a design goal of 0.5 kg yr⁻¹ in the demo phase, scaling to > 2 kg yr⁻¹ in a commercial 300 MWth unit. The higher beam energy in IADS yields a harder neutron spectrum, improving fission‑to‑capture ratios for curium isotopes, while MYRRHA’s lower energy reduces accelerator complexity. Both share LBE technology, but MYRRHA has advanced further in licensing, holding a construction licence since 2021, whereas IADS awaits AERB siting clearance.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a comparison, structure the answer in a three‑column table (Parameter – India – International) and highlight the unique Indian choices (thorium‑based MOX, 1 GeV linac). This format scores full marks for “comparative analysis” rubrics.

Additive Manufacturing of High‑Performance Alloys for Defence Aerospace Components: Qualification, Supply‑Chain Impact and Case Studies

The Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) launched the “Additive Manufacturing for Aerospace (AM‑Aero)” mission in 2017 to qualify laser‑powder‑bed‑fusion (L‑PBF) and directed‑energy‑deposition (DED) routes for nickel‑based superalloys (Inconel 718, René 80), titanium alloy Ti‑6Al‑4V, and the newly developed high‑entropy alloy (HEA) AlCoCrFeNi. Qualification follows the AS9100‑D quality management standard, the Directorate General of Aeronautical Quality Assurance (DGAQA) “AM‑Qual‑01” protocol, and the National Aerospace Laboratories (NAL) “Material‑Process‑Property” database.

Key achievements include: (i) successful L‑PBF printing of a first‑stage turbine blade for the Kaveri engine, meeting the 1 200 °C creep‑rupture requirement after a 200 h heat‑treatment cycle; (ii) DED repair of a cracked compressor disc on the Su‑30MKI’s AL‑31FP engine, restoring 95 % of baseline low‑cycle fatigue life; (iii) production of a 1.2 m‑diameter titanium‑alloy fuel‑tank dome for the Gaganyaan service module, reducing part count from 48 welded segments to a single monolithic component and cutting lead time from 14 months to 3 months.

Supply‑chain impact is quantified in the 2023 “AM‑Aero Economic Assessment”: indigenous powder production capacity at the Mishra Dhatu Nigam (MIDHANI) reached 150 t yr⁻¹ for Inconel 718 and 80 t yr⁻¹ for Ti‑6Al‑4V, eliminating import dependence on European atomisers. The programme also spawned a “Digital Thread” linking CAD, process simulation (ANSYS Additive), in‑situ melt‑pool monitoring (high‑speed IR camera), and post‑build CT‑scan inspection, enabling first‑article acceptance without destructive testing.

Future roadmap targets qualification of a 3 kW multi‑laser L‑PBF machine for serial production of 200 kg‑class turbine disks by 2027, and development of a field‑deployable DED system for forward‑base repair of helicopter gearbox housings.

Autonomous Swarm Drone Architecture for Tactical ISR: Control Algorithms, Communication Mesh and Operational Integration

The DRDO “SWARM‑ISR” programme, initiated in 2019, aims to field a heterogeneous swarm of 10‑20 kg class fixed‑wing and quad‑rotor UAVs for real‑time intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) in contested electromagnetic environments. Each node carries a modular payload bay (EO/IR, SAR‑lite, SIGINT) and a software‑defined radio (SDR) operating in the 2.4 GHz ISM band with frequency‑hopping spread spectrum (FHSS) and a secondary L‑band mesh link for beyond‑visual‑range (BVR) coordination.

Control is distributed: a ground‑station “Swarm Commander” issues high‑level mission intents (area‑search, target‑track, perimeter‑hold) which are decomposed by an on‑board behaviour‑tree engine into waypoint sequences. Conflict‑free trajectory generation uses a decentralized Model Predictive Control (MPC) algorithm with a 2 Hz replanning cycle, guaranteeing a minimum separation of 30 m in 3‑D space. The communication layer implements a Delay‑Tolerant Networking (DTN) bundle protocol over the mesh, allowing store‑and‑forward when links are intermittently jammed.

Integration with the Army’s Integrated Battlefield Management System (IBMS) is achieved through the “Tactical Data Link‑India (TDL‑I)” gateway, which translates swarm track files into Link‑16 compatible messages for fusion with radar and satellite feeds. Field trials in 2022 at the Pokhran range demonstrated a 12‑UAV swarm maintaining continuous coverage of a 25 km² sector for 3 hours, with a 92 % target‑detection probability for moving vehicles at 5 km range.

Ongoing work focuses on AI‑based automatic target recognition (ATR) using a quantised ResNet‑18 model running on an edge‑AI accelerator (NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin), reducing downlink bandwidth to < 200 kbps per UAV. The next milestone, slated for 2025, is a 30‑UAV heterogeneous swarm demonstrating autonomous hand‑over of a high‑value target to a loitering munition.

Space Traffic Management Framework: National Policy, Conjunction Assessment and International Coordination

India’s draft “National Space Traffic Management (STM) Policy” released by the Department of Space in March 2023 establishes a regulatory architecture for the safe, sustainable and equitable use of outer space. The policy designates the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) as the nodal agency for operational STM, with the newly formed National Space Situational Awareness Centre (NSSAC) at Byalalu serving as the single point of contact for conjunction data messages (CDMs).

Conjunction assessment follows the “Probability of Collision (Pc) ≥ 10⁻⁴” threshold for mandatory manoeuvre planning, consistent with the Inter‑Agency Space Debris Coordination Committee (IADC) guidelines. The NSSAC runs a high‑fidelity orbital propagator (SDP4 + high‑order gravitational harmonics up to 70 × 70) fed by radar tracks from the Multi‑Object Tracking Radar (MOTR) at Sriharikota, the optical telescope network at Mount Abu and Hanle, and space‑based observations from the upcoming “Netra‑2” SSA satellite (launch 2025). The system generates CDMs 72 hours before the predicted time of closest approach (TCA) and disseminates them via the Space Data Association (SDA) format to all registered operators.

International coordination is institutionalised through: (i) a bilateral data‑sharing MoU with the United States Space Command (USSPACECOM) signed in 2022, enabling real‑time exchange of Two‑Line Element (TLE) sets and high‑accuracy ephemerides; (ii) participation in the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS) “Long‑Term Sustainability” working group, where India co‑chairs the “Collision Avoidance Best Practices” subgroup; and (iii) membership in the IADC, contributing the “Indian Debris Environment Model (INDEM)” for global risk assessments.

The policy also mandates that all Indian launch vehicles and satellites launched after 1 January 2025 incorporate end‑of‑life disposal plans (controlled re‑entry or graveyard orbit) and a “design‑for‑demise” analysis. A compliance audit framework, overseen by the Space Commission, will issue “STM Clearance Certificates” prior to launch licensing.

  • Confusing the SBIR‑EW GEO payload’s staring‑array architecture with the LEO scanning sensor; they serve different revisit‑resolution trade‑offs.
  • Assuming the IADS linac will operate at 600 MeV like MYRRHA; the Indian design targets 1 GeV for a harder neutron spectrum.
  • Believing additive‑manufactured Inconel 718 parts are flight‑cleared without DGAQA “AM‑Qual‑01” certification; qualification is mandatory for each geometry.
  • Thinking the SWARM‑ISR mesh uses only commercial Wi‑Fi; it employs a military‑grade FHSS SDR with DTN bundle protocol.
  • Overlooking that the STM policy’s Pc threshold of 10⁻⁴ applies only to active Indian assets; foreign objects are monitored but not mandated for manoeuvre.
  • Mixing the Netra‑2 SSA satellite’s launch date (2025) with the earlier Netra‑1 technology demonstrator (2021).
  • Assuming the Gaganyaan service‑module fuel‑tank dome was produced by conventional forging; it was a single L‑PBF Ti‑6Al‑4V build.

Gaganyaan Human Spaceflight Programme: Life Support, Crew Escape and Mission Architecture

The Gaganyaan programme, approved by the Union Cabinet in December 2018, aims to demonstrate indigenous human spaceflight capability by launching a three‑member crew to a 400 km low‑Earth orbit for a mission duration of up to seven days. The programme is managed by the Human Space Flight Centre (HSFC) under ISRO, with the Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre (VSSC) responsible for the launch vehicle, the Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre (LPSC) for the service module propulsion, and the ISRO Telemetry, Tracking and Command Network (ISTRAC) for mission control.

The crew module (CM) is a 3.7 t, 3.5 m diameter capsule built around an aluminium‑lithium alloy pressure vessel. Its Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS) provides a mixed‑gas atmosphere (21 % O₂, 79 % N₂) at 101.3 kPa, temperature control between 22 °C and 26 °C, humidity regulation at 40‑60 % RH, and CO₂ removal using solid‑amine canisters rated for 8 h of continuous operation. Water recovery is achieved through a condensing heat exchanger that reclaims 85 % of metabolic water, while waste management uses a vacuum‑assisted compacting toilet. Redundancy is built into each subsystem: dual‑string oxygen generators, parallel CO₂ scrubbers, and cross‑strapped thermal loops.

The Crew Escape System (CES) is a solid‑propellant, high‑thrust (≈ 200 kN) motor mounted on the CM’s forward skirt. It can be triggered automatically by the Launch Vehicle’s Health Monitoring System (LVHMS) or manually by the crew via a dedicated abort handle. The CES provides a 10 g pull‑away for 3 s, delivering a Δv of ~300 m/s, sufficient to separate the CM from a failing GSLV‑Mk III at any point from lift‑off to 120 km altitude. Qualification tests include a Pad Abort Test (July 2018) and a High‑Altitude Abort Test (planned 2025) using a boiler‑plate CM on a sounding rocket.

The mission architecture follows a “launch‑to‑orbit‑to‑re‑entry” profile. GSLV‑Mk III (LVM3) lifts the 8.2 t composite (CM + Service Module) into a 170 × 400 km insertion orbit. The Service Module (SM) performs a circularisation burn at apogee using its 440 N liquid apogee motor (LAM) and 12 × 100 N reaction control thrusters. After mission completion, the SM is jettisoned, and the CM executes a de‑orbit burn using its own 4 × 100 N thrusters. Re‑entry follows a guided lifting‑body trajectory with a peak heat flux of 1.2 MW/m², managed by an ablative phenolic‑impregnated carbon ablator (PICA) heat shield. Parachute deployment sequence: two 2.5 m drogue chutes at 10 km, three 31 m main chutes at 5 km, and a final splashdown in the Bay of Bengal, recovered by Indian Navy ships.
