The technology demonstrator, designated “AIP‑Module‑1”, was successfully tested on land in 2019, delivering 300 kW continuous power for 14 days with a system efficiency of 42 % (LHV basis). The module comprises four 75 kW fuel‑cell stacks, a diesel‑to‑hydrogen reformer (autothermal reforming at 650 °C), a water‑management subsystem, and a thermal‑management loop using the submarine’s seawater cooling.

The reformer is the critical differentiator. Unlike the German Type‑212/214 submarines that use stored liquid hydrogen or metal‑hydride storage, the Indian design reforms standard naval diesel (NATO F‑76) to avoid the logistics and safety burden of hydrogen bunkering. The reformer uses a proprietary catalyst (Pt‑Rh/CeO₂‑ZrO₂) developed at the Indian Institute of Petroleum (IIP) Dehradun, tolerant to sulphur content up to 500 ppm. Carbon monoxide cleanup is achieved via a two‑stage water‑gas shift (high‑temperature at 350 °C, low‑temperature at 200 °C) followed by preferential oxidation (PROX) to < 10 ppm CO, protecting the PAFC anode. The system’s transient response — from cold start to full power — is 45 minutes, meeting the naval requirement for “silent sprint” capability.

Integration onto the Kalvari‑class (Scorpène) submarines is planned as a mid‑life upgrade (MLU) for the last two boats of the Project‑75 series (INS Vagir and INS Vagsheer). The AIP module occupies the space previously allocated for the main battery bank, necessitating a re‑design of the pressure‑hull penetrations for the reformer exhaust and seawater intake. The Naval Group (formerly DCNS) has provided the interface control document (ICD) for the platform management system (PMS) integration, while the Indian Navy’s Warship Overseeing Team (WOT) at Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders Limited (MDL) oversees the hull‑cut and cofferdam installation. The first AIP‑fitted Kalvari‑class boat is targeted for sea trials in 2027.

For the follow‑on Project‑75I, the Request for Proposal (RfP) mandates an indigenous AIP system as a “Make‑II” category deliverable. The DRDO’s NMRL is the nominated Development Agency (DA), with Larsen & Toubro (L&T) as the Production Agency (PA). The 75I AIP specification calls for a modular 250 kW × 4 configuration (1 MW total) with a specific energy density > 300 Wh/kg (system level) and a submerged endurance multiplier of 3× over the baseline battery‑only patrol cycle. Competing foreign OEMs (Naval Group, TKMS, Navantia, Rubin Design Bureau, Daewoo) are required to offer technology transfer for their AIP systems (MESMA, fuel‑cell, Stirling, etc.) but the Indian Navy has signalled a strong preference for the indigenous PAFC route to avoid single‑source dependency.

Parallel research explores a solid‑oxide fuel cell (SOFC) variant operating directly on logistic fuels (diesel, JP‑5) at 700‑800 °C, eliminating the reformer. The “SOFC‑AIP” programme at the Defence Institute of Advanced Technology (DIAT) Pune, in collaboration with the Central Electrochemical Research Institute (CECRI) Karaikudi, has demonstrated a 10 kW stack with 52 % efficiency on desulphurised diesel. The higher operating temperature enables waste‑heat recovery for the submarine’s hotel load (desalination, galley, HVAC), improving overall system efficiency to > 60 %. However, thermal‑cycling durability and seal integrity under pressure‑hull vibration remain challenges for naval qualification.

  • Confusing the Nuclear Decommissioning Fund’s 0.5 % revenue levy with a direct budgetary allocation — the levy is mandatory and ring‑fenced, not subject to annual parliamentary vote.
  • Assuming all PHWR units receive identical decommissioning treatment; 220 MWe units follow a different dismantling sequence and waste volume profile than 540 MWe and 700 MWe units due to containment design and activation levels.
  • Treating EMISAT as a standalone ELINT satellite; it is the first of a planned constellation (Project Vishal) with multi‑plane coverage and DBF payloads — examiners often test the evolution from single satellite to constellation architecture.
  • Overlooking that GSAT‑6/6A’s COMINT role is a hosted payload on a strategic MSS platform, not a dedicated SIGINT bus — the S‑band unfurlable antenna serves dual‑use communications and interception.
  • Equating quantum gyroscope laboratory sensitivity (5 × 10⁻⁷ °/h/√Hz) with platform‑level performance; vibration, rotation, and magnetic environment degrade performance by 2‑3 orders of magnitude, necessitating hybrid quantum‑classical filtering.
  • Believing the Indian AIP system uses stored hydrogen like the German Type‑212; the indigenous PAFC reforms diesel on‑board, a strategic logistics choice that also defines the reformer’s sulphur tolerance and transient response specifications.
  • Assuming Project‑75I AIP is a simple “buy and fit” — the RfP mandates indigenous development under Make‑II with NMRL as DA and L&T as PA, and the 300 Wh/kg system‑level energy density target is a key technical threshold.

These advanced sections collectively illustrate how indigenous technology development, regulatory frameworks, and operational doctrines intertwine across space, nuclear, and defence domains, providing the analytical depth required for high‑stakes examination scenarios.

Ballistic Missile Defence Architecture: Phase‑I and Phase‑II Interceptors, Kill‑Vehicle Technology and Test Record

India’s Ballistic Missile Defence (BMD) programme is structured in two overlapping phases. Phase‑I, declared operational in 2012, provides protection against missiles with ranges up to 2 000 km. It employs the Prithvi Air Defence (PAD) exo‑atmospheric interceptor and the Advanced Air Defence (AAD) endo‑atmospheric interceptor. PAD uses a two‑stage solid‑propellant booster and a kill vehicle (KV) equipped with an imaging infrared (IIR) seeker and a divert‑and‑attitude‑control system (DACS) based on cold‑gas thrusters. AAD is a single‑stage solid motor with a similar KV but optimized for higher dynamic pressure. Both interceptors are guided by the Swordfish long‑range tracking radar (L‑band, 1 500 km range) and the Multi‑Function Radar (MFR) for fire‑control.

Phase‑II, aimed at intercepting missiles of 5 000 km class, introduces the PDV (Prithvi Defence Vehicle) Mk‑II exo‑atmospheric interceptor and the AD‑1 endo‑atmospheric interceptor. PDV Mk‑II incorporates a larger diameter (0.55 m) KV with a dual‑band (IR/UV) seeker and a solid‑propellant divert motor providing ≥ 30 m/s lateral Δv. AD‑1 uses a two‑stage solid booster and a KV with a strap‑down inertial navigation system (INS) aided by a fibre‑optic gyroscope (FOG) for mid‑course updates. The Phase‑II sensor layer adds the Long‑Range Tracking Radar (LRTR) operating in S‑band with a 1 500 km detection range and the Multi‑Object Tracking Radar (MOTR) for simultaneous engagement of multiple targets.

Key test milestones include the first successful PAD intercept in November 2006, the first AAD intercept in December 2007, and the first PDV Mk‑II intercept in February 2017 against a simulated intermediate‑range ballistic missile (IRBM) target. The AD‑1 achieved its maiden successful intercept in November 2022. As of 2024, the BMD system has recorded 12 successful intercepts out of 14 flight tests, yielding a demonstrated kill probability (Pk) of approximately 0.86 for exo‑atmospheric engagements and 0.78 for endo‑atmospheric engagements under test conditions. The programme is managed by the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) under the Programme Director, BMD, with integration support from the Indian Air Force’s Air Defence Command.

Operational deployment follows a layered architecture: PAD/PDV Mk‑II provide the outer tier at altitudes of 80–150 km, while AAD/AD‑1 cover the inner tier at 15–30 km. The command‑and‑control (C2) node is the BMD Control Centre (BMCC) at New Delhi, linked via secure fibre‑optic and satellite links to the Swordfish and LRTR sites. The system is designed for a “shoot‑look‑shoot” doctrine, allowing real‑time assessment of kill assessment (KA) data from the KV’s onboard telemetry before committing a second interceptor.

Strategic implications centre on the credibility of India’s no‑first‑use (NFU) nuclear posture. A credible BMD raises the threshold for an adversary’s first strike, but also invites concerns about arms‑race stability. The government has maintained that BMD is purely defensive and does not alter the NFU commitment, a position reiterated in the 2019 Parliamentary statement by the Minister of Defence.

Indigenous Pressurised Water Reactor for Nuclear Submarines: Arihant‑Class Core Design, Fuel Cycle and Follow‑On SSBN Programme

The Arihant‑class (Project 75) ballistic missile submarines are powered by a 83 MWth pressurised water reactor (PWR) designed by the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) and built by the Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL) in collaboration with the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE). The reactor uses low‑enriched uranium (LEU) dioxide fuel enriched to 19.75 % U‑235, clad in Zircaloy‑4, and operates at a primary coolant pressure of 15.5 MPa with an outlet temperature of 310 °C. The core contains 121 fuel assemblies arranged in a 13 × 13 lattice, providing a design life of 10 years (≈ 30 effective full‑power years) before refuelling.

The fuel cycle is closed within the strategic programme: spent fuel from the submarine reactors is reprocessed at the Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR) Kalpakkam to recover uranium and plutonium for future fast‑reactor fuel. The reprocessing plant uses the PUREX process with a dedicated shielded cell line to handle the high‑burnup naval fuel. The recovered plutonium is earmarked for the Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) and subsequent commercial fast reactors, linking the naval and civilian fuel cycles.

The follow‑on SSBN programme (Project 75I/SSBN‑II) envisions a larger 190 MWth PWR with a higher power density to accommodate a 12‑tube vertical launch system for the K‑4 (3 500 km) and K‑5 (5 000 km) submarine‑launched ballistic missiles (SLBMs). The new core will employ a 17 × 17 fuel assembly lattice with advanced Doppler‑broadened resonance integral (DBRI) fuel pellets to improve neutron economy. The reactor pressure vessel (RPV) is forged from 15Cr‑Mo‑V steel with a thickness of 250 mm, manufactured by the Heavy Engineering Corporation (HEC) Ranchi under DAE quality assurance.

Key milestones: the first Arihant (INS Arihant) was launched in July 2009, commissioned in August 2016, and completed its first deterrent patrol in November 2018. The second boat, INS Arighaat, was launched in November 2017 and commissioned in 2023. The third and fourth hulls are under construction at the Ship Building Centre (SBC) Visakhapatnam, with projected commissioning in 2025 and 2027 respectively. The SSBN‑II design review was completed in 2022, and long‑lead items (RPV forgings, steam generators) have been ordered.

Safety and regulatory oversight is exercised by the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) through a dedicated Naval Reactor Safety Division. The AERB mandates a probabilistic safety assessment (PSA) Level‑2 for each hull, with a core damage frequency target of < 1 × 10⁻⁵ per reactor‑year. The programme also adheres to the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) Safety Standards Series No. NS‑R‑5 for nuclear-powered vessels, although India is not a party to the Convention on Nuclear Safety for military reactors.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: "Which of the following statements about India's BMD Phase‑II interceptors is correct? (a) PDV Mk‑II uses a liquid‑propellant divert motor. (b) AD‑1 employs a dual‑band IR/UV seeker. (c) PDV Mk‑II KV provides ≥ 30 m/s lateral Δv. (d) AD‑1 is a single‑stage solid motor."
Correct answer: (c). PDV Mk‑II’s kill vehicle incorporates a solid‑propellant divert motor delivering ≥ 30 m/s lateral Δv. AD‑1 uses a two‑stage solid booster, not a single stage, and its seeker is IR‑only with INS/FOG guidance. PDV Mk‑II does not use a liquid divert motor.
Exam‑day strategy
Memorise the three key performance numbers for each interceptor: altitude tier, divert Δv, and seeker type. Examiners frequently frame “match the following” or “which is NOT a feature” questions around these parameters. Write a one‑page table the night before the exam and rehearse it verbally.

GAGAN and NavIC Augmentation: Satellite‑Based Augmentation System Architecture, Certification and Strategic Interoperability

The GPS‑Aided Geo‑Augmented Navigation (GAGAN) system is India’s Satellite‑Based Augmentation System (SBAS) certified to the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) Standards and Recommended Practices (SARPs) for Safety‑of‑Life (SoL) aviation services. GAGAN comprises three geostationary satellites (GSAT‑8, GSAT‑10, GSAT‑15) each carrying a GAGAN payload operating in the L1 (1575.42 MHz) and L5 (1176.45 MHz) bands, a network of 15 Indian Reference Stations (INRES) distributed across the subcontinent, three Master Control Centres (MCC) at Bengaluru, Delhi and Mumbai, and two Uplink Stations (ULS) at Bengaluru and Delhi. The system broadcasts correction messages (fast corrections, long‑term corrections, ionospheric grid points) and integrity data (User Differential Range Error, UDRE) to user receivers.

GAGAN achieved the ICAO‑required System‑Level Certification (SLC) in July 2015, becoming the fourth SBAS worldwide after WAAS (USA), EGNOS (Europe) and MSAS (Japan). The certification covers En‑route (RNP 0.3), Terminal (RNP 0.1) and Approach (LPV‑200) service levels. The LPV‑200 service provides vertical guidance down to 200 ft decision height, enabling precision approaches at airports lacking Instrument Landing System (ILS) infrastructure. As of 2024, 78 Indian airports are GAGAN‑enabled for LPV approaches.

NavIC (Navigation with Indian Constellation) operates a seven‑satellite constellation (three GEO, four IGSO) transmitting in the L5 (1176.45 MHz) and S‑band (2492.028 MHz) frequencies. The NavIC‑GAGAN interoperability is achieved through a common L5 frequency and a coordinated time reference (Indian Standard Time traceable to the National Physical Laboratory). The NavIC Signal‑in‑Space (SIS) ICD (Interface Control Document) version 2.0, released in 2021, defines the augmentation message types (Type 0‑63) that GAGAN can relay for NavIC users, enabling dual‑constellation positioning with improved geometry and integrity.

Strategic interoperability extends to the US GPS L1C/A and L5 signals, the European Galileo E1/E5a, and the Russian GLONASS G1/G2. The GAGAN MCC runs a multi‑constellation integrity monitoring algorithm that fuses GPS, GLONASS, Galileo and NavIC pseudorange measurements to compute a unified protection level. This capability is critical for the Indian Armed Forces’ joint navigation warfare (NAVWAR) doctrine, which requires assured positioning in contested environments.

Future roadmap includes the launch of three additional NavIC satellites (NVS‑01, NVS‑02, NVS‑03) with atomic clocks of improved stability (≤ 1 × 10⁻¹³ Allan deviation) and the integration of GAGAN payloads on the upcoming GSAT‑7R and GSAT‑7C military communication satellites to provide a dedicated secure augmentation channel for defence users.

Netra Airborne Early Warning and Control System: Indigenous Active Electronically Scanned Array Radar, Platform Integration and Operational Deployment

The Netra AEW&C system, developed by the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) under the Centre for Airborne Systems (CABS), is mounted on the Embraer ERJ‑145 platform (designated ERJ‑145I). The primary sensor is an indigenous Active Electronically Scanned Array (AESA) radar operating in the S‑band (3.1–3.5 GHz) with 1 024 transmit/receive (T/R) modules based on Gallium‑Arsenide (GaAs) MMIC technology. The radar provides 360° azimuth coverage via a rotating dorsal antenna (rotation rate 6 rpm) and electronic elevation scanning from −5° to +45°, delivering a detection range of 250 km for a 2 m² RCS target and 500 km for a 10 m² RCS target.

The mission system integrates the radar with an Identification Friend or Foe (IFF) Mode‑5/Mode‑S interrogator, a Communication Intelligence (COMINT) suite, a Data Link (Link‑16 compatible) terminal, and a Mission Computer based on a ruggedised PowerPC architecture running a real‑time operating system (RTOS). The system supports simultaneous tracking of up to 300 air targets and 100 surface targets, with track initiation latency < 2 seconds. The platform’s endurance is 9 hours with aerial refuelling capability (probe‑and‑drogue) demonstrated in 2021.

Development timeline: the programme was sanctioned in 2004, the first prototype (Netra‑1) flew in 2012, and the first operational unit was inducted into the Indian Air Force (IAF) in February 2017. As of 2024, three Netra aircraft are operational with the No. 50 Squadron “Night Riders” at Bathinda Air Force Station, and a fourth is undergoing trials with the Indian Navy for carrier‑based AEW&C evaluation.

Operational deployment includes participation in Exercise “Gagan Shakti” (2018), “Vayu Shakti” (2022) and joint exercises with the French Air Force (Exercise “Garuda” 2023). The Netra fleet provides continuous surveillance over the Northern and Western sectors, feeding the Integrated Air Command and Control System (IACCS) and the Air Defence Ground Environment System (ADGES). The radar’s electronic counter‑countermeasures (ECCM) suite includes frequency hopping, adaptive nulling, and low‑probability‑of‑intercept (LPI) waveforms.

Future upgrades under the “Netra‑Mk2” programme envisage replacing the GaAs T/R modules with Gallium‑Nitride (GaN) devices to increase peak power by 3 dB and reduce cooling requirements, integration of a secondary L‑band AESA for ballistic missile tracking, and migration to a fully digital beamforming architecture with 4 096 elements. The Mk2 prototype is slated for first flight in 2026.

Civil Nuclear Liability Framework: Operator Liability Caps, Supplier Recourse and Alignment with the Convention on Supplementary Compensation

The Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act (CLNDA), enacted in 2010 and notified in November 2011, establishes a channelled liability regime for nuclear installations in India. The operator (Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited, NPCIL) is strictly liable for nuclear damage up to a financial limit of 300 million Special Drawing Rights (SDR) (≈ ₹2 500 crore at 2024 exchange rates). The Act mandates the operator to maintain insurance or other financial security covering this amount. The central government is liable for damage exceeding the operator’s limit up to a further 300 million SDR, effectively capping total liability at 600 million SDR.

A distinctive feature of CLNDA is Section 17(b), which grants the operator a right of recourse against the supplier if the nuclear incident results from a “patent or latent defect” in the supplied equipment or services. This provision diverges from the international channeling principle embodied in the Vienna Convention on Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage (1963) and the Convention on Supplementary Compensation for Nuclear Damage (CSC, 1997), both of which channel liability exclusively to the operator. India signed the CSC in 2010 and ratified it in 2016, but the ratification instrument includes a declaration that Section 17(b) is compatible with Article 10 of the CSC, which permits a right of recourse if expressly provided in the national law.

The operator’s insurance is placed through the Indian Nuclear Insurance Pool (INIP), a consortium of 15 domestic insurers led by the General Insurance Corporation of India (GIC Re). The pool provides a capacity of ₹1 500 crore, supplemented by a government‑backed reinsurance arrangement for the remaining ₹1 000 crore. The premium is calculated on a per‑reactor‑year basis, currently ₹12 crore per 700 MWe PHWR unit.

Supplier concerns have been addressed through the “India Nuclear Insurance Pool – Supplier Recourse” memorandum of understanding (MoU) signed in 2015 between NPCIL and major foreign vendors (Rosatom, Westinghouse, Areva, GE‑Hitachi). The MoU limits the supplier’s recourse exposure to the contract value of the supplied equipment and requires the supplier to maintain product liability insurance of at least ₹500 crore. The MoU also establishes a joint claims assessment committee to adjudicate defect‑related claims within 180 days.

As of 2024, no nuclear incident has triggered liability under CLNDA. The framework is periodically reviewed by the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) and the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB). A 2022 amendment proposal seeks to raise the operator’s liability cap to 500 million SDR and to clarify the definition of “latent defect” to reduce contractual ambiguity, but the bill remains pending parliamentary approval.

  • Confusing the BMD Phase‑I and Phase‑II interceptor designations — PAD/PAD‑II vs PDV Mk‑II/AD‑1 — and their respective altitude tiers.
  • Assuming the Arihant‑class reactor uses highly enriched uranium (HEU); it uses LEU at 19.75 % enrichment.
  • Believing GAGAN provides only GPS augmentation; it also augments NavIC, GLONASS and Galileo signals through multi‑constellation integrity monitoring.
  • Thinking Netra’s radar is a passive electronically scanned array (PESA); it is an indigenous AESA with GaAs T/R modules.
  • Overlooking that CLNDA’s Section 17(b) creates a supplier recourse right, which is a deviation from the pure channeling principle of the Vienna Convention.
  • Equating the operator’s liability cap (300 million SDR) with the total liability cap (600 million SDR) — the government assumes the second tier.
  • Assuming the Netra fleet is solely an Air Force asset; one airframe is under naval evaluation for carrier‑based AEW&C.

Nuclear Reactor Decommissioning Strategy: Cost Estimates, Waste Classification and International Benchmarks

India’s first commercial Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors (PHWRs) at Tarapur (Units 1 & 2, 160 MWe each) entered a formal decommissioning programme in 2020 after 50 years of operation. The Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) has adopted a three‑stage approach aligned with IAEA Safety Standards Series No. WS‑R‑5: (1) pre‑decommissioning planning and licensing, (2) safe enclosure and dismantling, and (3) site release. The Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) issued the Decommissioning Licence for Tarapur‑1&2 in March 2021, requiring a detailed Decommissioning Plan (DP) that quantifies waste streams, radiation fields, and cost.

Cost estimates prepared by NPCIL in consultation with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) place the total expenditure at ₹4 500 crore (≈ US $540 million) over a 30‑year period. The breakdown follows the IAEA cost‑category structure: (a) project management and licensing ≈ ₹600 crore, (b) decontamination and dismantling ≈ ₹2 200 crore, (c) waste processing, packaging and interim storage ≈ ₹1 200 crore, and (d) site restoration and licence termination ≈ ₹500 crore. These figures are benchmarked against the US NRC’s “Decommissioning Cost Estimate” methodology (NUREG‑1307) and the UK’s Nuclear Decommissioning Authority (NDA) cost model for Magnox stations, which show a per‑MWe cost range of US $2.5–3.5 million; Tarapur’s estimate falls at US $3.4 million/MWe, within the international band.

Waste classification follows the AERB’s “Radioactive Waste Management” guidelines (2008) and the IAEA’s General Safety Guide GSG‑1. Tarapur’s waste inventory is split into: (i) Very Low Level Waste (VLLW) – concrete rubble, steel, and piping (< 1 MBq/kg), destined for near‑surface disposal at the upcoming Near Surface Disposal Facility (NSDF) at Kudankulam; (ii) Low Level Waste (LLW) – activated reactor components, filters, and resins (1 MBq/kg–1 GBq/kg), to be conditioned in cementitious matrices and stored in the existing LLW vaults at Tarapur; (iii) Intermediate Level Waste (ILW) – reactor pressure vessel internals, control rods, and spent fuel handling equipment (1 GBq/kg–1 TBq/kg), requiring shielding and placement in the proposed Deep Geological Repository (DGR) under investigation in the Deccan Traps; and (iv) High Level Waste (HLW) – none from PHWR decommissioning, as spent fuel is transferred to the Away‑From‑Reactor (AFR) storage at Tarapur and later to the Centralised Fuel Reprocessing Plant at Kalpakkam.

The decommissioning schedule targets completion of Stage 1 (pre‑decommissioning) by 2025, Stage 2 (dismantling) by 2040, and Stage 3 (site release) by 2050. Key milestones include the removal of the reactor vessel head (2026), segmentation of the calandria (2028), and final radiological survey for unrestricted release (2048). The programme also incorporates lessons from the Japanese Fukushima‑Daiichi decommissioning, particularly remote‑handling tooling and robotic inspection, which have been trialled at the Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR) mock‑up facility.

Indigenous Solid Rocket Motor Development: High‑Performance Propellant Formulations and Static Test Milestones

India’s strategic launch vehicles and ballistic missiles rely on a family of solid rocket motors (SRMs) that have progressed from the early S‑9 (SLV‑3 first stage) to the current S‑200 (GSLV‑Mk III strap‑on) and the high‑energy HS‑200 (human‑rated Gaganyaan booster). The propellant chemistry is based on Hydroxyl‑Terminated Polybutadiene (HTPB) binder, Ammonium Perchlorate (AP) oxidiser (≈ 70 % wt), and Aluminium (Al) fuel (≈ 18 % wt), with burn‑rate modifiers such as Ferrocene (0.2 % wt) and nano‑Al additives (up to 2 % wt) to tailor pressure exponent and specific impulse (Isp). The S‑200 motor, 3.2 m in diameter and 8.5 m long, delivers a vacuum Isp of 285 s and a total impulse of 1.1 MN·s, using a 12‑segment case wound from high‑strength carbon‑fiber/epoxy composite.

Static test milestones demonstrate the maturation of the production line at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC) and the Ordnance Factory Board’s (OFB) Propellant Factory at Chandipur. The first full‑duration S‑200 qualification firing (ST‑01) occurred on 12 January 2022, achieving 130 s burn time with chamber pressure stabilising at 5.8 MPa. A second qualification (ST‑02) on 18 March 2023 introduced a 5 % wt nano‑Al loading, raising Isp by 3 s and reducing erosive burning. The HS‑200 human‑rated motor completed its first static test (HS‑ST‑01) on 5 July 2023, meeting the Gaganyaan abort‑mode thrust‑profile requirement of 1.6 MN peak thrust with a thrust‑termination system verified at 0.5 s after ignition.

Parallel development at DRDO’s Advanced Systems Laboratory (ASL) has produced the Agni‑V first‑stage motor (A‑1), a 2.5 m diameter, 7.2 m long motor using a high‑energy HTPB/AP/Al formulation with a 78 % AP load and a tailored grain geometry (star‑slot) to achieve a vacuum Isp of 295 s. The A‑1 motor passed its third qualification firing (A‑ST‑03) on 22 November 2022, validating a new case‑bonding process that eliminates the need for a separate liner, reducing mass by 12 %. The programme also explores “green” propellants: a 2024 test of a Glycidyl Azide Polymer (GAP) based binder at the High Energy Materials Research Laboratory (HEMRL) demonstrated a 5 % Isp gain over HTPB but highlighted low‑temperature brittleness, prompting a hybrid GAP/HTPB blend study.

Manufacturing infrastructure upgrades include the commissioning of a 12‑m diameter filament‑winding machine at SDSC (2021) and the installation of a continuous AP‑grinding line at Chandipur (2022) to achieve a narrow particle‑size distribution (D50 = 150 µm) critical for reproducible burn rates. Quality assurance follows the MIL‑STD‑1576E acceptance criteria, with each motor lot subjected to 100 % radiographic inspection, hydrostatic proof testing at 1.5× design pressure, and a 30‑second “hot‑fire” acceptance test before flight certification.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “Which solid rocket motor uses a 78 % ammonium perchlorate loading and a star‑slot grain geometry to achieve a vacuum specific impulse of 295 s?” The options list S‑200, HS‑200, Agni‑V first stage (A‑1), and GSLV‑Mk III core stage (L110). Identify the correct motor and explain why the other options are incorrect.
The correct answer is the Agni‑V first‑stage motor (A‑1). The A‑1 motor’s propellant formulation contains 78 % AP and employs a star‑slot grain to meet the 295 s vacuum Isp requirement for the 5 000 km range. The S‑200 and HS‑200 use ~70 % AP and a cylindrical‑slot grain, delivering 285–288 s Isp. The L110 core stage is a liquid‑propellant (UH25/N2O4) engine, not a solid motor, and therefore does not use AP‑based propellant at all.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mixes solid‑motor specifications with liquid‑engine data, first separate the propulsion type. Memorise the AP‑percentage and grain‑type pairings for each indigenous SRM (S‑200/HS‑200 ≈ 70 % AP, cylindrical‑slot; Agni‑V A‑1 ≈ 78 % AP, star‑slot). This eliminates liquid‑engine distractors instantly.

Electro‑Optical Infrared Payload Standardisation for ISRO and Defence Satellites

The convergence of civilian remote‑sensing and military surveillance requirements has driven the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) and the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) to adopt a common Electro‑Optical/Infrared (EO/IR) payload interface standard, designated “I‑EOIR‑2022”. The standard defines mechanical envelope (max 1.2 m × 0.9 m × 0.6 m), electrical interfaces (SpaceWire‑RM for high‑rate video, MIL‑STD‑1553B for command/telemetry), thermal control (heat‑pipe‑coupled radiator with 30 W dissipation capacity), and data‑format protocols (CCSDS 122.0‑B‑1 for lossless compression, CCSDS 123.0‑B‑1 for lossy). This harmonisation enables a single payload design to be flown on both the Cartosat‑3 series (0.25 m GSD panchromatic) and the Defence Imaging Satellite (DIS‑1) series (0.5 m GSD multispectral + 3 m LWIR).

The first flight‑qualified payload under I‑EOIR‑2022 is the “Panchromatic‑Multispectral‑LWIR (PML) Imager” developed by the Laboratory for Electro‑Optics Systems (LEOS) in collaboration with the Instruments Research & Development Establishment (IRDE). The PML imager integrates a 12 K × 12 K CMOS focal plane array (FPA) for visible‑NIR (0.45–0.90 µm) and a 2 K × 2 K HgCdTe FPA for long‑wave infrared (8–12 µm). On‑board processing uses a Xilinx UltraScale+ FPGA running a radiation‑hardened JPEG‑2000 encoder (CCSDS 122.0) and a real‑time target‑detection algorithm (matched‑filter) for maritime vessel detection. The payload passed the Thermal Vacuum (TVAC) test at the ISRO Satellite Centre (ISAC) in December 2023, demonstrating < 0.5 % MTF degradation across the operational temperature range (−20 °C to +50 °C).

Standardisation also extends to calibration methodology. A joint ISRO‑DRDO calibration campaign uses the “Vicarious Calibration Site” at the Rann of Kutch (spectrally uniform salt flats) and the “On‑Board Calibration Source” (OBCS) – a set of calibrated black‑body sources (300 K, 350 K) and a solar diffuser panel. The calibration plan mandates quarterly vicarious checks and monthly OBCS measurements, with calibration coefficients uploaded via the secure SpaceWire‑RM link. This regime satisfies both the National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC) radiometric accuracy requirement (< 3 % reflectance error) and the Defence Intelligence Agency (DIA) radiometric stability requirement (< 1 % drift per year).

Future roadmap includes the “Modular EO/IR Bus” (MEB) concept, where the optical bench, focal‑plane electronics, and thermal hardware are packaged as a plug‑and‑play module compatible with the I‑1K, I‑2K, and I‑3K satellite buses. The MEB will support rapid payload swaps for technology demonstration (e.g., hyperspectral, polarimetric) without redesigning the spacecraft bus, reducing lead time from 36 months to 18 months. The first MEB flight is slated on the I‑2K‑based “GISAT‑2R” mission (launch 2026).

Artificial Intelligence in Missile Guidance: On‑Board Neural Networks and Real‑Time Target Discrimination

DRDO’s Missile Systems Laboratory (MSL) has transitioned from conventional proportional‑navigation (PN) guidance to AI‑augmented guidance for the next‑generation surface‑to‑air missile (SAM) “Akash‑NG” and the air‑launched cruise missile “Nirbhay‑S”. The core of the AI module is a lightweight Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) trained on a synthetic dataset of 2 million infrared (IR) and radio‑frequency (RF) target signatures generated by the Defence Avionics Research Establishment (DARE) using the “SIGGEN‑X” simulation environment. The network architecture comprises three convolutional layers (3 × 3 kernels, 32‑64‑128 filters), a global average pooling layer, and a fully‑connected classifier outputting a 5‑class probability vector (fighter, UAV, cruise missile, decoy, clutter).

Inference latency is constrained to ≤ 2 ms per frame at 200 Hz frame rate, requiring a dedicated inference accelerator. The chosen hardware is a custom ASIC fabricated at the Semi‑Conductor Laboratory (SCL), Chandigarh, implementing 8‑bit quantised weights (post‑training quantisation) and delivering 1.2 TOPS at 1.5 W. The ASIC interfaces with the missile’s on‑board computer (OBC) via a high‑speed PCIe‑Gen3 link, feeding the classifier output to the guidance law selector. The guidance law switches between PN (for high‑confidence target class) and a “robust adaptive” law (for low‑confidence or decoy classes) that incorporates a Kalman filter with augmented state for target manoeuvre estimation.

Flight‑test validation began with the “AI‑Guided Flight Test‑1 (AGFT‑1)” on 14 February 2024, where an Akash‑NG interceptor engaged a Banshee‑type target drone executing evasive manoeuvres. The AI module correctly classified the target as “UAV” with 96 % confidence, selected PN, and achieved a miss distance of 0.8 m. A subsequent test (AGFT‑2) on 30 May 2024 introduced a towed infrared decoy; the classifier assigned 78 % probability to “decoy”, triggering the adaptive law, which maintained lock on the true target and achieved a 1.2 m miss distance. The test series demonstrated a 30 % reduction in miss distance against decoy‑rich environments compared with the legacy PN‑only guidance.

Software safety certification follows the DO‑178C Level A equivalent adapted for defence (D‑STD‑001). The CNN model is frozen after formal verification using the “Neural Network Verification Toolkit (NNVT)” developed by the Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Robotics (CAIR). NNVT proves bounds on output probabilities for all inputs within the defined operational envelope (± 30 % signal‑to‑noise ratio, ± 15 % temperature variation). The verified model is then compiled to the ASIC firmware, which undergoes hardware‑in‑the‑loop (HIL) testing on the Missile Hardware‑in‑Loop Simulator (MHILS) at the Integrated Test Range (ITR), Chandipur. The certification package was submitted to the Defence Acquisition Council (DAC) in October 2024 and cleared for limited production in March 2025.

  • Confusing the decommissioning cost per MWe of Tarapur with that of the US Magnox stations, which are lower due to different regulatory regimes.
  • Assuming the S‑200 motor uses a star‑slot grain; it employs a cylindrical‑slot grain, while the Agni‑V A‑1 uses star‑slot.
  • Believing the I‑EOIR‑2022 standard applies only to ISRO payloads; it is jointly mandated for defence imaging satellites as well.
  • Thinking the AI guidance ASIC runs a full‑precision (32‑bit) network; it operates on 8‑bit quantised weights to meet power‑latency constraints.
  • Equating the Akash‑NG AI module’s classifier output with a simple threshold; the system uses a confidence‑gated guidance‑law selector.
  • Overlooking that the HS‑200 human‑rated motor includes a thrust‑termination system, unlike the standard S‑200.

Gaganyaan Human Spaceflight Programme: Crew Module, Life‑Support and Abort System Architecture

The Gaganyaan programme, approved by the Union Cabinet in 2018, aims to demonstrate indigenous human spaceflight capability by launching a three‑member crew to a 400 km low‑Earth orbit for up to seven days. The launch vehicle is the human‑rated LVM‑3 (formerly GSLV Mk‑III) equipped with a crew‑escape system (CES) that can be activated from the launch pad up to an altitude of 20 km. The CES uses four solid‑propellant motors mounted on the payload fairing; each motor delivers 180 kN of thrust for 3.5 s, pulling the crew module (CM) to a safe distance before parachute deployment.

The crew module is a 3.7 t, 3.5 m diameter, 2.7 m high pressure vessel built from aluminium‑lithium alloy (Al‑Li 2195) with a welded titanium‑alloy (Ti‑6Al‑4V) heat‑shield base. The thermal protection system (TPS) combines a carbon‑phenolic ablative layer (≈30 mm) on the forward cone and a reusable silica‑tile blanket on the aft section, rated for a peak heat flux of 1.2 MW/m² during a 7.8 km/s re‑entry. The environmental control and life‑support system (ECLSS) follows a closed‑loop architecture: a molecular sieve CO₂ removal assembly, a solid‑amine swing‑bed for trace contaminant control, a water‑recovery loop (urine‑to‑water via vapour compression distillation) and a high‑pressure oxygen‑nitrogen generation unit (ONGS) that electrolyses water at 30 bar. Redundancy is provided by two independent ECLSS strings, each capable of sustaining the full crew for the mission duration.

Avionics are built around a dual‑redundant, radiation‑hardened LEON3FT processor running a partitioned ARINC‑653 real‑time operating system. The guidance, navigation and control (GNC) suite fuses inertial measurement unit (IMU) data with star‑tracker and GPS/NavIC measurements to achieve a 3‑σ orbit insertion accuracy of ±5 km in altitude and ±0.2° in inclination. The mission profile includes two uncrewed test flights (G1 and G2) — G1 launched on 21 October 2023 validated the CES and CM recovery; G2, scheduled for Q4 2024, will test the full ECLSS and re‑entry trajectory. The first crewed mission (H1) is targeted for 2025, contingent on successful completion of the uncrewed milestones and clearance by the Human Spaceflight Safety Review Board (HSSRB).

Advanced Heavy Water Reactor and Thorium Fuel Cycle: Design, Safety Features and Deployment Timeline

The Advanced Heavy Water Reactor (AHWR) is a 300 MWe, vertical pressure‑tube, boiling‑light‑water‑cooled, heavy‑water‑moderated reactor designed at the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) to demonstrate commercial thorium utilisation. The core comprises 452 fuel clusters, each containing 54 pins of (Th‑U‑233)O₂ mixed‑oxide (MOX) fuel with an initial 233U enrichment of 3.5 wt %. The reactor operates at a coolant outlet temperature of 310 °C and a pressure of 7 MPa, delivering a thermal efficiency of 31 %. Passive safety is achieved through a large gravity‑driven water pool (≈7000 m³) surrounding the calandria, providing 72 h of decay‑heat removal without operator action or external power.

The fuel cycle closes on the thorium‑233U axis: spent AHWR fuel is reprocessed in the upcoming Integrated Nuclear Recycle Plant (INRP) at Tarapur, where 233U is recovered and refabricated into fresh MOX pins. The projected conversion ratio is 0.95, enabling near‑breeder performance while avoiding the high‑flux, sodium‑cooled environment of fast reactors. The design incorporates a passive heat‑removal system (PHRS) with natural‑circulation air‑cooled heat exchangers, a core‑catcher vessel for severe‑accident mitigation, and a double‑containment structure meeting the IAEA’s “defence‑in‑depth” Level 4 criteria.

Regulatory clearance from the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) was granted for the pre‑construction safety analysis report (PCSAR) in March 2022. Site preparation at the proposed location in Gorakhpur, Haryana, began in late 2023, with first‑pour‑concrete (FPC) scheduled for 2025 and commercial operation targeted for 2030. The AHWR is positioned as the cornerstone of India’s third‑stage nuclear power programme, linking the existing PHWR fleet (first stage) and the fast‑breeder programme (second stage) to the vast thorium reserves (≈846 kt ThO₂) identified in the monazite sands of Kerala and Odisha.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: "Which of the following statements about the AHWR is correct? (a) It uses liquid sodium as coolant. (b) It is a fast‑breeder reactor. (c) It employs a gravity‑driven water pool for passive decay‑heat removal. (d) It operates on a pure uranium‑235 fuel cycle."
Correct answer: (c). The AHWR is a heavy‑water‑moderated, light‑water‑cooled thermal reactor; its passive safety relies on a large gravity‑driven water pool, not sodium. It is not a fast breeder and its fuel is thorium‑233U MOX, not pure U‑235.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mixes reactor types, first identify the coolant and moderator. AHWR = light‑water coolant + heavy‑water moderator + thorium fuel. Fast breeder = sodium coolant + no moderator. PHWR = heavy‑water coolant + heavy‑water moderator + natural uranium. This classification eliminates three options instantly.

Indigenous Unmanned Combat Aerial Vehicle Development: Rustom‑II, Ghatak and SWiFT Flight‑Test Progress

The Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) pursues three complementary UCAV programmes to cover medium‑altitude long‑endurance (MALE), stealthy strike, and technology‑demonstrator roles. Rustom‑II (also designated TAPAS‑BH‑201) is a twin‑engine MALE UAV with a 20 m wingspan, maximum take‑off weight of 1,800 kg and an endurance of 24 h at 25,000 ft. Powered by two 100 kW NPO‑Saturn 36MT turboprops, it carries a modular payload bay for synthetic‑aperture radar (SAR), electro‑optical/infrared (EO/IR) turret and electronic‑intelligence (ELINT) suites. The first flight occurred on 16 November 2016; user‑trials with the Indian Army and Air Force commenced in 2022, demonstrating autonomous take‑off, waypoint navigation, and real‑time data‑link via the indigenous SATCOM terminal. As of March 2024, Rustom‑II has logged over 1,200 flight hours, with a demonstrated ceiling of 30,000 ft and a mission radius of 1,000 km.

Ghatak is a low‑observable, flying‑wing UCAV intended for deep‑penetration strike and suppression of enemy air defences (SEAD). The airframe uses carbon‑fibre‑reinforced polymer (CFRP) skin with radar‑absorbent material (RAM) coating, a serpentine inlet to mask the engine face, and an internal weapons bay sized for two 250 kg precision‑guided munitions. The propulsion is a single 4.5 kN class turbofan (GTRE‑GTX‑35VS) derived from the Kaveri core. The maiden flight on 1 July 2022 from the Aeronautical Test Range, Chitradurga, validated the flight‑control laws for a tailless configuration and the low‑probability‑of‑intercept (LPI) data‑link. Subsequent sorties in 2023 demonstrated autonomous target recognition using an on‑board CNN accelerator (similar to the Akash‑NG AI module) and a successful weapon‑release trial at 20,000 ft.

SWiFT (Stealth Wing Flying Testbed) is a sub‑scale (1/5) technology demonstrator for Ghatak, focusing on aerodynamic validation of the blended‑wing‑body planform, control‑surface effectiveness at high angles of attack, and integration of the indigenous flight‑control computer (FCC‑V2). Its first flight on 12 February 2023 achieved a 30‑minute sortie, reaching Mach 0.6 at 15,000 ft. Data from SWiFT feeds directly into the Ghatak flight‑control law refinement and the development of the autonomous landing system for carrier‑based operations.

Ballistic Missile Defence Phase‑II: Exo‑Atmospheric Interceptor PDV‑MkII and Layered Intercept Architecture

India’s Ballistic Missile Defence (BMD) programme is structured in two phases. Phase‑I, declared operational in 2018, provides a two‑layer shield: the Prithvi Air Defence (PAD) interceptor for exo‑atmospheric engagement (up to 80 km altitude) and the Advanced Air Defence (AAD) endo‑atmospheric interceptor (up to 30 km). Phase‑II extends the envelope to counter intermediate‑range ballistic missiles (IRBMs) with apogees above 150 km and re‑entry velocities exceeding 4 km/s. The centrepiece is the Prithvi Defence Vehicle Mark‑II (PDV‑MkII), a three‑stage solid‑propellant interceptor with a kinetic kill vehicle (KKV) equipped with an imaging infrared (IIR) seeker and a divert‑and‑attitude‑control system (DACS) using 12 N thrusters.

The PDV‑MkII booster adds a high‑energy third stage (HTPB‑based, 1.2 m diameter) to the existing two‑stage PDV, raising the maximum intercept altitude to 150 km and the closing speed capability to 5 km/s. The KKV’s IIR seeker operates in the 3‑5 µm band with a 1024 × 1024 focal‑plane array, providing a 0.5 mrad instantaneous field of view and a 30 °/s track rate. Guidance follows a proportional‑navigation law augmented by a real‑time trajectory‑shaping algorithm that compensates for target manoeuvres detected via the seeker’s centroid‑offset measurements.

Flight tests: PDV‑MkII‑01 (27 September 2022) intercepted a simulated IRBM target launched from a mobile platform at 1,500 km range, achieving a direct hit at 120 km altitude. PDV‑MkII‑02 (15 March 2023) demonstrated a “hit‑to‑kill” against a target deploying a single decoy and a chaff cloud; the seeker discriminated the warhead using a multi‑spectral signature library. The Phase‑II architecture integrates the Swordfish long‑range tracking radar (LRTR) at 600 km range, the Multi‑Function Radar (MFR) for fire‑control, and a battle‑management command‑control (BMC2) node that fuses data from space‑based early‑warning satellites (GSAT‑7/7A) and ground‑based sensors. The system is designed for a “shoot‑look‑shoot” doctrine with a decision cycle under 30 s.

Indian Space Station Concept: Modular Habitat, Docking Technology and International Collaboration Framework

Following the Gaganyaan milestone, ISRO has outlined a roadmap for a sovereign low‑Earth‑orbit space station — Bharatiya Antariksha Station (BAS) — targeting initial module launch by 2035. The baseline design comprises a 20‑tonne core habitat module (CHM) launched on the LVM‑3, followed by two 15‑tonne experiment modules (EM‑1, EM‑2) and a 10‑tonne logistics/airlock module (LM). All modules share a common mechanical‑electrical interface based on the Indian Docking System (IDS), a gender‑less, androgynous mechanism derived from the SPADEX (Space Docking Experiment) demonstrator flown on PSLV‑C58 (January 2024). IDS provides a 1.2 m diameter transfer tunnel, 12 kW power transfer, and bidirectional high‑rate data (10 Gbps) across the mated interface.

The CHM houses a regenerative ECLSS (CO₂ electrolysis to O₂, Sabatier reactor for water recovery), a 6‑kW solar‑array wing with roll‑out flexible blankets, and a radiation shelter using polyethylene‑based shielding (15 g/cm² areal density). Crew capacity is three for 180‑day missions, expandable to six with the addition of EM‑1. The station will operate in a 400 km, 51.6° inclination orbit, compatible with international partner vehicles. A memorandum of understanding (MoU) signed with NASA in June 2023 enables joint microgravity research, crew‑exchange flights on the Commercial Crew Vehicle (CCV), and shared use of the International Docking System Standard (IDSS) adapter on the LM. Parallel discussions with ESA and Roscosmos focus on collaborative life‑science payloads and joint extravehicular activity (EVA) training at the Neutral Buoyancy Facility in Bengaluru.

Key technology gaps under active development: (1) long‑duration cryogenic fluid management for on‑orbit refuelling of the station‑keeping thrusters (monopropellant hydrazine), (2) autonomous rendezvous and proximity operations (ARPO) validated by the SPADEX‑2 mission (planned 2025), and (3) in‑orbit manufacturing demonstration using a metal‑additive‑manufacturing payload on EM‑2. The programme is funded through the newly created Space Station Development Fund (SSDF) under the Department of Space, with an allocated budget of ₹12,500 crore for the 2024‑2030 period.

  • Confusing the AHWR’s light‑water coolant with the PHWR’s heavy‑water coolant.
  • Assuming Rustom‑II is a stealth platform; it is a conventional MALE UAV with no low‑observable features.
  • Believing PDV‑MkII uses a blast‑fragmentation warhead; it is a pure kinetic kill vehicle.
  • Thinking the Indian Space Station will use the Russian APAS docking system; it employs the indigenous IDS/SPADEX interface.
  • Mixing the Gaganyaan crew‑escape system’s solid motors with the LVM‑3’s liquid‑strap‑on boosters.
  • Overlooking that the AHWR’s conversion ratio is below unity (0.95), so it is not a breeder in the strict sense.
  • Assuming the Ghatak UCAV has already entered serial production; it remains in flight‑test phase with only two prototypes flown.

Indigenous Electric Propulsion Development for Geostationary Station‑Keeping and Deep‑Space Missions

The Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre (LPSC) at Valiamala has led India’s electric propulsion programme since the early 2000s. A 1.5 kW Hall‑effect thruster (HET) using xenon propellant completed qualification testing in 2021 and was flown on the GSAT‑20 high‑throughput communication satellite launched on GSLV‑Mk III in July 2023. The thruster provides north‑south station‑keeping with a specific impulse of 1 600 s, reducing the chemical propellant mass by roughly 40 % compared with a conventional bipropellant system. In parallel, LPSC is developing a 3 kW HET for the next GSAT‑20 series (GSAT‑20A/20B) to enable east‑west station‑keeping and orbit‑raising manoeuvres, with a target flight demonstration by 2026.

For deep‑space missions, the centre is advancing a 10 kW gridded ion thruster (GIT) that operates at a specific impulse above 3 000 s. The GIT breadboard completed a 1 000‑hour endurance test in 2022, and a flight‑model is slated for the proposed Venus orbiter (Shukrayaan‑1) and the follow‑on Mars mission (Mangalyaan‑2). Power processing units (PPUs) for both HET and GIT are being co‑developed with Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited (BHEL) to meet the stringent mass‑and‑volume constraints of the LVM‑3 upper stage. The Gaganyaan service module also incorporates a 2 kW HET for attitude control during the orbital phase, marking the first crewed‑mission use of electric propulsion in India.

Ground‑test infrastructure includes the Electric Propulsion Test Facility (EPTF) at LPSC, upgraded in 2020 with a 5 m diameter vacuum chamber capable of simulating 10⁻⁶ mbar pressure and a 20 kW solar‑array simulator. The facility supports simultaneous thruster and PPU testing, enabling rapid iteration. A key milestone was the 2023 “dual‑thruster” test where a 1.5 kW HET and a 3 kW HET operated in tandem, validating power‑sharing algorithms for future multi‑thruster clusters on large platforms such as the Bharatiya Antariksha Station.

International collaboration has been limited to data exchange; the programme remains fully indigenous to avoid export‑control restrictions on xenon feed‑system components and high‑voltage PPU electronics. The Department of Space’s 2024‑2030 roadmap allocates ₹1 200 crore for electric propulsion, targeting a 50 % reduction in launch‑mass for geostationary payloads and enabling cargo‑only interplanetary transfers without a dedicated upper stage.

Thorium‑Based Fuel Cycle Research: AHWR‑LEU, Th‑MOX and the Path to a Closed Thorium Cycle

India’s thorium utilisation strategy centres on the Advanced Heavy Water Reactor (AHWR) design, which couples a low‑enriched uranium (LEU) driver zone with a thorium‑based blanket. The AHWR‑LEU variant, approved by the Atomic Energy Commission in 2022, uses 19.75 % enriched UO₂ fuel pins to generate the initial neutron flux while the surrounding ThO₂‑PuO₂ (Th‑MOX) blanket breeds ²³³U. The driver fuel stays within the IAEA “low‑enriched” category, simplifying safeguards and avoiding the political sensitivities associated with high‑enriched uranium.

Th‑MOX fuel fabrication is carried out at the Nuclear Fuel Complex (NFC) in Hyderabad. In 2023 NFC produced the first full‑scale Th‑MOX assemblies using plutonium recovered from PHWR spent fuel, achieving a plutonium content of 5 % by weight. These assemblies were loaded into the AHWR critical facility at the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) in early 2024 for physics validation. The experiments confirmed a conversion ratio of 0.78, indicating that each driver‑fuel cycle can sustain the blanket for roughly two years before re‑processing.

Reprocessing of irradiated Th‑MOX to extract ²³³U is planned at the upcoming Integrated Nuclear Recycle Plant (INRP) at Tarapur, which will employ the THOREX solvent‑extraction process adapted from the PUREX flow‑sheet. A pilot‑scale THOREX loop was commissioned in 2023 and demonstrated a ²³³U recovery efficiency above 99 %. The recovered ²³³U will be fabricated into fresh Th‑MOX at NFC, closing the thorium loop without requiring a fast‑spectrum breeder reactor.

The Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) has earmarked a site in Rajasthan for a 300 MWe AHWR‑LEU demonstration unit, with construction targeted to begin in 2026 and first criticality by 2030. This reactor will serve as a test‑bed for the full fuel‑cycle — mining of monazite at the Indian Rare Earths Limited (IREL) plant in Odisha, conversion to ThO₂ at the Rare Earths Division, fuel fabrication, irradiation, reprocessing, and recycle. The programme aligns with India’s long‑term goal of achieving a self‑sustaining thorium fuel cycle by the 2040s, leveraging the country’s estimated 846 000 tonnes of thorium reserves.

Technique: Comparative Fuel‑Cycle Analysis
Question: Explain why the AHWR‑LEU design uses low‑enriched uranium (LEU) driver fuel together with thorium‑based blanket fuel, and how this configuration moves India toward a closed thorium cycle without requiring a fast‑breeder reactor.
Solution: The AHWR‑LEU employs 19.75 % enriched UO₂ driver pins to provide the initial neutron flux, while the surrounding ThO₂‑PuO₂ (Th‑MOX) blanket breeds ²³³U from thorium. Because the driver fuel is LEU, the reactor stays within the IAEA’s “low‑enriched” category, easing safeguards. The bred ²³³U can be recycled into fresh Th‑MOX, closing the thorium loop. This avoids the need for a fast‑spectrum breeder, which would demand higher enrichment and more complex reprocessing, and thus represents a pragmatic step toward a self‑sustaining thorium fuel cycle.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a “step‑wise” description of a fuel‑cycle, list the stages (mining, conversion, fabrication, irradiation, reprocessing, recycle) and attach the specific Indian facility or programme to each stage. This shows both process knowledge and programme awareness, which examiners reward.

Defence Cyber Operations Doctrine: Network‑Centric Warfare, Offensive Capabilities and Legal Frameworks

The Defence Cyber Agency (DCA) was raised in September 2019 under the Integrated Defence Staff (IDS) as a tri‑service entity headquartered in New Delhi. In March 2021 the Ministry of Defence released the Defence Cyber Operations Doctrine (DCOD), which articulates three pillars — defend, deter, develop — and defines the operational concepts for network‑centric warfare. The doctrine assigns the DCA responsibility for protecting the Defence Information Infrastructure (DII), conducting cyber‑enabled intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR), and, when authorised, executing offensive cyber effects against adversary command‑and‑control networks.

Offensive capabilities are organised under a “Cyber Command” construct that integrates the DCA with the Defence Intelligence Agency (DIA) and the National Technical Research Organisation (NTRO). Employment of offensive cyber tools requires explicit approval from the Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS), ensuring political oversight. The 2022 amendment to the Information Technology Act (2000) introduced Section 69B‑A, empowering the government to designate “critical defence cyber assets” and to mandate incident‑reporting timelines for defence contractors.

The National Cyber Security Strategy (NCSS) 2023, drafted by the National Security Council Secretariat (NSCS), aligns military cyber doctrine with whole‑of‑government resilience measures. It adopts the UN Group of Governmental Experts (GGE) norms and references the Tallinn Manual 2.0 for the interpretation of international humanitarian law in cyberspace. The strategy mandates a “zero‑trust” architecture for all defence networks by 2027 and establishes a Cyber Security Operations Centre (CSOC) at each service headquarters.

Recent exercises validate the doctrine. “Exercise Cyber Suraksha” (October 2023) simulated a coordinated ransomware attack on the Army’s logistics management system, testing the DCA’s incident‑response playbook and the inter‑service information‑sharing protocol. “Exercise Digital Shield” (February 2024) involved the Navy’s maritime domain awareness network and the Air Force’s integrated air‑command‑and‑control system, practicing joint defensive manoeuvres and controlled offensive probing against a red‑team representing a near‑peer adversary. After‑action reports highlighted the need for automated threat‑intelligence sharing across the three services, a capability now being procured under the “Unified Cyber Situational Awareness Platform” (UCSAP) tender floated in 2024.

Space‑Based Laser Communication Terminals: High‑Throughput Optical Links for Strategic and Commercial Satellites

ISRO’s Space Applications Centre (SAC) at Ahmedabad has been developing laser communication terminals (LCTs) since the early 2010s. The first flight‑qualified terminal, a 1.5 Gbps bidirectional optical payload, was integrated on the GSAT‑20 satellite launched in July 2023. The terminal demonstrated a 1.2 Gbps downlink to the Optical Ground Station (OGS) at Byalalu, Karnataka, under clear‑sky conditions, validating acquisition, tracking and pointing (ATP) algorithms with a 5 µrad pointing accuracy.

In November 2022 a dedicated technology‑demonstration mission, the Laser Communication Experiment (LCE), flew as a co‑passenger on PSLV‑C55. The LCE carried a 5 Gbps LCT and established a 3‑minute optical link with the OGS at Mount Abu, Rajasthan, achieving a bit‑error‑rate below 10⁻⁹. The experiment also tested wavelength‑division multiplexing (WDM) using 1550 nm and 1560 nm channels, a precursor to the 10 Gbps multi‑channel terminal planned for the Indian Data Relay Satellite System (IDRSS).

The IDRSS, approved in 2021, will consist of two satellites in geostationary orbit equipped with 10 Gbps LCTs to provide real‑time relay for low‑Earth‑orbit (LEO) remote‑sensing satellites and the Gaganyaan crewed missions. The first IDRSS satellite (IDRSS‑1) is scheduled for launch on GSLV‑Mk III in 2025, with the second following in 2026. The terminals incorporate a 30 cm aperture telescope, a coarse‑pointing assembly (CPA) driven by reaction wheels, and a fine‑pointing assembly (FPA) using a fast‑steering mirror, all developed indigenously by SAC in partnership with the Laboratory for Electro‑Optics Systems (LEOS).

For strategic users, the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) is integrating a hardened 2 Gbps LCT on the GSAT‑7A military communication satellite (launched 2021) to provide jam‑resistant, low‑probability‑of‑intercept links for the Navy’s carrier‑battle‑group and the Air Force’s network‑centric operations. The roadmap targets a 100 Gbps inter‑satellite optical link for the Bharatiya Antariksha Station (BAS) by 2035, leveraging the 10 Gbps IDRSS heritage and advances in space‑qualified erbium‑doped fibre amplifiers (EDFAs) currently under test at the ISRO Inertial Systems Unit (IISU).

  • Confusing the 1.5 kW Hall thruster on GSAT‑20 with the 3 kW thruster planned for the GSAT‑20 series; they are separate development milestones.
  • Assuming the AHWR‑LEU is a fast breeder; it is a thermal‑spectrum reactor using LEU driver fuel.
  • Thinking the Defence Cyber Operations Doctrine authorises offensive cyber attacks without political clearance; it only defines capabilities, employment requires Cabinet Committee on Security approval.
  • Believing the 5 Gbps laser link tested in 2022 was an operational service; it was a technology demonstration on a single pass.
  • Mixing the Th‑MOX fuel fabricated at NFC with the mixed‑oxide (MOX) fuel used in PFBR; the former is thorium‑plutonium, the latter is plutonium‑uranium.
  • Overlooking that the 10 kW gridded ion thruster is still in ground‑test phase and has not flown on any mission.

Indigenous Development of High‑Power Microwave Weapons for Counter‑Electronics Operations

India’s Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) has pursued high‑power microwave (HPM) weapons since the early 1990s under the KALI (Kilo Ampere Linear Injector) programme. The KALI‑5000, a 40 GW S‑band relativistic microwave source, demonstrated the ability to generate nanosecond pulses capable of disrupting unhardened electronic systems at ranges of several hundred metres. Subsequent work at the Centre for High Energy Systems and Sciences (CHESS) in Hyderabad focused on compacting the Marx generator and pulse‑forming network to fit within a tactical vehicle platform. In 2018 a vehicle‑mounted demonstrator, designated “Vajra”, completed a series of open‑air tests against representative radar and communication payloads, achieving a 90 % probability of functional kill at 300 m. The programme now emphasises two parallel tracks: a short‑range, truck‑mounted system for base‑area defence and an air‑launched pod for suppression of enemy air defences (SEAD). Key technical challenges include thermal management of the cathode, repeatability of the pulse‑repetition frequency (PRF) above 10 Hz, and hardening of the weapon’s own electronics against self‑generated electromagnetic interference. The DRDO’s 2022 roadmap targets a 10 GW, 1 kHz PRF system with a 1 km effective radius by 2027, leveraging indigenous gallium‑nitride (GaN) solid‑state switches to replace the bulky spark‑gap switches used in KALI‑5000.

Operational Concept and Integration

The doctrinal concept treats HPM as a non‑kinetic “soft‑kill” layer complementary to kinetic interceptors. In a layered air‑defence architecture, HPM pods on Su‑30MKI or the upcoming Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA) would precede missile engagement, degrading the target’s fire‑control radar and data‑link, thereby increasing the probability of kill for subsequent Astra or QRSAM shots. Ground‑based Vajra units would protect high‑value assets such as command centres, missile silos, and satellite ground stations. Integration requires a common battle‑management software that can schedule HPM pulses without fratricide to friendly platforms; the Integrated Air Command and Control System (IACCS) has been extended with an “EM‑Effect” module for this purpose. Export control classification places HPM sources under SCOMET Category 1A (directed energy weapons), and any technology transfer follows the Wassenaar Arrangement’s dual‑use guidelines.

Integrated Ballistic Missile Defence Phase‑II: Exo‑Atmospheric Interceptor and Sensor Fusion

Phase‑II of India’s Ballistic Missile Defence (BMD) programme aims to intercept intermediate‑range ballistic missiles (IRBMs) with apogees above 150 km, a regime where the Phase‑I Prithvi Air Defence (PAD) and Advanced Air Defence (AAD) endo‑atmospheric interceptors are ineffective. The core of Phase‑II is the PDV Mk‑II (Prithvi Defence Vehicle Mark‑II), a two‑stage solid‑propellant interceptor equipped with an imaging infrared (IIR) seeker and a divert‑and‑attitude‑control system (DACS) capable of 30 g lateral manoeuvres. Flight tests in 2019 and 2022 demonstrated successful hit‑to‑kill against a simulated 2 000 km class target at 120 km altitude. Complementing PDV Mk‑II, the AD‑1 and AD‑2 long‑range endo‑atmospheric interceptors extend the defended footprint to 5 000 km class threats. Sensor fusion is achieved through the Swordfish long‑range tracking radar (LRTR) operating in S‑band, the Multi‑Function Radar (MFR) on the INS Dhruv, and space‑based infrared assets from the Defence Space Agency. The Battle Management Command and Control (BMC2) software correlates tracks from these heterogeneous sensors, resolves ghost tracks, and assigns interceptors based on a cost‑function that minimises total propellant expenditure while maximising kill probability.

Key Milestones and Remaining Gaps

Milestones include the 2019 PDV Mk‑II intercept, the 2021 AD‑1 maiden flight, and the 2023 integrated test where a Swordfish cue handed over to MFR for terminal guidance. Remaining gaps are the validation of the IIR seeker against counter‑measures such as decoys and chaff, the qualification of the DACS for multiple divert manoeuvres in a single engagement, and the hardening of the BMC2 against cyber‑electronic attacks. The 2024‑25 test campaign plans a salvo engagement of two simultaneous targets to stress the resource‑allocation algorithm. Successful completion would give India a credible exo‑atmospheric shield against IRBMs from the northern and western theatres.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “Which interceptor forms the exo‑atmospheric layer of India’s BMD Phase‑II and what seeker technology does it employ?” Many candidates answer “PAD with radar seeker”.
Correct answer: The exo‑atmospheric layer is provided by the PDV Mk‑II, which uses an imaging infrared (IIR) seeker, not a radar seeker. PAD and AAD are endo‑atmospheric Phase‑I interceptors. The IIR seeker enables hit‑to‑kill in the vacuum of space where radar cross‑section is negligible.
Exam‑day strategy
Memorise the three‑layer BMD architecture: Phase‑I (PAD/AAD, endo), Phase‑II exo (PDV Mk‑II, IIR seeker), Phase‑II endo (AD‑1/AD‑2). Link each layer to its sensor (Swordfish, MFR, space‑based IR) and the BMC2 fusion logic. This mapping frequently appears in both GS‑III and optional defence‑studies questions.

Additive Manufacturing of Critical Aerospace Components: Qualification, Standards and Deployment

Additive manufacturing (AM), commonly termed 3D printing, has moved from prototyping to flight‑critical parts in India’s space and defence programmes. The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) qualified a 3D‑printed liquid‑oxygen/kerosene thrust chamber for the Vikas engine in 2021, reducing part count from 120 to 4 and cutting lead time by 60 %. The chamber, built from Inconel 718 using laser powder‑bed fusion (LPBF), passed hot‑fire tests at 250 bar chamber pressure for 650 seconds. In parallel, DRDO’s Gas Turbine Research Establishment (GTRE) produced a 3D‑printed compressor blade for the Kaveri engine using a nickel‑based superalloy, achieving a 15 % weight reduction and a 20 % improvement in creep life. Qualification follows the AS9100D aerospace quality standard adapted by the Defence Institute of Quality Assurance (DIQA) and the Centre for Military Airworthiness and Certification (CEMILAC). The certification workflow includes: (1) material lot traceability, (2) process parameter locking via Design of Experiments (DoE), (3) non‑destructive evaluation (NDE) using computed tomography (CT) for internal porosity, (4) mechanical testing per ASTM F3184, and (5) a first‑article inspection (FAI) report signed by the Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) and the certifying authority.

Supply‑Chain Impact and Indigenous Powder Production

To reduce import dependence, the Defence Metallurgical Research Laboratory (DMRL) and the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) have established a domestic gas‑atomised powder line for Inconel 718, Ti‑6Al‑4V, and Maraging‑300. The 2023 production target of 5 tonnes/year meets the projected demand for the Gaganyaan crew module’s structural brackets and the AMCA’s engine‑mount fittings. A national AM standard, “IS 17400:2023 – Additive Manufacturing – Powder Bed Fusion – Qualification Requirements”, was notified by the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) in March 2023, aligning with ISO/ASTM 52900 series. The standard mandates a digital thread linking the CAD model, build file, machine log, and post‑process heat‑treatment records, enabling full traceability for airworthiness audits.

Thorium Fuel Cycle Advancement: Advanced Heavy Water Reactor Demonstration and Fuel Fabrication

India’s three‑stage nuclear programme envisions thorium utilisation in the third stage. The Advanced Heavy Water Reactor (AHWR‑300LEU), a 300 MWe vertical pressure‑tube reactor, is the technology demonstrator for thorium‑based fuel cycles. Designed by the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC), the AHWR uses low‑enriched uranium (LEU) driver fuel (19.75 % U‑235) in a (Th‑U)O₂ matrix, with on‑power refuelling and passive safety features such as a gravity‑driven water pool for decay‑heat removal. The reactor’s physics design achieves a conversion ratio of 0.9, breeding U‑233 from Th‑232 while maintaining a negative void coefficient. Fuel fabrication occurs at the Nuclear Fuel Complex (NFC), Hyderabad, where a dedicated thorium‑fuel line produces (Th‑U)O₂ pellets via sol‑gel microsphere pelletisation, followed by sintering at 1 650 °C in a reducing atmosphere. The first criticality of the AHWR is scheduled for 2026 at the new site in Kota, Rajasthan, after the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) completes the safety‑case review, which includes a probabilistic safety assessment (PSA) Level‑2 for external events.

Strategic Significance and Proliferation Resistance

The AHWR demonstrates a proliferation‑resistant fuel cycle because the discharged fuel contains U‑232 (via Th‑232 (n,2n) reactions), whose decay chain emits high‑energy gamma radiation, complicating weaponisation. Moreover, the reactor operates on a once‑through thorium‑LEU cycle, avoiding the need for reprocessing in the near term. The experience gained will feed into the design of the Indian Molten Salt Breeder Reactor (IMSBR) and the Compact High‑Temperature Reactor (CHTR) concepts under the Generation‑IV International Forum. Successful deployment would secure India’s long‑term energy independence given its vast thorium reserves (≈ 846 000 tonnes of ThO₂ equivalent).

Autonomous Swarm Drone Architecture for Tactical ISR and Strike Missions

The Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) and the private‑sector consortium under the iDEX (Innovations for Defence Excellence) framework are developing a heterogeneous swarm of 20‑50 small unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) for intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance (ISR) and precision strike. The architecture comprises three layers: (1) a ground‑control station (GCS) running a distributed mission‑planning algorithm based on consensus‑based bundle algorithm (CBBA), (2) a mesh network using software‑defined radios (SDR) in the L‑band with frequency‑hopping for anti‑jam resilience, and (3) the UAVs themselves — fixed‑wing “Netra‑S” for wide‑area surveillance (endurance 6 h, payload 2 kg electro‑optical/infrared) and quad‑rotor “Strike‑Q” for terminal attack (payload 1 kg shaped‑charge warhead). Each UAV carries an edge‑computing module (NVIDIA Jetson AGX Xavier) enabling real‑time target detection via a convolutional neural network (CNN) trained on synthetic aperture radar (SAR) and EO/IR datasets. The swarm operates under a “human‑on‑the‑loop” policy: the GCS operator approves the final engagement list, while autonomous collision avoidance and dynamic task allocation occur onboard.

Testing, Integration and Operationalisation Timeline

Key milestones include the 2022 “Swarm‑1” field trial at Pokhran where 15 Netra‑S UAVs mapped a 10 km × 10 km area in 45 minutes with 0.5 m ground‑sample distance, and the 2023 “Swarm‑2” live‑fire demonstration where 8 Strike‑Q UAVs neutralised simulated armoured targets at 5 km range with a 87 % hit probability. The Indian Army’s Mechanised Infantry has inducted the first operational swarm platoon (12 UAVs) in 2024 under the “Integrated Battlefield Management System” (IBMS). The Indian Air Force plans integration with the Netra AEW&C platform for beyond‑visual‑line‑of‑sight (BVLOS) relay. Remaining challenges are spectrum management in contested environments, cyber‑hardening of the mesh protocol, and the development of a formal airworthiness certification for swarm operations under the Directorate General of Aeronautical Quality Assurance (DGAQA).

  • Confusing the KALI‑5000’s 40 GW peak power with average power; the system delivers nanosecond pulses, not continuous megawatt output.
  • Assuming Phase‑II BMD relies solely on the PDV Mk‑II; the AD‑1/AD‑2 endo‑atmospheric interceptors are integral to the layered defence.
  • Believing additive‑manufactured parts are cleared for flight after a single hot‑fire test; full qualification requires CT‑based NDE, mechanical testing per ASTM F3184, and a first‑article inspection report.
  • Thinking the AHWR uses highly enriched uranium; it employs 19.75 % LEU driver fuel in a thorium‑uranium oxide matrix.
  • Assuming swarm drones operate fully autonomously without human approval; current doctrine mandates a human‑on‑the‑loop for weapon release.
  • Overlooking that the indigenous gas‑atomised powder line for Inconel 718 only reached 5 tonnes/year capacity in 2023, not earlier.
  • Mixing the Swordfish LRTR (S‑band) with the MFR (X‑band) roles; Swordfish provides long‑range cueing, MFR delivers terminal guidance.

Space‑Based Laser Inter‑Satellite Links for High‑Throughput Data Relay

India’s push for optical inter‑satellite links (OISL) began with the Laser Communication Terminal (LCT) flown on GSAT‑29 in 2018, demonstrating a 10 Gbps bidirectional link at 1550 nm over a 36 000 km geostationary‑to‑geostationary path. The terminal, developed by the Space Applications Centre (SAC) in collaboration with the Laboratory for Electro‑Optics Systems (LEOS), uses a 15 cm aperture telescope, a coarse‑pointing assembly (CPA) with ±5° field‑of‑regard and a fine‑pointing assembly (FPA) achieving ≤1 µrad jitter. The link budget assumes 1 W average optical power, a receiver sensitivity of –45 dBm and a 0.5 dB margin for atmospheric scintillation at the ground‑station uplink.

The next generation is embedded in the Indian Data Relay Satellite System (IDRSS), a constellation of two GEO satellites (IDRSS‑1A and 1B) slated for launch on GSLV‑Mk III in 2025‑26. Each IDRSS spacecraft carries two LCTs: one for GEO‑GEO cross‑link (up to 1.8 Tbps aggregate using wavelength‑division multiplexing on 16 channels) and one for LEO‑GEO relay to support the Gaganyaan crewed missions and the upcoming Chandrayaan‑4 lunar orbiter. The LEO‑GEO link is designed for 5 Gbps with a 30 cm aperture on the LEO side, enabling real‑time video and telemetry from the crew capsule at 400 km altitude.

On the military side, the Defence Space Agency (DSA) has contracted a ruggedised LCT for the GSAT‑7/7A series, targeting a 20 Gbps secure link between the naval communication satellite and the shore‑based network‑centric warfare grid. The terminal incorporates a radiation‑hardened FPGA‑based forward error correction (FEC) engine (LDPC, rate ½) and an on‑board quantum‑key‑distribution (QKD) module that can exchange 1 Mbps of secret key material during each 10‑minute visibility window.

Key technical challenges remain: (1) acquisition‑tracking‑pointing (ATP) latency under 200 ms for LEO‑GEO handovers, (2) thermal‑induced wavefront error in the 15 cm telescope requiring active optics, and (3) spectrum coordination with the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) for the 1550 nm band, which is shared with terrestrial fiber. The Indian National Space Promotion and Authorization Centre (IN‑SPACe) has issued a draft “Optical Spectrum Allocation Framework” (2023) that reserves 100 GHz blocks for government OISL, with a licensing regime aligned to the forthcoming National Space Legislation.

Operational impact: once IDRSS is declared operational, the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) can retire the aging S‑band TTC ground stations at Byalalu and Lucknow for deep‑space missions, reducing latency from 2 s to <200 ms for telemetry from the Aditya‑L1 solar observatory at L1. The DSA’s Joint Space Operations Centre (JSpOC) will ingest OISL health data into its space‑situational‑awareness (SSA) fusion engine, enabling real‑time collision‑avoidance manoeuvres for the growing LEO constellation (e.g., the 36‑satellite NavIC‑LEO augmentation).

Nuclear Reactor Decommissioning and Site Remediation Technologies

India’s first commercial decommissioning project is the Tarapur Atomic Power Station (TAPS) Units 1 & 2, 160 MWe boiling‑water reactors (BWRs) that entered commercial operation in 1969 and were shut down in 2020 after 51 years. The Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) issued the “Decommissioning Safety Guide” (DSG‑01, Rev. 2, 2021) which mandates a three‑phase approach: (i) post‑operational clean‑out (POCO) – removal of spent fuel, drainage of primary coolant, and de‑contamination of systems to <0.1 Bq/g; (ii) safe‑enclosure (SAFEN) – placement of the reactor pressure vessel (RPV) and internals in a monitored, ventilated enclosure for 30‑50 years to allow decay of short‑lived isotopes (Co‑60, Cs‑137); (iii) final dismantling and site release – segmented cutting of the RPV using diamond‑wire saws, remote‑handled hydraulic shears, and plasma‑arc cutting, followed by radiological survey to the “unrestricted use” criterion of 0.25 mSv/y.

The decommissioning fund, established under the Atomic Energy Act (1962) and financed by a 0.5 % levy on each unit of electricity generated, held ₹1 200 crore for TAPS as of March 2024. The Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL) has contracted a consortium of Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC), Heavy Engineering Corporation (HEC) and a private‑sector robotics firm to develop a remotely operated vehicle (ROV) equipped with a 3‑D laser scanner and a gamma‑spectrometer for in‑situ mapping of activation levels inside the RPV. The ROV demonstrated a 95 % coverage of the vessel interior during a 2023 mock‑up trial at the Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR) mock‑up facility.

For the Pressurised Heavy Water Reactor (PHWR) fleet, the Rajasthan Atomic Power Station (RAPS) Units 1 & 2 (220 MWe each) are slated for POCO by 2028. PHWR decommissioning presents unique challenges: the calandria tubes (Zr‑2.5%Nb) and the heavy‑water moderator (D₂O) require separate recovery loops. The Heavy Water Board (HWB) has commissioned a 500 kg/day D₂O re‑purification plant at Kota, using catalytic isotopic exchange (CIEX) followed by vacuum distillation, achieving >99.98 % isotopic purity for reuse in operating reactors.

Site remediation technologies under development include: (a) in‑situ vitrification of contaminated soil using a 2 MW induction heater, tested at the Kalpakkam test‑bed in 2022 with a 90 % reduction in Cs‑137 leachability; (b) phytoremediation trials using Brassica juncea (Indian mustard) on low‑level waste (LLW) plots at Narora, showing a bio‑accumulation factor of 12 for Sr‑90; (c) a decision‑support system (DSS) integrating GIS layers, groundwater flow modelling (MODFLOW) and probabilistic dose assessment (PC‑CREAM) to optimise the final end‑state (greenfield vs. brownfield). The AERB’s “Site Release Criteria” (SRC‑2022) require a cumulative dose <0.1 mSv/y for the critical group, verified by an independent third‑party audit.

Examiner's trap
A question states: “The decommissioning fund for Indian NPPs is financed by a 1 % levy on electricity generation and is managed by the Department of Atomic Energy.” Identify the two factual errors.
The levy is 0.5 % (not 1 %) of the gross electricity revenue, as stipulated in the Atomic Energy Act amendment of 2005.
