Nuclear Reactor Coolant Chemistry Control: Advanced Water Chemistry for PHWRs and Fast Reactors

Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors (PHWRs) operate with heavy water (D₂O) as both coolant and moderator. The primary chemistry objective is to minimise corrosion of zirconium‑alloy pressure tubes and steam generator tubes while suppressing radiolytic decomposition of D₂O. The current “Advanced Heavy Water Chemistry” (AHWC) regime maintains a dissolved deuterium (D₂) concentration of 2–3 mg/kg to scavenge oxidising radiolytic species (D₂O₂, O₂) and keeps the pD (deuterium‑equivalent pH) at 10.5 ± 0.2 using lithium‑7 deuteroxide (⁷LiOD) as the alkalising agent. Zinc injection (as Zn(D₂O)₂) at 5–10 µg/kg further reduces cobalt‑60 deposition on out‑of‑core surfaces, lowering radiation fields during maintenance.

Fast reactors, exemplified by the Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) at Kalpakkam, use liquid sodium as coolant. Sodium chemistry control focuses on oxygen and hydrogen impurity management. The target dissolved oxygen concentration is ≤ 2 ppm (by weight) to avoid sodium oxide (Na₂O) precipitation that can plug narrow fuel‑assembly flow channels. A cold‑trap system, operating at 120–150 °C, continuously removes oxygen by forming Na₂O on a packed‑bed of nickel‑based getter material. Hydrogen is controlled at 0.5–1 ppm to prevent sodium hydride formation; a hot‑trap at 300 °C removes excess hydrogen via reaction with a zirconium getter.

Both reactor types employ on‑line monitoring: PHWRs use a suite of conductivity, pD, and dissolved deuterium analysers sampling the primary heat transport (PHT) loop every 15 minutes. PFBR deploys electrochemical oxygen meters (based on yttria‑stabilised zirconia sensors) and plugging‑meter hydrogen detectors in the sodium purification circuit. Data feed into the plant’s Distributed Control System (DCS) where automated set‑point adjustments trigger deuterium or zinc dosing pumps (PHWR) or cold‑trap regeneration cycles (PFBR).

Recent advances include the deployment of “hydrogen water chemistry” (HWC) in the 700 MWe PHWRs at Kakrapar (KAPP‑3/4). HWC raises the dissolved hydrogen (H₂) level in the light‑water secondary side to 30–50 cc/kg, suppressing intergranular stress corrosion cracking (IGSCC) of stainless‑steel steam generator tubing. The transition from conventional oxygenated water chemistry to HWC required a licensing amendment from the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) and a comprehensive probabilistic safety assessment (PSA) demonstrating a net reduction in core damage frequency.

For the upcoming Commercial Fast Reactor (CFR‑600) fleet, a “sodium‑bonded fuel” design demands even tighter oxygen control (≤ 1 ppm) to preserve fuel‑cladding chemical interaction (FCCI) margins. BARC’s Sodium Chemistry Division is qualifying a next‑generation cold‑trap using a nanostructured nickel‑titanium alloy getter that offers a 3× higher oxygen capacity per unit volume, reducing trap size and regeneration frequency. The design is slated for demonstration in the PFBR’s secondary sodium loop during the 2025‑26 refuelling outage.

Examiner's trap: conflating coolant chemistry strategies across reactor types
A question asks: “Which of the following statements about coolant chemistry control in Indian nuclear reactors is correct? (a) PHWRs use cold‑traps to control dissolved oxygen in heavy water. (b) PFBR maintains a dissolved deuterium concentration of 2–3 mg/kg in sodium. (c) The AHWC regime in PHWRs employs lithium‑7 deuteroxide for pD control and zinc injection for cobalt‑60 mitigation. (d) Fast reactors use hydrogen water chemistry on the secondary side to prevent IGSCC.”
Correct answer: (c). PHWRs indeed use the Advanced Heavy Water Chemistry (AHWC) regime with ⁷LiOD for pD control and zinc injection to reduce cobalt‑60 deposition. Cold‑traps are a sodium‑coolant feature (PFBR), not used in heavy‑water systems. Dissolved deuterium control applies to PHWR primary coolant, not sodium. Hydrogen water chemistry is applied to the light‑water secondary side of PHWRs, not to fast‑reactor sodium loops.
Exam‑day strategy
Memorise the three key chemistry parameters for each reactor type: PHWR – D₂ (2–3 mg/kg), pD (10.5 ± 0.2), Zn (5–10 µg/kg); PFBR – O₂ (≤ 2 ppm), H₂ (0.5–1 ppm), cold‑trap temperature (120–150 °C). A quick table in your notes lets you eliminate cross‑reactor distractors in seconds.

Indigenous High‑Power Microwave Weapon Programme: DRDO’s HPM Development and Platform Integration

The Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) has pursued high‑power microwave (HPM) weapons since the late 1990s under the “KALI” (Kilo Ampere Linear Injector) series at the Centre for High Energy Systems and Sciences (CHESS), Hyderabad. KALI‑2000, commissioned in 2001, generated 200 kV, 20 kA electron beams producing S‑band microwave pulses of 1 GW peak power with a pulse width of 100 ns. The subsequent KALI‑5000 (2008) scaled to 500 kV, 50 kA, delivering 5 GW peak power in L‑band, establishing a testbed for component hardening and effects evaluation.

HPM weaponisation requires transitioning from laboratory pulsed‑power drivers to compact, ruggedised sources suitable for airborne or ground‑based platforms. DRDO’s “Microwave Weapon System (MWS)” programme, initiated in 2015, focuses on a solid‑state, relativistic magnetron driven by a Marx‑generator‑based pulsed‑power module. The target specification: 3 GW peak power at 3 GHz (S‑band), pulse repetition frequency (PRF) of 100 Hz, and a total system weight under 500 kg for integration on a modified Su‑30MKI hardpoint. The magnetron uses a cathode‑emission‑enhanced dispenser cathode and a mode‑selective cavity to suppress parasitic modes, achieving > 70 % electronic efficiency in bench tests.

Platform integration studies address antenna design, beam‑forming, and platform‑generated electromagnetic interference (EMI). A conformal phased‑array antenna (16 × 16 elements) with GaN‑based high‑electron‑mobility transistors (HEMTs) provides electronic beam steering ± 30° in azimuth and elevation, enabling target engagement without mechanical gimbal. The array’s radiated field is shaped to produce a narrow main‑lobe (~3°) for standoff engagement of electronic systems at ranges up to 5 km. EMI mitigation includes a Faraday‑cage enclosure for the pulsed‑power module and common‑mode choke filters on all power‑bus lines.

Effects testing follows the “HPM Susceptibility Assessment Protocol” (HSAP) defined by the Defence Institute of Advanced Technology (DIAT). Representative targets — avionics suites, radar front‑ends, communication transceivers — are exposed in an anechoic chamber to calibrated HPM pulses. Test metrics include upset threshold (field strength causing bit‑flips), latch‑up current, and permanent damage (junction burnout). Results from 2022‑23 campaigns indicate that modern COTS‑based mission computers exhibit upset at 10 kV/m, while hardened MIL‑STD‑461F compliant units withstand up to 50 kV/m, guiding the required on‑target field strength for operational effectiveness.

The programme’s roadmap envisions a “HPM Pod” for the Light Combat Aircraft (LCA) Tejas Mk‑2 by 2028, leveraging the same GaN array technology developed for the Uttam AESA radar. A parallel effort explores a ground‑based “Area Denial HPM System” mounted on a 8 × 8 high‑mobility vehicle, intended for protection of forward airbases against swarm UAVs. Both systems will be governed by the Defence AI Ethics Framework’s human‑in‑the‑loop requirement for directed‑energy engagements.

Autonomous Satellite Servicing and On‑Orbit Assembly: SpaDeX Follow‑On Missions and International Cooperation

ISRO’s Space Docking Experiment (SpaDeX), launched in December 2024, demonstrated autonomous rendezvous, proximity operations, and hard‑capture docking between two 400 kg class satellites (Chaser and Target) in a 450 km circular orbit. The mission validated a six‑degree‑of‑freedom (6‑DOF) relative navigation suite comprising a laser rangefinder, a vision‑based sensor (VBS) with a 1 MP CMOS imager, and a differential GPS receiver. The docking mechanism used a gender‑neutral, androgynous interface compliant with the International Docking System Standard (IDSS) Rev. C, enabling future interoperability with international vehicles.

The follow‑on programme, “SpaDeX‑2”, approved by the Space Commission in 2023, aims to extend capabilities to on‑orbit servicing (OOS) tasks: propellant transfer, payload exchange, and structural assembly. SpaDeX‑2 will employ a 1 500 kg chaser equipped with a robotic manipulator (7‑DOF, force‑torque sensing) developed by the Laboratory for Electro‑Optics Systems (LEOS). The manipulator’s end‑effector incorporates a standardised “Grapple Fixture” compatible with the IDSS berthing ring, allowing capture of non‑cooperative client satellites. A dedicated “Propellant Transfer Module” (PTM) will demonstrate cryogenic (LOX/LH₂) and storable (MMH/N₂O₄) fluid transfer using a pressure‑driven, zero‑leak quick‑disconnect coupling qualified for micro‑gravity.

On‑orbit assembly demonstrations will focus on constructing a 3‑meter truss segment from modular “building‑block” units launched as secondary payloads. The chaser’s manipulator, guided by a visual‑servoing algorithm trained on synthetic imagery, will perform bolt‑driving and latch‑engagement operations. Telemetry from the assembly sequence will be downlinked via the Indian Data Relay Satellite System (IDRSS) to the Mission Control Centre (MCC) at ISTRAC, where a ground‑in‑the‑loop supervisory console can intervene if autonomy confidence drops below a predefined threshold.

International cooperation is formalised through the “Global On‑Orbit Servicing Forum” (GOOSF), where ISRO participates alongside NASA (OSAM‑1), ESA (ClearSpace‑1), JAXA (CRD2), and commercial entities (Northrop Grumman’s Mission Extension Vehicle). A memorandum of understanding (MoU) signed with NASA in 2022 enables cross‑support of docking interfaces and sharing of relative navigation filter algorithms. Joint simulation campaigns in 2023‑24 validated interoperability of ISRO’s VBS with NASA’s “Relative Navigation Sensor” (RNS) using a common coordinate frame and time reference (GPS‑disciplined).

Regulatory and policy aspects are addressed in the draft National Space Legislation, which defines liability for servicing operations, licensing of servicing vehicles, and debris‑mitigation obligations for client‑satellite disposal. The legislation proposes a “Servicing Authorization Certificate” issued by the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorization Centre (IN‑SPACe) after a safety case review that includes collision‑risk assessment, propellant‑transfer hazard analysis, and end‑of‑life disposal planning. This framework positions India to offer commercial OOS services to foreign operators while safeguarding national security assets.

Defence Cyber Operations Doctrine: Offensive, Defensive and Resilience Frameworks

The Defence Cyber Agency (DCA), raised in September 2019 under the Integrated Defence Staff (IDS), released the “Defence Cyber Operations Doctrine (DCOD)” in March 2022 after extensive tri‑service consultation. The doctrine structures cyber operations into three pillars: Offensive Cyber Operations (OCO), Defensive Cyber Operations (DCO), and Cyber Resilience (CR). Each pillar is governed by a distinct authority chain, rules of engagement (RoE), and capability development roadmap, ensuring alignment with the National Security Council Secretariat (NSCS) directives and the Information Technology Act, 2000 (as amended).

OCO capabilities are developed by the “Cyber Offensive Group” (COG) within DCA, focusing on network exploitation, malware development, and electromagnetic spectrum manipulation to degrade, disrupt, or destroy adversary command‑and‑control (C2) infrastructure. The doctrine mandates that any OCO mission requires a “Cyber Tasking Order” (CTO) approved by the Chief of Defence Staff (CDS) and the National Security Advisor (NSA), with a mandatory legal review by the Judge Advocate General (JAG) branch. Target sets are limited to military‑grade networks, critical logistics nodes, and integrated air‑defence systems; civilian critical infrastructure is excluded unless a declared state of war exists.

DCO is executed by the “Cyber Defence Group” (CDG) operating a 24 × 7 Security Operations Centre (SOC) at the Defence Cyber Operations Centre (DCOC) in New Delhi. The SOC ingests telemetry from the “Defence Network Sensor Grid” (DNSG) — a fabric of host‑based agents, network traffic analysers, and deception honeypots deployed across the three services’ intranets. Detection employs a hybrid signature‑behavioural engine enriched with threat‑intelligence feeds from the National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre (NCIIPC) and allied partners under the “Cyber Information Sharing Agreement” (CISA). Response playbooks follow the “Detect‑Contain‑Eradicate‑Recover” (DCER) cycle, with automated containment actions (e.g., VLAN quarantine, credential revocation) authorised at the SOC tier‑2 level.

Cyber Resilience focuses on “design‑in” security for new weapon systems and legacy platform hardening. The “Secure Software Development Lifecycle (D‑SSDL)” mandates threat modelling, static analysis, and formal verification for all mission‑critical code. Legacy platforms undergo “Cyber Survivability Upgrade Packages” (CSUP) — e.g., the Su‑30MKI’s mission computer received a hardware‑root‑of‑trust (HRoT) module and a measured‑boot chain in 2021. The doctrine also prescribes “Red Team / Blue Team” exercises at the joint‑force level annually, with the “Exercise Cyber Shield” series (2020‑2024) progressively expanding scope from network defence to integrated kinetic‑cyber scenarios.

Capability development is tracked through the “Cyber Capability Maturity Model (C2M2)” adapted from the US DoD framework, with five maturity levels assessed biennially by the Defence Audit Organisation. As of the 2023 assessment, DCA achieved Level 3 (“Defined”) for OCO and DCO, and Level 2 (“Managed”) for CR. The roadmap targets Level 4 (“Quantitatively Managed”) across all pillars by 2027, contingent on induction of indigenous AI‑driven threat‑hunting platforms (under the “Project Shakti” at CAIR) and the operationalisation of a dedicated “Cyber Test Range” at the Defence Electronics Research Laboratory (DLRL), Hyderabad.

  • Confusing the PHWR AHWC regime’s deuterium control with the PFBR’s sodium oxygen control; they address different radiolytic and corrosion mechanisms.
  • Assuming the KALI‑5000 pulsed‑power driver is already weaponised; it remains a laboratory testbed for component hardening.
  • Believing SpaDeX‑2 will perform on‑orbit refuelling of cryogenic propellants without a qualified zero‑leak coupling; the PTM is still in qualification.
  • Thinking the Defence Cyber Operations Doctrine permits offensive actions against civilian critical infrastructure in peacetime; such targets are excluded unless a formal war declaration exists.
  • Mixing the IDSS docking standard used on SpaDeX with the older APAS‑95 interface; they are not mechanically compatible.
  • Overlooking that the GaN‑based phased array for the HPM pod shares the same epitaxial wafer process as the Uttam AESA radar, creating a common supply‑chain dependency.
  • Assuming the National Space Legislation has already been enacted; it remains a draft pending parliamentary approval.

Thorium‑Based Advanced Heavy Water Reactor (AHWR) Development and the Closed Fuel Cycle Roadmap

The Advanced Heavy Water Reactor (AHWR) is a 300 MWe vertical pressure‑tube design conceived by the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) to demonstrate commercial thorium utilisation. Unlike the Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors (PHWRs) that operate on natural uranium, the AHWR core is seeded with low‑enriched uranium (LEU) or plutonium while the bulk of the fuel is thorium‑oxide (ThO₂) mixed with a small fraction of 233U bred in‑situ. The reactor uses heavy water as moderator and light water as coolant, allowing a high neutron economy that converts 232Th to 233U with a conversion ratio above 1.0. The design incorporates passive safety systems — gravity‑driven water injection, passive decay heat removal through natural circulation, and a large water inventory in the calandria vault — eliminating the need for active pumps during a station blackout.

The closed fuel cycle roadmap for the AHWR envisions three stages: (1) irradiation of ThO₂‑LEU seed assemblies in existing PHWRs to generate 233U, (2) reprocessing of spent AHWR fuel in a dedicated thorium‑fuel reprocessing plant (TFRP) using the THOREX solvent‑extraction process, and (3) fabrication of 233U‑ThO₂ fuel pins for subsequent AHWR cores. BARC has commissioned a laboratory‑scale THOREX loop at the Radiometallurgy Division, Tarapur, and demonstrated >99.9 % recovery of 233U with decontamination factors exceeding 10⁴ for fission products. The TFRP design targets a throughput of 0.5 tHM yr⁻¹, sufficient for a fleet of 4–6 AHWR units.

Licensing milestones: the Pre‑Project Safety Report (PPSR) was submitted to the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) in 2015; the Site Evaluation Report for a proposed location at Tarapur (adjacent to the existing PHWR complex) was cleared in 2018. Construction approval awaits the finalisation of the Nuclear Liability Act amendments and the allocation of budgetary support under the 15th Finance Commission. The first concrete pour is projected for 2026‑27, with criticality expected by 2030. Successful operation would validate thorium‑fuel cycle economics, reduce uranium import dependence by an estimated 30 % for a 10 GW(e) AHWR fleet, and provide a proliferation‑resistant pathway because 233U is always denatured with 238U in the fuel matrix.

Key Technical Parameters

  • Thermal power: 920 MWth; Electrical output: 300 MWe (net)
  • Core height: 3.5 m; 452 fuel channels; 12 kg ThO₂ per channel
  • Coolant inlet/outlet temperature: 266 °C / 310 °C (light water)
  • Moderator temperature: 70 °C (heavy water)
  • Target burn‑up: 25 GWd tHM⁻¹ for seed, 15 GWd tHM⁻¹ for thorium blanket

Indigenous Small Satellite Launch Vehicle (SSLV) Programme: Design, Test Flights and Commercial Positioning

The Small Satellite Launch Vehicle (SSLV) is ISRO’s three‑stage, all‑solid‑propellant launcher designed to place up to 500 kg into a 500 km low‑Earth orbit (LEO) or 300 kg into Sun‑synchronous orbit (SSO). The vehicle stands 34 m tall, has a lift‑off mass of 120 t, and uses the S‑85, S‑7 and S‑4 solid motors for the first, second and third stages respectively. A liquid‑propellant Velocity Trimming Module (VTM) based on the Monomethylhydrazine‑Mixed Oxides of Nitrogen (MMH‑MON) system provides precise orbit insertion. The SSLV is assembled vertically in a mobile launch pad, enabling a launch‑campaign duration of less than 72 hours — a key differentiator for responsive space access.

Developmental flights: SSLV‑D1 (7 August 2022) suffered a sensor anomaly in the VTM that caused a loss of attitude control, resulting in the payloads (EOS‑02 and AzaadiSAT) being placed in an elliptical, unstable orbit. The Failure Analysis Committee identified a missing “loss‑of‑signal” detection logic in the onboard computer. SSLV‑D2 (10 February 2023) incorporated the corrected logic, a redesigned VTM thrust‑vector control, and an enhanced telemetry suite; it successfully injected EOS‑07, Janus‑1 and AzaadiSAT‑2 into a 450 km circular orbit. SSLV‑D3 (2024) is slated to demonstrate a commercial multi‑payload mission for a foreign customer, marking the transition from developmental to operational status.

Commercial positioning: Antrix Corporation and NewSpace India Limited (NSIL) have marketed SSLV as a “dedicated ride‑share” alternative to the PSLV’s piggy‑back model. The vehicle’s low per‑kg cost (target ≤ US$ 25,000 kg⁻¹ to LEO) and rapid integration timeline aim to capture the growing small‑sat constellation market (e.g., IoT, Earth‑observation cubesats). NSIL has signed launch service agreements with two international operators for 2025‑26 slots. The SSLV programme also serves as a testbed for solid‑motor scaling technologies that feed into the future Unified Launch Vehicle (ULV) concept.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “Which of the following statements about SSLV‑D1 is correct? (a) It placed its payloads in the intended circular orbit. (b) The failure was due to a solid‑motor malfunction. (c) The anomaly originated in the Velocity Trimming Module’s onboard computer logic. (d) The mission was declared a partial success because one payload separated.”
Correct answer: (c). The Failure Analysis Committee report explicitly attributes the loss of attitude control to a missing loss‑of‑signal detection logic in the VTM’s onboard computer, not to solid‑motor performance. The payloads were inserted into an unstable elliptical orbit and subsequently decayed; no payload achieved the intended orbit.
Exam‑day strategy
Memorise the SSLV developmental flight sequence (D1 failure cause, D2 corrective actions, D3 commercial target) and the three‑stage solid motor designations (S‑85, S‑7, S‑4). Questions often test the distinction between the VTM’s liquid propulsion and the solid stages, and the payload mass differences between LEO and SSO.

Autonomous Swarm Drone Architecture for Network‑Centric Warfare: DRDO’s SWiFT, NETRA and the Indigenous AI Stack

The Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) has pursued a layered approach to autonomous swarm capability, combining platform development, communication middleware, and an artificial‑intelligence (AI) decision‑making stack. The Stealth Wing Flying Testbed (SWiFT) — a sub‑scale, low‑observable flying‑wing UCAV demonstrator — completed its maiden autonomous flight in July 2022 at the Aeronautical Test Range, Chitradurga. SWiFT validates autonomous take‑off, waypoint navigation, and recovery using an onboard flight‑control computer running the “AutoPilot‑X” real‑time operating system developed by the Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Robotics (CAIR).

In parallel, the NETRA (Network‑Enabled Tactical Reconnaissance Aircraft) family — NETRA‑1 (fixed‑wing) and NETRA‑2 (VTOL) — provides persistent ISR with electro‑optical/infrared (EO/IR) and synthetic‑aperture radar (SAR) payloads. NETRA platforms have been integrated into the Army’s “Integrated Battlefield Management System” (IBMS) via the “Tactical Data Link‑India” (TDL‑I) waveform, enabling beyond‑line‑of‑sight (BLOS) connectivity through the GSAT‑6/6A satellites.

The swarm layer is orchestrated by the “Multi‑Agent Collaborative Engagement” (MACE) framework, which implements a decentralized consensus algorithm (based on the Raft protocol) for task allocation, collision avoidance, and dynamic re‑planning. In a 2021 demonstration at the Pokhran Field Firing Range, the Indian Army operated a heterogeneous swarm of 75 indigenous quad‑rotor drones (developed by the Defence Electronics Research Laboratory, DLRL) that executed a coordinated area‑search, target‑identification, and simulated strike mission under a single commander’s intent. The AI stack includes a convolutional neural network (CNN) for real‑time target classification (trained on the “Bharat‑DRDO” dataset of 1.2 million labelled images) and a reinforcement‑learning module for adaptive formation keeping under GPS‑denied conditions.

Key technical challenges addressed: (1) secure, low‑latency mesh networking using frequency‑hopping spread spectrum (FHSS) radios with AES‑256 encryption; (2) power management for 30‑minute endurance on 2 kg platforms — solved by high‑energy‑density Li‑S cells (350 Wh kg⁻¹) developed by the High Energy Materials Research Laboratory (HEMRL); (3) regulatory compliance with the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) “Unmanned Aircraft System Rules, 2021” for beyond‑visual‑line‑of‑sight (BVLOS) operations in segregated airspace.

Swarm Architecture Layers

  • Platform layer: SWiFT (UCAV), NETRA‑1/2 (ISR), DLRL quad‑rotors (tactical)
  • Communication layer: TDL‑I, FHSS mesh, SATCOM backhaul via GSAT‑6/6A
  • Autonomy layer: AutoPilot‑X, MACE consensus, CNN target classifier, RL formation controller
  • Decision‑support layer: IBMS integration, commander‑intent parsing, rules‑of‑engagement engine

Quantum‑Resistant Cryptography Migration for Strategic Communication Networks: NIST Standards, Indian Implementation Timeline and Key Management

The advent of cryptographically relevant quantum computers (CRQCs) threatens the asymmetric primitives — RSA, ECC, DH — that underpin India’s strategic communication infrastructure, including the Defence Communication Network (DCN), the Naval Satellite Link (NSL), and the Air Force’s Secure Voice‑Data Network (SVDN). The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) concluded its Post‑Quantum Cryptography (PQC) standardisation process in 2024, selecting CRYSTALS‑Kyber (KEM), CRYSTALS‑Dilithium (signature), and SPHINCS+ (hash‑based signature) as primary algorithms, with Falcon and Classic McEliece as alternates.

India’s migration roadmap, coordinated by the National Security Council Secretariat (NSCS) and the National Technical Research Organisation (NTRO), adopts a “hybrid‑first” approach: existing TLS 1.3 and IPsec sessions will negotiate both a classical (X25519) and a PQC (Kyber‑768) key‑exchange, deriving a combined session key via a KDF. This ensures backward compatibility while providing quantum‑resistant forward secrecy. The Defence Information Assurance and Research Agency (DIARA) has mandated that all new procurement of cryptographic modules (Hardware Security Modules, inline network encryptors) must support at least one NIST‑approved PQC algorithm by FY 2025‑26.

Key management infrastructure upgrades: the existing “Key Management System‑India” (KMS‑I) — a hierarchical PKI rooted in the “Root Certifying Authority of India” (RCAI) — is being extended with a “PQC‑Ready Certificate Profile” that includes algorithm identifiers for Dilithium‑3 and Kyber‑768. Certificate lifetimes are reduced to 90 days for tactical nodes to limit exposure. The “Quantum‑Safe Key Distribution” (QSKD) pilot, launched in 2023 between the Delhi and Bengaluru DCN nodes, combines Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) over a dedicated dark‑fibre link with PQC‑based key encapsulation for the metropolitan segment, demonstrating a composite security model.

Timeline milestones: (1) FY 2024‑25 — completion of PQC algorithm validation on indigenous HSMs (developed by the Society for Electronic Transactions and Security, SETS); (2) FY 2025‑26 — mandatory hybrid TLS/IPsec deployment on all strategic gateways; (3) FY 2027‑28 — full deprecation of RSA‑2048 and ECC‑P‑256 for classified traffic; (4) FY 2030 — attainment of “Quantum‑Resilient” certification for the entire DCN as per the “National Cyber Security Strategy 2023” framework.

Indigenous Development of Radar Absorbing Materials (RAM) and Structural Stealth Technologies for Fighter Aircraft

Reducing the radar cross‑section (RCS) of frontline fighters is a force‑multiplier for survivability in contested airspace. The Defence Metallurgical Research Laboratory (DMRL), Hyderabad, leads the indigenous RAM programme, delivering three generations of absorbers tailored for the Light Combat Aircraft (LCA) Tejas Mk‑1A, the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA) and the Su‑30MKI upgrade.

First‑generation ferrite‑based RAM tiles (Fe‑Ni‑Zn composition) were qualified for the Tejas inlet duct and engine bay in 2016. They provide > 15 dB reduction in the 8‑12 GHz (X‑band) with a thickness of 3 mm and areal density of 1.2 kg m⁻². Second‑generation “graded‑impedance” RAM uses a multilayer stack of carbon‑loaded polyurethane foam and conductive polymer sheets, achieving broadband attenuation (2‑18 GHz) of 20‑25 dB at 5 mm thickness. This variant has been integrated into the AMCA’s leading‑edge and weapon‑bay doors during the Critical Design Review (CDR) phase (2022).

Third‑generation structural stealth employs “conductive carbon‑carbon (C‑C) composite skins” where the laminate itself acts as a resonant absorber. DMRL, in collaboration with the Gas Turbine Research Establishment (GTRE), has developed a C‑C preform infiltrated with a silicon‑carbide (SiC) matrix doped with nano‑ferrite particles. Coupon tests at the Radar Cross‑Section Measurement Facility (RCSMF), Kolar, demonstrate > 30 dB RCS reduction across 6‑40 GHz while retaining structural load‑bearing capability (tensile strength > 350 MPa). The material is slated for the AMCA’s internal weapon‑bay bulkheads and the Su‑30MKI’s conformal fuel‑tank fairings under the “Super Sukhoi” modernisation.

Manufacturing scale‑up: a dedicated RAM production line at the Ordnance Factory, Medak, commissioned in 2021, produces 2 000 m² yr⁻¹ of ferrite tiles. The graded‑impedance foam line at the Defence Materials and Stores Research and Development Establishment (DMSRDE), Kanpur, achieved a 500 m² yr⁻¹ capacity in 2023. The C‑C composite facility at the Advanced Composites Division, HAL, Bengaluru, is undergoing qualification for autoclave‑free resin‑transfer moulding (RTM) to meet the AMCA’s 2028 first‑flight target.
