  • Confusing the NNFL's pre‑detonation forensics capability with post‑detonation fallout analysis; India currently lacks a dedicated rapid‑deployment radiochemical lab for the latter.

Advanced Heavy Water Reactor: Thorium Fuel Cycle, Demonstration Reactor and Deployment Roadmap

The Advanced Heavy Water Reactor (AHWR) is a 300 MWe vertical pressure‑tube type reactor designed by the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) to demonstrate the commercial viability of the thorium‑uranium‑233 fuel cycle. The core uses a heterogeneous lattice: a driver fuel of 19.75 % low‑enriched uranium dioxide (LEU‑UO₂) surrounded by a blanket of natural thorium dioxide (ThO₂). Only the blanket breeds 233U, which is subsequently recycled as fissile material in later fuel cycles, closing the thorium loop. The reactor operates at a coolant outlet temperature of 310 °C, using heavy water as both moderator and coolant, and incorporates passive safety systems — gravity‑driven water pools, natural‑circulation decay‑heat removal, and a large‑volume containment — that meet Generation‑III+ safety goals without active pumps.

The AHWR design was finalised in 2014 and received the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) design safety clearance in 2017. A technology demonstration unit (AHWR‑TD) is planned at the Tarapur site, with construction expected to begin after the completion of the Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) commissioning at Kalpakkam. The Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) has indicated a target of first criticality for the AHWR‑TD by the early 2030s, followed by a 5‑year operational campaign to validate fuel performance, online refuelling, and thorium‑blanket irradiation behaviour. Successful demonstration would enable the deployment of commercial AHWR‑300 units at multiple sites, leveraging India’s vast thorium reserves (≈ 846 kt Th) and reducing dependence on imported uranium.

Key technical challenges include the development of high‑burnup thorium‑based fuel pins capable of achieving > 70 GWd/tHM, qualification of the 233U‑recovery reprocessing flow‑sheet at the Integrated Nuclear Recycle Plant (INRP) at Tarapur, and the establishment of a dedicated fuel fabrication line for (Th,U)O₂ mixed‑oxide pellets. The DAE has initiated a coordinated programme involving the Nuclear Fuel Complex (NFC), the Radiometallurgy Division of BARC, and the Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR) to address these issues. The AHWR also serves as a test‑bed for advanced structural materials such as Zr‑2.5 %Nb pressure tubes and for the integration of hydrogen‑production modules using high‑temperature steam electrolysis (HTSE) coupled to the reactor’s secondary circuit.

From a strategic perspective, the AHWR aligns with India’s three‑stage nuclear power programme articulated by Homi Bhabha: Stage 1 (PHWRs using natural uranium), Stage 2 (Fast Breeder Reactors breeding plutonium), and Stage 3 (Thorium‑based reactors using 233U). The successful commercialisation of the AHWR would mark the transition to Stage 3, providing a near‑inexhaustible fuel base and enhancing energy security. The roadmap envisions a fleet of 10‑12 AHWR‑300 units by 2050, contributing roughly 3‑4 GW of baseload capacity and supporting the national target of 22 GW nuclear capacity by 2031.

Future Ready Combat Vehicle Programme: Spiral Development, Private Lead Integrator and Commonality Drive

The Future Ready Combat Vehicle (FRCV) programme, launched by the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) in 2022, aims to replace the Indian Army’s T‑72 and T‑90 main battle tank fleets from the 2030s onward. Unlike the Arjun MBT programme, which was DRDO‑led with limited industry participation, the FRCV adopts a “spiral development” model with a private‑industry lead integrator — Larsen & Toubro (L&T), Tata Advanced Systems, or Mahindra Defence — while the Combat Vehicles Research and Development Establishment (CVRDE) acts as technology partner. The Expression of Interest (EoI) issued in March 2023 specifies a 1,500‑1,800 hp indigenous DATRAN engine family, an unmanned turret with autoloader enabling a three‑man crew, modular composite armour with active protection system (APS) integration, AI‑enabled situational awareness, and full network‑centric warfare compatibility.

The spiral timeline sets a Technology Demonstrator (TD) by 2028, a Prototype Vehicle (PV) by 2031, and series production from 2035. Each spiral incorporates incremental capability insertions: Spiral‑1 validates the power‑pack, suspension, and baseline fire‑control; Spiral‑2 adds the unmanned turret, APS, and sensor fusion; Spiral‑3 integrates the AI decision‑support suite and manned‑unmanned teaming (MUM‑T) interfaces. The commonality drive extends beyond the FRCV: the Wheeled Armoured Platform (WhAP) 8×8, developed jointly by CVRDE and Tata, shares the DATRAN 1,000 hp engine, transmission, and track‑system components, reducing logistics footprint across tracked and wheeled fleets. An amphibious WhAP variant has been cleared for riverine operations, and limited production has commenced for mechanised infantry and United Nations peacekeeping roles.

Critical subsystems under indigenous development include the DATRAN 1,500 hp turbo‑charged diesel engine (in partnership with BEML), a 120 mm smoothbore gun with electro‑thermal chemical (ETC) ignition for higher muzzle energy, and a multispectral panoramic sight fused with millimetre‑wave radar for APS cueing. The programme also leverages the Defence Acquisition Procedure (DAP) 2023 amendments that raise the indigenous content threshold to 60 % for “Buy (Indian‑IDDM)” categories and introduce offset‑credit reforms favouring technology transfer to the private lead integrator. The FRCV’s acquisition strategy thus shifts procurement risk and intellectual‑property ownership to industry, a structural change intended to accelerate delivery timelines and foster a sustainable defence‑industrial ecosystem.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “Which of the following statements about the FRCV programme is correct? (a) It is a DRDO‑led programme with no private‑industry lead integrator. (b) The Technology Demonstrator is scheduled for 2028 and series production from 2035. (c) The FRCV will use the same MTU engine as the Arjun Mk‑1. (d) The programme does not mandate an active protection system.”
Correct answer: (b). The FRCV adopts a private‑industry lead integrator model (unlike the Arjun), targets a TD by 2028 and series production from 2035, fields the indigenous DATRAN engine (not the MTU), and explicitly requires APS integration as per the 2023 EoI.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question compares two indigenous programmes (e.g., Arjun vs. FRCV), focus on the procurement model (DRDO‑led vs. private lead integrator), engine lineage (MTU vs. DATRAN), and spiral‑development milestones. These three discriminators appear repeatedly in UPSC GS‑III and defence‑specific papers.

Dual‑Use Technology Governance: Civil‑Military Integration Framework for Space and Nuclear Sectors

India’s dual‑use technology governance rests on the Strategic Commodities and Technologies Export Control (SCOMET) list, administered by the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) under the Foreign Trade (Development & Regulation) Act, 1992. The list is periodically updated to reflect multilateral regime commitments — Wassenaar Arrangement (WA), Missile Technology Control Regime (MTCR), Australia Group (AG), and Nuclear Suppliers Group (NSG) — and to capture emerging domains such as artificial intelligence, quantum computing, and synthetic biology. The 2022 amendment added 23 entries covering AI training algorithms with potential military decision‑support applications, quantum key distribution (QKD) hardware, and gene‑editing toolkits (CRISPR‑Cas9) that could be weaponised. Compliance is enforced through end‑use certificates (EUCs), post‑shipment verification (PSV) visits, and a risk‑based licensing framework that classifies applicants into “trusted” and “non‑trusted” categories based on past adherence.

At the institutional level, the National Security Council Secretariat (NSCS) chairs the Dual‑Use Technology Coordination Committee (DUTCC), which includes representatives from the Department of Space (DoS), Department of Atomic Energy (DAE), DRDO, Ministry of Defence (MoD), and the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY). The DUTCC meets quarterly to review technology‑transfer requests, assess proliferation risk, and recommend “controlled” or “monitored” classification for new R&D outputs. A notable mechanism is the “Technology Readiness Level (TRL) gating” policy: any project crossing TRL 6 (system/subsystem demonstration in relevant environment) must undergo a mandatory dual‑use screening before further funding or foreign collaboration is approved.

In the space sector, the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN‑SPACe) acts as the single‑window authorisation body for non‑governmental entities (NGEs). IN‑SPACe’s licensing framework incorporates a dual‑use annex that requires applicants to declare any payload or subsystem with potential military utility — e.g., high‑resolution optical imagers (< 0.5 m GSD), synthetic aperture radar (SAR) with sub‑meter resolution, or on‑board signal‑intelligence (SIGINT) processors. The annex is cross‑referenced with the SCOMET list, and any positive declaration triggers a referral to the DUTCC. For nuclear technologies, the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) and the DAE’s Nuclear Controls and Planning Wing (NCPW) jointly evaluate proposals involving enrichment, reprocessing, or advanced fuel‑cycle R&D for dual‑use implications, especially concerning the potential diversion of 233U or plutonium streams.

Recent case studies illustrate the framework’s operation: the 2023 export licence for a quantum‑random‑number‑generator (QRNG) chip to a European research consortium was granted after a DUTCC review confirmed the device’s TRL 5 status and absence of cryptographic‑key‑generation capability beyond 256 bits. Conversely, a 2024 request to transfer a high‑power fibre‑laser (2 kW continuous wave) to a Southeast Asian university was denied because the laser’s beam‑quality parameters matched the SCOMET threshold for directed‑energy‑weapon (DEW) subsystems. These decisions demonstrate the calibrated approach — enabling legitimate scientific exchange while preventing leakage of strategic capabilities.

Space‑Based Laser Communication Terminals: High‑Throughput Optical Links for Strategic Satellites

The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) has been developing free‑space optical communication (FSOC) terminals since the early 2010s to overcome the bandwidth and spectrum‑congestion limits of radio‑frequency (RF) links. The first on‑orbit demonstration flew on GSAT‑29 (launched 14 November 2018) carrying a Laser Communication Terminal (LCT) operating at 1550 nm with a 10 Gbps bidirectional data rate. The terminal, built by the Laboratory for Electro‑Optics Systems (LEOS), uses a 135 mm aperture telescope, a coarse‑pointing assembly (CPA) with ±5° field of regard, and a fine‑pointing assembly (FPA) achieving < 2 µrad jitter. The link was established between GSAT‑29 in geostationary orbit and the Optical Ground Station (OGS) at the Space Applications Centre (SAC), Ahmedabad, demonstrating acquisition, tracking, and pointing (ATP) under varying atmospheric turbulence conditions.

Building on this heritage, ISRO’s next‑generation LCT — designated LCT‑2 — targets 100 Gbps per channel using wavelength‑division multiplexing (WDM) across four 25 Gbps lanes. The terminal incorporates a monolithic integrated photonics transceiver fabricated at the Semi‑Conductor Laboratory (SCL), Chandigarh, and a deformable‑mirror adaptive optics (AO) subsystem to compensate for wavefront distortion during low‑elevation passes. LCT‑2 is slated for flight on the GSAT‑30 series (planned 2025‑26) and on the upcoming Indian Data Relay Satellite System (IDRSS) constellation, which will provide continuous high‑rate connectivity for low‑earth‑orbit (LEO) remote‑sensing satellites and the Gaganyaan crewed missions.

Strategic implications are significant. Optical links offer inherent low‑probability‑of‑intercept (LPI) and low‑probability‑of‑detection (LPD) characteristics, making them attractive for secure military communications, space‑based electronic intelligence (ELINT) data downlink, and command‑and‑control (C2) of strategic assets. The Defence Space Agency (DSA) has identified FSOC as a critical enabler for the Joint Space Operations Centre (JSpOC) to achieve real‑time sensor‑to‑shooter latency < 1 second across the Indian Ocean Region (IOR). To this end, a joint ISRO‑DRDO programme — “Project Tejas” — is developing a ruggedised, radiation‑hardened LCT variant (LCT‑M) with a 200 Gbps aggregate throughput, compatible with the I‑6K satellite bus and the future Geo‑Imaging Satellite (GISAT) series.

Key technical hurdles remain: atmospheric attenuation during monsoon clouds (optical depth > 3), pointing‑acquisition time < 30 seconds for LEO‑to‑GEO links, and qualification of space‑qualified erbium‑doped fibre amplifiers (EDFAs) for > 15 years mission life. ISRO’s ongoing ground‑test campaign at the OGS network (Ahmedabad, Shillong, Port Blair) uses site‑diversity and adaptive coding and modulation (ACM) to mitigate weather outages, targeting > 99.9 % link availability for operational services by 2028.

  • Confusing the AHWR’s thorium blanket with the driver fuel; the blanket is natural ThO₂, while the driver is 19.75 % LEU — only the blanket breeds 233U.
  • Assuming the FRCV programme is DRDO‑led like the Arjun; it mandates a private‑industry lead integrator, shifting procurement risk and IP ownership.
  • Believing dual‑use screening applies only to export licences; the TRL‑gating policy requires mandatory screening at TRL 6 for all domestic R&D projects before further funding.
  • Thinking space‑based laser terminals are immune to weather; monsoon clouds cause severe attenuation, requiring site‑diversity and ACM for operational availability.
  • Overlooking that the DATRAN engine family is common across FRCV and WhAP platforms; this commonality drive is a deliberate logistics‑footprint reduction measure.
  • Assuming the SCOMET list is static; it is dynamically updated to include AI, quantum, and biotechnology entries, with the 2022 amendment adding 23 new controls.
  • Confusing the LCT‑M military variant with the civilian LCT‑2; LCT‑M incorporates radiation‑hardened components and higher throughput for strategic C2.

The advanced sections above integrate technical depth with policy context, equipping aspirants to tackle both factual and analytical questions in the examination.

Thorium Fuel Cycle and the Advanced Heavy Water Reactor (AHWR) Development

India’s three‑stage nuclear programme positions thorium as the ultimate fissile resource because the country holds roughly 25 % of the world’s known thorium reserves, principally in monazite sands along the coastal belts of Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Kerala. The first stage (PHWRs) produces plutonium, the second stage (fast breeder reactors) breeds 233U from thorium, and the third stage deploys thorium‑based reactors that fission 233U. The Advanced Heavy Water Reactor (AHWR) is the flagship third‑stage demonstrator: a 300 MWe vertical pressure‑tube reactor cooled by boiling light water and moderated by heavy water. Its core uses a low‑enriched uranium (LEU) driver (19.75 % 235U) surrounded by a thorium oxide blanket that breeds 233U in‑situ. The design incorporates passive safety systems — gravity‑driven emergency core cooling, a large water inventory in the calandria vault, and a passive containment cooling system — eliminating the need for active pumps during a station blackout.

Design work began in the early 2000s at the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) with the conceptual design report completed in 2004. The detailed design phase (2008‑2015) produced a safety analysis report that was reviewed by the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) and cleared in 2016. Site selection studies identified Tarapur (Maharashtra) as the preferred location because of existing infrastructure, proximity to the coast for seawater cooling, and an established emergency planning zone. In 2023 the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) accorded “in‑principle” approval for construction, and site‑preparation activities — land acquisition, environmental clearance, and access‑road upgrades — commenced in early 2024. The first concrete pour is targeted for 2026, with criticality expected around 2030.

Key technical milestones include the qualification of the thorium‑oxide blanket fuel pins (irradiated in the Fast Breeder Test Reactor at Kalpakkam up to 70 GWd/t), the development of a high‑temperature steam‑generator tube material (Alloy 800) compatible with boiling light‑water conditions, and the validation of the passive decay‑heat removal system through integral tests at the Thermal‑Hydraulic Test Facility (THTF) in Trombay. The AHWR also serves as a test‑bed for advanced instrumentation: fibre‑optic temperature sensors, neutron‑flux monitors based on 10B‑lined proportional counters, and a digital twin platform for real‑time safety margin monitoring.

Strategically, the AHWR demonstrates the feasibility of a near‑breeder thorium cycle that can be deployed without the high‑enrichment infrastructure required for conventional fast reactors. It also provides a pathway to reduce the long‑term radiotoxicity of spent fuel because the 233U‑thorium cycle generates fewer minor actinides. The reactor’s design data are being shared with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) under the Thorium Fuel Cycle Technical Working Group, positioning India as a technology provider for countries exploring thorium‑based power.

Integrated Battlefield Management System (IBMS) and Network‑Centric Warfare Architecture

The Integrated Battlefield Management System (IBMS) is the Indian Army’s flagship programme to realise network‑centric operations (NCO) across the tactical, operational and strategic levels. Conceived under the aegis of the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) and executed by the Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Robotics (CAIR) in collaboration with Bharat Electronics Limited (BEL), IBMS integrates heterogeneous sensor feeds — ground‑based radars (e.g., Swathi, Rajendra), electro‑optical platforms (UAVs, handheld thermal imagers), space‑based assets (RISAT, Cartosat, GSAT‑7/7A) and signals‑intelligence (SIGINT) nodes — into a common operational picture (COP) displayed on ruggedised command‑post terminals and soldier‑worn devices.

The architecture follows a four‑layer model: (1) Sensor Layer — multi‑domain sensors with standardized NATO‑STANAG‑4586 compliant interfaces; (2) Communication Layer — a hybrid backbone combining software‑defined radios (SDR) operating in VHF/UHF/L‑band, tactical SATCOM terminals (Ku/Ka‑band) and the Army’s Wide‑Area Network (WAN) built on MPLS‑over‑fibre and microwave hops; (3) Processing & Fusion Layer — a distributed cloud‑edge compute fabric running the “Shakti” data‑fusion engine, which employs Kalman‑filter tracking, multi‑hypothesis association, and AI‑based threat classification (trained on a curated dataset of 1.2 million labelled radar/IR signatures); (4) Decision & Effector Layer — a command‑and‑control (C2) suite that supports collaborative planning, automated fire‑control solutions for artillery (K9 Vajra, Pinaka) and air‑defence (Akash‑NG, QRSAM), and real‑time tasking of loitering munitions (e.g., Nag‑ML, ALFA‑S).

Field trials conducted in 2022‑2024 at the Mahajan Field Firing Range (Rajasthan) and the High‑Altitude Warfare School (Gulmarg) validated end‑to‑end latency of < 2 seconds from sensor detection to shooter engagement for a simulated armoured column. The system demonstrated interoperability with the Indian Air Force’s Integrated Air Command and Control System (IACCS) via the Joint Tactical Data Link (JTDL) and with the Navy’s Maritime Domain Awareness (MDA) network through the Information Fusion Centre – Indian Ocean Region (IFC‑IOR). A notable capability is the “plug‑and‑play” sensor onboarding framework, which allows new platforms (e.g., the upcoming Future Infantry Combat Vehicle) to be integrated within 48 hours using a standardised data‑model schema.

IBMS also incorporates a cyber‑resilience subsystem: a hardware‑root‑of‑trust (TPM 2.0) on every node, continuous attestation via a blockchain‑based ledger, and an AI‑driven anomaly detection module that flags lateral movement attempts in the tactical network. The programme’s roadmap includes the induction of IBMS‑v2 (2027) with quantum‑key‑distribution (QKD) links for the most sensitive command nodes, and the migration to a micro‑services architecture on the Defence Information Infrastructure (DII) cloud to enable rapid software updates.

Comparative Table Construction
Compare the communication architecture of IBMS with the legacy Army Tactical Communication System (ATCS) in terms of bandwidth, latency, and interoperability.
Answer:
Bandwidth: ATCS relies on narrowband VHF/UHF voice nets (≤ 25 kbps) and limited data bursts; IBMS uses SDRs with adaptive coding delivering 2‑10 Mbps per link and aggregates multiple bearers (SATCOM, fibre, microwave) for > 100 Mbps aggregate throughput at division level.
Latency: ATCS store‑and‑forward messaging incurs 5‑30 seconds end‑to‑end; IBMS’s IP‑based mesh with edge compute reduces sensor‑to‑shooter latency to < 2 seconds (validated in 2023 trials).
Interoperability: ATCS uses proprietary protocols, requiring gateway boxes for joint ops; IBMS adopts STANAG‑4586, JTDL, and Link‑16 compatible waveforms, enabling native data exchange with IAF IACCS, Navy MDA, and allied forces without intermediate translators.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for “network‑centric warfare enablers”, list SATCOM, SDR, data‑fusion engine, AI decision support, and interoperability standards (STANAG‑4586, JTDL). Pair each enabler with a concrete Indian programme (IBMS, IACCS, IFC‑IOR) to score full marks.

Small Satellite Launch Vehicle (SSLV) Development, Commercial Launch Services and Market Positioning

The Small Satellite Launch Vehicle (SSLV) is ISRO’s dedicated three‑stage launch system designed to place up to 500 kg into a 500 km low‑Earth orbit (LEO) with a launch‑on‑demand cadence of 7‑10 days. The vehicle uses solid‑propellant first (SS1) and second (SS2) stages derived from the PSLV’s S‑139 and S‑12 motors, and a liquid‑propellant velocity‑trimming module (VTM) as the third stage, providing precise orbital insertion. Development began in 2016 under the Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre (VSSC) with the objective of capturing the burgeoning small‑satellite market — constellation deployments, technology demonstrators, and university payloads — that larger vehicles (PSLV, GSLV) cannot serve economically.

The inaugural flight SSLV‑D1 (7 August 2022) suffered a guidance anomaly during the VTM burn, resulting in an elliptical orbit that caused the two payloads (EOS‑02 and AzaadiSAT) to re‑enter. The failure investigation identified a sensor‑fusion error in the inertial navigation unit (INU) and led to a redesign of the VTM’s thrust‑vector‑control logic. SSLV‑D2 (10 February 2023) successfully injected EOS‑07, Janus‑1 and AzaadiSAT‑2 into a 450 km circular orbit, validating the corrected guidance algorithm and the new “quick‑turnaround” integration flow that reduces vehicle stacking time from 30 days (PSLV) to 72 hours. SSLV‑D3 (16 August 2024) carried the first commercial payload — a 120 kg Earth‑observation microsat for a Southeast Asian operator — under a contract signed with NewSpace India Limited (NSIL) at a quoted price of US $4.2 million, positioning SSLV competitively against Rocket Lab’s Electron (US $7.5 million) and Arianespace’s Vega‑C (US $12 million for rideshare slots).

NSIL’s commercial strategy leverages the “launch‑as‑a‑service” model: customers procure a dedicated SSLV flight with a fixed schedule, while NSIL manages licensing, range safety, and payload integration through a single‑window portal. As of March 2025, NSIL has secured five firm launch contracts (two domestic, three international) and a memorandum of understanding with a European small‑sat constellation operator for up to eight launches through 2028. The vehicle’s low‑cost architecture — solid motors produced at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre’s propellant plant, VTM assembled at the Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre (LPSC) — yields a recurring cost estimate of ₹30 crore per launch, roughly one‑third of a PSLV‑XL mission.

Future upgrades include SSLV‑D4 (planned 2026) featuring an upgraded avionics suite with a radiation‑hardened RISC‑V flight computer, a restartable VTM for multi‑orbit deployment, and a payload‑adapter ring compatible with the 12‑U CubeSat standard. Parallel studies at VSSC explore a reusable first‑stage concept (SSLV‑R) using a para‑foil recovery system, targeting a 30 % cost reduction per flight by 2030. The programme also feeds into the “Gaganyaan‑Lite” abort‑test vehicle, sharing the SS1 motor and VTM heritage.

Fast Reactor Metal Fuel Development and Pyroprocessing for Closed Fuel Cycle

The Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) at Kalpakkam currently operates with mixed‑oxide (MOX) fuel (UO₂‑PuO₂) but the next‑generation Commercial Fast Reactor (CFR‑600) is slated to adopt metallic fuel (U‑Pu‑Zr alloy) because of its higher breeding ratio (≈ 1.25 vs 1.05 for MOX), superior thermal conductivity (≈ 20 W/m·K), and simpler fabrication route. Metallic fuel development is coordinated by the Nuclear Fuel Complex (NFC), Hyderabad, with irradiation testing in the Fast Breeder Test Reactor (FBTR) at Kalpakkam. Since 2018, NFC has produced over 200 fuel pins (6 mm diameter, 1 m active length) with Pu content ranging from 15‑25 wt %. Post‑irradiation examinations (PIE) at the Hot Cell Facility show swelling < 2 % at 100 GWd/t burn‑up, meeting the design limit for CFR‑600.

Complementing metal fuel, pyroprocessing — a high‑temperature electro‑refining technique in molten LiCl‑KCl eutectic (450‑500 °C) — is being developed to close the fuel cycle without aqueous reprocessing. The process separates uranium, plutonium and minor actinides into a metallic ingot while fission products remain in the salt waste form, which is subsequently immobilised in a glass‑ceramic matrix. A pilot‑scale pyroprocessing facility (5 kg HM/day) was commissioned at the Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR) in 2022. Demonstration runs using spent FBTR MOX fuel achieved > 99.9 % U/Pu recovery and a decontamination factor > 10⁴ for cesium and strontium.

Key advantages of pyroprocessing for India include: (1) proliferation resistance — the product stream never isolates pure plutonium; (2) compact footprint — the facility occupies < 200 m² versus > 2000 m² for a PUREX plant; (3) compatibility with metal fuel — the metallic product can be directly cast into fresh fuel pins. The regulatory pathway is being defined by the AERB through a dedicated “Pyroprocessing Safety Guide” (draft 2023) that addresses criticality safety in the electro‑refiner, off‑gas treatment for volatile fission products (Kr, Xe, I), and waste‑form qualification for deep geological disposal.

The integrated timeline targets metal‑fuel qualification for CFR‑600 by 2025, commissioning of a 50 kg HM/day demonstration pyroprocessing line by 2027, and full‑scale commercial pyroprocessing (200 kg HM/day) co‑located with the CFR‑600 fuel fabrication plant by the early 2030s. This closed‑cycle capability is essential for sustaining India’s fast‑reactor fleet beyond the limited plutonium inventory from PHWR spent fuel, and it positions the country as a technology holder for the Generation‑IV Sodium‑cooled Fast Reactor (SFR) system.

Artificial Intelligence Applications in Defence: Project Defence AI, Centre for AI and Robotics and Autonomous Systems

Project Defence AI, launched in 2020 under the aegis of the Department of Defence Production, coordinates AI research across DRDO laboratories, the three services, and the private sector. The programme’s charter identifies five thrust areas: (1) Intelligence, Surveillance & Reconnaissance (ISR) analytics — automated target recognition (ATR) from multi‑sensor imagery; (2) Predictive maintenance — health‑monitoring of gas‑turbine engines (Kaveri, HTFE‑25) and naval propulsion shafts using vibration‑signature ML models; (3) Autonomous navigation — path‑planning for unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) and swarm UAVs in GPS‑denied environments; (4) Decision‑support systems — real‑time course‑of‑action (COA) generation for brigade‑level commanders; (5) Cyber defence — anomaly detection in tactical networks using graph‑neural networks.

The Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Robotics (CAIR), Bengaluru, serves as the nodal laboratory. CAIR’s flagship products include NETRA — a deep‑learning pipeline that processes high‑resolution Cartosat‑3 and RISAT‑1A SAR imagery to detect camouflaged vehicles with a reported F1‑score of 0.92 on the 2023 validation set; and the AI‑enabled Radar Signal Processor (ARSP) integrated into the Akash‑NG fire‑control radar, which reduces false‑alarm rate by 40 % through clutter‑map learning. In 2023, CAIR demonstrated a 25‑drone swarm (ALFA‑S) performing collaborative area‑search and target‑hand‑over using a decentralized consensus algorithm, all operating on edge‑AI modules (NVIDIA Jetson AGX) with inter‑drone mesh links.

Service‑specific programmes leverage this backbone. The Army’s “Project SAKSHAM” integrates AI‑based logistics forecasting (demand prediction for ammunition, fuel) into the IBMS decision layer. The Navy’s “Maritime Autonomous Surface Ship (MASS)” programme uses CAIR’s collision‑avoidance stack on the 12‑m unmanned surface vessel (USV) “Matangi”, which completed a 48‑hour autonomous patrol in the Arabian Sea in 2024. The Air Force’s “Project VAYU” embeds AI‑driven electronic‑warfare (EW) threat‑library updates into the Su‑30MKI’s DARIN‑III mission computer, enabling real‑time jammer classification.

Governance is provided by the Defence AI Ethics Framework (2023), which mandates a human‑in‑the‑loop for any kinetic action, requires algorithmic audit trails stored on a tamper‑evident ledger, and establishes a Defence AI Ethics Committee (DAIEC) reporting to the Chief of Defence Staff. The framework also defines a Technology Readiness Level (TRL) gating policy: AI models must achieve TRL 6 (demonstrated in relevant environment) before integration into weapon systems, and TRL 8 (operational qualification) before deployment in combat units. This structured approach aims to balance rapid innovation with accountability, ensuring that autonomous capabilities enhance — rather than erode — command authority.

  • Confusing the AHWR’s thorium blanket with the driver fuel; the blanket is natural ThO₂, while the driver is 19.75 % LEU — only the blanket breeds 233U.
  • Assuming the IBMS architecture is a single monolithic software; it is a micro‑services stack on a hybrid cloud‑edge fabric with plug‑and‑play sensor onboarding.
  • Believing SSLV’s commercial price is fixed at US $4 million; NSIL quotes vary with payload mass, orbit inclination, and launch‑window flexibility.
  • Thinking pyroprocessing yields pure plutonium; the electro‑refiner produces a mixed U‑Pu‑MA ingot, never separating Pu alone.
  • Overlooking that the Defence AI Ethics Framework applies to all domestic R&D projects at TRL 6, not only to export‑controlled items.
  • Assuming the CAIR swarm demo used satellite links; the 2023 trial relied solely on line‑of‑sight mesh radios.
  • Confusing the CFR‑600 metal‑fuel qualification date with the PFBR’s MOX fuel; they are distinct programmes with separate timelines.

Gaganyaan Human Spaceflight Programme: Crew Escape System, Environmental Control and Life Support, and Mission Architecture

The Gaganyaan programme, announced by the Prime Minister in August 2018, aims to demonstrate indigenous human spaceflight capability by launching a three‑member crew to a 400 km low‑Earth orbit for up to seven days. The launch vehicle is the human‑rated LVM3 (formerly GSLV Mk‑III), which incorporates a reinforced payload fairing, an upgraded C25 cryogenic upper stage with a higher thrust margin, and a dedicated crew‑escape system (CES) that can be activated from the launch pad up to an altitude of 20 km. The CES completed a successful pad‑abort test in July 2023 at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre, demonstrating a 20‑second burn of the solid‑propellant abort motor and a clean separation of the crew module (CM) from the launch vehicle.

The crew module, a 3.7 t conical capsule, houses the Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS) that regulates cabin pressure at 101.3 kPa, temperature at 22 ± 2 °C, and humidity at 40‑60 %. The ECLSS uses a closed‑loop carbon‑dioxide removal assembly based on molecular‑sieve beds, a water‑recovery loop that condenses exhaled moisture, and a fire‑suppression subsystem employing inert gas generators. Redundancy is built to a 2‑out‑of‑3 voting logic for critical sensors, and the system has been qualified through thermal‑vacuum tests at the ISRO Propulsion Complex, Mahendragiri, and acoustic tests at the National Aerospace Laboratories, Bengaluru.

Astronaut selection, conducted jointly by the Indian Air Force (IAF) and ISRO, shortlisted four IAF test pilots in 2020. The candidates completed basic spaceflight training at the Yuri Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Centre, Star City, Russia, including centrifuge exposure up to 8 g, parabolic‑flight microgravity familiarisation, and Soyuz simulator sessions. In 2022, the crew returned to India for mission‑specific training on the Gaganyaan CM mock‑up, ECLSS operations, and emergency egress drills at the newly built Human Spaceflight Centre (HSFC) in Bengaluru. The HSFC also hosts the Mission Control Centre (MCC) for Gaganyaan, which will operate in tandem with the existing ISRO Telemetry, Tracking and Command Network (ISTRAC) for real‑time health monitoring.

The mission profile calls for a launch window that aligns the orbital plane with the ground‑track over the Indian Ocean for optimal recovery. After orbital insertion, the CM will perform a phasing manoeuvre using its onboard reaction control thrusters (monopropellant hydrazine) to rendezvous with a pre‑positioned recovery ship in the Bay of Bengal. The service module (SM), which provides propulsion, power, and thermal control during the orbital phase, is jettisoned prior to re‑entry. The CM’s ablative thermal protection system (TPS), based on a carbon‑phenolic composite, is designed for a peak heat flux of 1.2 MW/m² during a 7.8 km/s re‑entry. Parachute deployment follows a mortar‑fired pilot‑chute sequence, culminating in a main‑chute cluster of three 35 m diameter ringsail parachutes that decelerate the capsule to a splashdown velocity below 8 m/s.

Programme governance is vested in the Gaganyaan National Advisory Council, chaired by the National Security Advisor, with representation from the Department of Space, Ministry of Defence, and the Prime Minister’s Office. Funding of ₹10,000 crore was approved in the 2019‑20 budget, with subsequent allocations for the human‑rating of LVM3, CES qualification, and ground‑segment upgrades. The first uncrewed test flight (G1) is slated for late 2024, followed by a second uncrewed mission (G2) carrying a humanoid payload (Vyommitra) to validate life‑support and avionics, before the crewed mission (H1) targeted for 2025‑26.

Advanced Heavy Water Reactor (AHWR) and Thorium Fuel Cycle Roadmap

The Advanced Heavy Water Reactor (AHWR) is a 300 MWe vertical pressure‑tube reactor designed to demonstrate the commercial viability of the thorium‑uranium‑233 fuel cycle, the third stage of India’s three‑stage nuclear power programme. The reactor uses boiling light water as coolant and heavy water as moderator, a configuration that decouples the coolant temperature (≈ 300 °C) from the moderator temperature (≈ 70 °C), enabling passive heat removal through natural circulation of the coolant and a large gravity‑driven water pool (the “passive decay heat removal system”) that can sustain core cooling for 72 hours without operator action or external power.

The reference fuel for AHWR is a mixed‑oxide (MOX) comprising 19.75 % low‑enriched uranium (LEU) as the driver and natural thorium dioxide (ThO₂) as the blanket. In‑core, the thorium blanket breeds uranium‑233, which is subsequently fissioned, while the LEU driver maintains reactivity. The fuel pins are arranged in 12‑pin clusters within each pressure tube, and the reactor core contains 452 fuel assemblies. The design targets a discharge burn‑up of 25 GWd/tHM for the driver and a conversion ratio of 0.8 for the blanket, yielding a net fissile production that can feed future fast‑reactor cores.

Design completion was declared in 2020 by the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) after extensive safety analyses, including a Level‑2 Probabilistic Safety Assessment (PSA) that confirmed a core‑damage frequency below 10⁻⁶ per reactor‑year. The site identified for the first AHWR is Tarapur, Maharashtra, where a dedicated fuel‑fabrication facility for ThO₂‑LEU MOX is being commissioned under the Nuclear Fuel Complex (NFC). Construction licensing is under review by the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB), with a target first‑pour‑concrete date of 2026 and commercial operation by 2030, contingent on the successful demonstration of the prototype fast breeder reactor (PFBR) at Kalpakkam, which will supply the initial plutonium inventory for the driver fuel.

The thorium roadmap envisions a fleet of 12‑15 AHWRs by 2050, each contributing to a closed thorium‑uranium‑233 cycle that reduces uranium ore demand by > 80 % relative to the current PHWR fleet. The programme also includes the development of a thorium‑based fuel reprocessing line (the “Thorium Reprocessing Plant”) at the upcoming Integrated Nuclear Recycle Plant (INRP) in Tarapur, employing a modified PUREX flow‑sheet with selective extraction of U‑233 using a tributyl phosphate‑nitric acid system. This plant is slated for hot‑commissioning by 2032, aligning with the AHWR fuel‑cycle closure timeline.

International collaboration on thorium technology is pursued through the IAEA’s Coordinated Research Project on Thorium Fuel Cycles, where India contributes experimental data from the AHWR critical facility at BARC. Domestically, the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) has established a Thorium Utilisation Working Group that coordinates research on advanced fuel forms (e.g., thorium‑based metallic fuels for fast reactors), radiation‑damage modelling of ThO₂, and the economics of thorium‑fuelled SMRs. The AHWR thus serves as both a technology demonstrator and a strategic bridge to a sustainable, resource‑independent nuclear energy future.

Examiner's trap
A question states: "The AHWR uses natural thorium as the driver fuel and low‑enriched uranium as the blanket." Identify the error and explain the correct fuel configuration.
The statement reverses the roles. In the AHWR, the driver fuel is 19.75 % low‑enriched uranium dioxide (LEU) which provides the initial neutrons, while the blanket surrounding the driver pins is natural thorium dioxide (ThO₂) that breeds uranium‑233. The driver sustains reactivity; the blanket converts thorium to fissile U‑233. Remember: driver = LEU, blanket = natural ThO₂.
Exam‑day strategy
For nuclear fuel‑cycle questions, sketch a quick two‑column table: Driver vs Blanket, Coolant vs Moderator, Burn‑up vs Conversion Ratio. This visual cue prevents the common reversal of driver/blanket roles and helps you recall the passive safety features (gravity‑driven pool, natural circulation) that are unique to AHWR.

Indigenous Unmanned Combat Aerial Vehicle Development: Ghatak, SWiFT, and the Loyal Wingman Concept

The Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) is pursuing a family of stealthy unmanned combat aerial vehicles (UCAVs) under the Autonomous Unmanned Research Aircraft (AURA) programme. The technology demonstrator, designated SWiFT (Scalable Winged Flight Testbed), performed its maiden flight on 1 July 2022 from the Aeronautical Test Range, Chitradurga. SWiFT is a low‑observable, tailless flying‑wing configuration powered by a single indigenous Kaveri‑derivative turbofan (dry thrust 49 kN) and incorporates an internal weapons bay capable of carrying two 250 kg precision‑guided munitions. The airframe uses carbon‑fibre‑reinforced polymer (CFRP) skins with radar‑absorbent material (RAM) coatings, and the flight‑control system employs a triplex digital fly‑by‑wire architecture with autonomous waypoint navigation and terrain‑following modes.

Building on SWiFT data, the full‑scale Ghatak UCAV is being designed for a maximum take‑off weight of 13 t, a combat radius of 1,200 km, and a service ceiling of 15 km. Ghatak will feature a modular mission system that can swap between strike, electronic‑attack, and ISR payloads. The propulsion baseline is the after‑burning Kaveri‑K9 engine (wet thrust 81 kN), currently undergoing altitude‑test validation at the Gas Turbine Research Establishment (GTRE). The weapons bay is sized for four 500 kg class stand‑off weapons (e.g., the indigenous SAAW or the BrahMos‑NG) and includes a retractable electro‑optical targeting pod for terminal guidance.

A key operational concept is the “Loyal Wingman” mode, where a pair of Ghatak UCAVs operate under the tactical command of a manned Tejas Mk‑1A or Su‑30MKI. The manned platform provides high‑level mission planning and rules‑of‑engagement authority, while the UCAVs execute autonomous ingress, target prosecution, and egress using a secure line‑of‑sight datalink (L‑band, frequency‑hopping) and a beyond‑visual‑range satellite link for over‑the‑horizon missions. In 2023, DRDO conducted a simulated loyal‑wingman trial at the Integrated Test Range, Chandipur, where a Tejas‑mounted mission computer tasked a SWiFT surrogate to prosecute a simulated radar emitter; the UCAV autonomously planned a low‑observable route, released a dummy weapon, and returned to a predefined recovery point.

Integration challenges include the development of a certifiable autonomous decision‑making stack that satisfies the Defence AI Ethics Framework’s human‑in‑the‑loop requirement for kinetic release. The Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Robotics (CAIR) is supplying a reinforcement‑learning based tactical planner that has been validated to Technology Readiness Level (TRL) 6 in a hardware‑in‑the‑loop environment. Additionally, the airframe’s low‑observable coatings must withstand the thermal cycle of after‑burner operation; the Defence Materials and Stores Research and Development Establishment (DMSRDE) has qualified a ceramic‑based RAM that retains > 90 % reflectivity reduction after 200 hours at 600 °C.

Programme governance is overseen by the AURA Project Monitoring Committee, chaired by the Scientific Adviser to the Defence Minister, with representation from the Indian Air Force, Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL), and the private‑sector partner NewSpace Research & Technologies. The current roadmap targets Ghatak prototype rollout by 2026, first flight by 2027, and initial operational capability (IOC) for the loyal‑wingman team by 2030, aligning with the IAF’s 2035 force‑structure plan for 48 UCAVs across six squadrons.

Indian Lunar Exploration Roadmap: Chandrayaan‑3, Chandrayaan‑4, LUPEX Collaboration, and In‑Situ Resource Utilisation Demonstrations

Following the successful soft landing of Chandrayaan‑3 on 23 August 2023 at the lunar south‑polar region (69.37° S, 32.35° E), ISRO has formalised a multi‑mission roadmap extending to 2035. Chandrayaan‑3’s lander Vikram and rover Pragyan demonstrated end‑to‑end landing, roving, and in‑situ scientific measurements, including the first ever in‑situ detection of sulphur and the measurement of near‑surface thermal conductivity (≈ 0.01 W/m·K). The mission also validated the Laser‑Induced Breakdown Spectroscope (LIBS) and the Alpha Particle X‑ray Spectrometer (APXS) for elemental analysis.

Chandrayaan‑4, approved in principle by the Space Commission in 2024, is conceived as a sample‑return mission targeting the same high‑latitude region. The architecture comprises a lander‑ascender module, a transfer module, and an Earth‑return capsule. The ascender will use a newly developed 440 N liquid‑oxygen/liquid‑methane (LOX/LCH₄) engine, currently under hot‑fire testing at the ISRO Propulsion Complex, to lift ~ 30 kg of regolith to a low‑lunar orbit where it will dock autonomously with the transfer module. The Earth‑return capsule incorporates a carbon‑phenolic ablative heat shield rated for 11 km/s re‑entry, and a parachute system derived from the Gaganyaan crew module. Launch is targeted for 2028 on an LVM3 with an extended payload fairing.

The Lunar Polar Exploration (LUPEX) mission is a joint venture with the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), signed in 2023. JAXA provides the launch vehicle (H3) and a 350 kg rover equipped with a ground‑penetrating radar and a water‑ice drill capable of 1.5 m depth. ISRO contributes the lander, based on the Chandrayaan‑3 heritage, and the mission operations centre. LUPEX aims to map the vertical distribution of water‑ice in permanently shadowed regions (PSRs) and to demonstrate a 10 W radio‑isotope heater unit (RHU) for thermal survival during the 14‑day lunar night. The launch window is set for 2026‑27, with a landing site near the Shackleton crater rim.

In‑Situ Resource Utilisation (ISRU) demonstrations are embedded across these missions. Chandrayaan‑3 carried the “Lunar Thermal Probe” to assess regolith thermal properties for future extraction plants. LUPEX will test a solid‑oxide electrolysis cell (SOEC) that converts extracted water‑ice into oxygen and hydrogen at 800 °C, using waste heat from the RHU. Chandrayaan‑4’s sample‑return canister includes a miniature ISRU payload to validate the reduction of ilmenite (FeTiO₃) with hydrogen to produce iron, titanium dioxide, and water — a pathway for in‑situ metal production. The long‑term goal, articulated in the ISRO “Lunar Exploration Vision 2040” document, is to establish a semi‑permanent robotic outpost at the south pole by 2035, capable of producing 1 t of oxygen per year to support human‑rated missions under the Gaganyaan‑Lunar extension concept.

Programme coordination is managed by the Lunar Exploration Programme Office (LEPO) at ISRO Headquarters, with technical oversight from the U.R. Rao Satellite Centre (URSC) for orbiters, the Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre (LPSC) for propulsion, and the Laboratory for Electro‑Optics Systems (LEOS) for scientific instruments. Funding of ₹12,000 crore has been earmarked for the 2024‑2030 phase, with a review gate at the completion of LUPEX to assess ISRU technology readiness before committing to the outpost phase.

Integrated Battlefield Management System (IBMS) Architecture: Micro‑Services Stack, Sensor Fusion, and Joint All‑Domain Command and Control Alignment

The Integrated Battlefield Management System (IBMS) is the Indian Army’s flagship network‑centric warfare platform, designed to provide a common operational picture (COP) from the tactical edge to the strategic headquarters. Unlike the legacy “single‑monolith” battlefield management software, IBMS is built on a micro‑services architecture deployed over a hybrid cloud‑edge fabric. Each micro‑service — track management, sensor onboarding, mission planning, logistics forecasting, and electronic‑order‑of‑battle — runs in a containerised environment (Kubernetes‑based) that can be instantiated on ruggedised edge servers mounted on command vehicles (BMP‑2/3, Arjun) as well as on central data centres at Corps and Command levels.

Sensor fusion is achieved through a publish‑subscribe middleware that ingests data from heterogeneous sources: the Swathi weapon‑locating radar, the Akash‑NG fire‑control radar, the Netra airborne early‑warning platform, the RISAT‑1A synthetic‑aperture radar, and the Navy’s maritime domain awareness feed via the Information Fusion Centre – Indian Ocean Region (IFC‑IOR). The fusion engine employs a multi‑hypothesis tracking (MHT) algorithm with a Gaussian‑mixture implementation, delivering a fused track update rate of 5 Hz for high‑priority targets. The system also integrates the Army’s “Project SAKSHAM” AI‑based logistics predictor, which consumes ammunition consumption patterns and fuel‑usage telemetry to generate 48‑hour demand forecasts with a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) below 12 %.

Interoperability with the Indian Air Force’s Integrated Air Command and Control System (IACCS) and the Navy’s Maritime Domain Awareness (MDA) grid is realised through the Joint All‑Domain Command and Control (JADC2) reference architecture adopted by the Integrated Defence Staff (IDS) in 2022. IBMS exposes a set of RESTful APIs conforming to the NATO STANAG 4586‑compliant “UAV Control Segment” profile, enabling cross‑service tasking of unmanned assets such as the DRDO “Matangi” USV and the “ALFA‑S” drone swarm. The security layer implements a zero‑trust model with mutual TLS authentication, hardware‑rooted identity modules (TPM 2.0) on every edge node, and a continuous‑monitoring Security Operations Centre (SOC) at the Defence Cyber Agency.

Deployment follows a spiral‑development model. Spiral‑1 (2021‑22) fielded the core COP and track‑management micro‑services to two Corps headquarters. Spiral‑2 (2023‑24) added sensor‑onboarding plug‑ins for the new QRSAM and Akash‑NG radars, and integrated the AI‑enabled Radar Signal Processor (ARSP) from CAIR to reduce false‑alarm rates. Spiral‑3 (planned 2025‑26) will introduce a decision‑support module that generates real‑time courses of action (COAs) for brigade commanders using a Monte‑Carlo tree search over the fused battlespace model, with a human‑in‑the‑loop approval gate mandated by the Defence AI Ethics Framework.

Industrial partnership is led by Bharat Electronics Limited (BEL) as the system integrator, with software development contributions from the Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C‑DAC), the Defence Research and Development Organisation’s (DRDO) Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Robotics (CAIR), and private‑sector firms specialising in container orchestration and cyber‑resilience. The programme’s acquisition follows the Defence Acquisition Procedure (DAP) 2023 “Make‑II” category, with a 60 % indigenous content threshold verified through the Defence Indigenisation Committee’s bill‑of‑materials audit. The total sanctioned cost is ₹8,500 crore, with a target of full operational capability across all three services by 2029.

  • Confusing the AHWR driver fuel (LEU) with the blanket (natural ThO₂) — the driver provides neutrons, the blanket breeds U‑233.
  • Assuming Gaganyaan’s crew escape system is only a launch‑pad abort; it is certified up to 20 km altitude and includes a high‑altitude abort mode.
  • Believing the Ghatak UCAV is a direct copy of foreign stealth drones; its flying‑wing airframe and Kaveri‑derivative engine are indigenous designs.
  • Thinking Chandrayaan‑4 will use the same lander as Chandrayaan‑3; it requires a new ascender with LOX/LCH₄ propulsion for sample return.
  • Overlooking that IBMS micro‑services run on edge servers at the tactical level, not solely in central data centres.
  • Mixing up LUPEX’s Japanese rover (water‑ice drill) with ISRO’s lander responsibilities; the drill is a JAXA payload.
  • Assuming the Defence AI Ethics Framework applies only to exported systems; it governs all domestic R&D projects at TRL 6 and above.

The advanced sections above cover human spaceflight, thorium reactor technology, autonomous combat aircraft, lunar exploration, and network‑centric battlefield management, providing the depth and specificity required for high‑stakes examination questions.

Indigenous Small Satellite Launch Vehicle (SSLV) Development: Architecture, Flight History and Commercial Positioning

The Small Satellite Launch Vehicle (SSLV) is ISRO’s dedicated three‑stage launch system designed to place 500 kg class payloads into 500 km low‑Earth orbit (LEO) and 300 kg into Sun‑synchronous orbit (SSO). The vehicle uses a solid‑propellant first stage (SS1) derived from the PSLV’s S‑139 motor, a solid second stage (SS2) based on the PSLV’s S‑139‑derived motor with a reduced propellant load, and a liquid‑propellant third stage (SS3) employing a pressure‑fed monomethylhydrazine (MMH) / mixed oxides of nitrogen (MON‑3) engine derived from the PSLV’s fourth‑stage reaction control thrusters. The entire stack stands 34 m tall, has a lift‑off mass of approximately 120 t, and is assembled vertically on a mobile launch platform that can be transported to the launch pad on a standard rail‑gauge transporter, reducing pad‑occupancy time to under 72 hours.

The first developmental flight, SSLV‑D1 (7 August 2022), suffered a guidance anomaly during the second‑stage burn that resulted in the payloads being injected into an elliptical orbit with a perigee below 200 km, causing premature re‑entry. The failure investigation identified a sensor‑fusion error in the inertial navigation system (INS) when the vehicle transitioned from open‑loop to closed‑loop guidance. Corrective actions included a redesign of the INS filter logic, addition of a redundant star‑tracker for attitude verification, and a revised flight‑software verification campaign using hardware‑in‑the‑loop (HIL) simulation at the Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre (VSSC).

SSLV‑D2 (10 February 2023) successfully placed the EOS‑07, Janus‑1 and AzaadiSAT‑2 satellites into a 450 km circular SSO, validating the corrected guidance algorithm and demonstrating a 15‑minute launch‑to‑orbit timeline. The third developmental flight, SSLV‑D3 (16 August 2024), carried the commercial payloads of two foreign customers (a 120 kg Earth‑observation microsat and a 80 kg technology demonstrator) alongside the Indian EOS‑08, achieving a 500 km SSO insertion with a payload mass of 460 kg. The mission also qualified the new “quick‑turnaround” payload integration flow, where the satellite encapsulation and mate‑to‑vehicle operations are completed within 48 hours of arrival at the launch complex.

Commercially, SSLV is positioned to capture the growing small‑sat ride‑share market, competing with international providers such as Rocket Lab’s Electron and Virgin Orbit’s LauncherOne. ISRO’s commercial arm, NewSpace India Limited (NSIL), offers a standardised launch service contract with a fixed price of US $4.5 million for a 300 kg SSO slot, inclusive of launch‑vehicle integration, range safety, and post‑launch telemetry support. The vehicle’s all‑solid first two stages eliminate the need for cryogenic ground infrastructure, enabling launch from the newly commissioned SSLV Launch Complex (SLC) at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC‑SHAR) and, in the future, from a mobile sea‑based platform under the “Sea‑Launch” concept study.

Key performance metrics after SSLV‑D3: lift‑off thrust 1 800 kN, first‑stage burn time 110 s, second‑stage burn time 85 s, third‑stage burn time 300 s, total Δv ≈ 9.2 km/s. The vehicle’s modular avionics suite, based on the “Vikram‑100” radiation‑hardened processor, supports autonomous flight termination and real‑time health monitoring via a C‑band telemetry link. Ongoing work includes qualification of a restartable third‑stage engine for multi‑orbit deployment and integration of a payload‑adapter with a standardised 24‑inch bolt‑pattern to accommodate CubeSat dispensers up to 12U.

Space‑Based Optical Inter‑Satellite Links: Indian Laser Communication Terminals and Network Architecture

India’s entry into free‑space optical communication (FSOC) for satellite‑to‑satellite and satellite‑to‑ground links began with the Laser Communication Terminal (LCT) flown on GSAT‑29 (launched 14 November 2018). The LCT, developed by the Space Applications Centre (SAC) in collaboration with the Laboratory for Electro‑Optics Systems (LEOS), operates at 1550 nm wavelength, delivering a bidirectional data rate of 1.25 Gbps over a 40 000 km inter‑satellite range with a 10 cm aperture telescope. The terminal uses a coarse‑pointing assembly (CPA) driven by a two‑axis gimbal and a fine‑pointing assembly (FPA) based on a fast‑steering mirror (FSM) with a bandwidth of 2 kHz, achieving a pointing accuracy of < 2 µrad.

The GSAT‑29 demonstration established a 5‑minute optical link with the ground station at the Indian Deep Space Network (IDSN) in Byalalu, validating acquisition, tracking and pointing (ATP) algorithms under realistic atmospheric turbulence. Subsequent ground‑to‑satellite tests from the Optical Ground Station (OGS) at Mount Abu (Rajasthan) achieved a 2.5 Gbps downlink using adaptive optics (AO) to compensate for scintillation, confirming the feasibility of high‑rate feeder links for future high‑throughput satellites (HTS).

The next generation of Indian optical terminals is being integrated into the Indian Data Relay Satellite System (IDRSS), a constellation of two geostationary relay satellites (IDRSS‑1A and IDRSS‑1B) slated for launch in 2025‑26. Each IDRSS satellite will carry a dual‑head LCT capable of simultaneous inter‑satellite links (ISL) to low‑Earth‑orbit (LEO) Earth‑observation satellites (e.g., RISAT‑1A, Cartosat‑3) and a high‑rate Ka‑band feeder link to the ground. The ISL architecture follows a mesh topology: each LEO satellite equipped with a compact LCT (mass < 15 kg, power < 80 W) can hand over data to either IDRSS node, providing near‑continuous coverage for real‑time synthetic‑aperture radar (SAR) and hyperspectral imaging downlinks.

Network‑level management is handled by the “Optical Network Control Centre” (ONCC) at the ISRO Telemetry, Tracking and Command Network (ISTRAC). The ONCC runs a software‑defined networking (SDN) stack that schedules link windows, performs dynamic routing based on link‑budget margins, and executes autonomous hand‑over procedures when a LEO satellite transitions between IDRSS footprints. The control plane uses the Consultative Committee for Space Data Systems (CCSDS) Optical Communications Standard (OCS) protocol suite, ensuring interoperability with international partners such as ESA’s European Data Relay System (EDRS) and NASA’s Laser Communications Relay Demonstration (LCRD).

Key technical challenges addressed in the development programme include radiation‑hardened avalanche photodiodes (APDs) for the receiver, space‑qualified erbium‑doped fibre amplifiers (EDFAs) for the transmitter, and a thermal‑control subsystem that maintains the laser diode junction temperature within ±0.5 °C across the ‑40 °C to +60 °C orbital environment. The programme also conducted a series of vibration and thermal‑vacuum tests at the ISRO Satellite Integration and Test Establishment (ISITE) to qualify the terminal for a 15‑year GEO lifetime.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: "Which Indian satellite first demonstrated a space‑to‑ground laser communication link at 1.25 Gbps?" The distractors include GSAT‑30, GSAT‑29, RISAT‑1A and Cartosat‑3.
The correct answer is GSAT‑29. The Laser Communication Terminal (LCT) on GSAT‑29, launched in November 2018, performed the first Indian space‑to‑ground optical link at 1.25 Gbps with the IDSN ground station. GSAT‑30 carries only Ka‑band and Ku‑band transponders; RISAT‑1A and Cartosat‑3 are radar and optical imaging satellites without laser‑com terminals.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question cites a data‑rate and wavelength for an Indian laser‑com demo, associate 1550 nm and 1.25 Gbps with GSAT‑29. Remember that the IDRSS constellation will use the same wavelength but higher rates (up to 10 Gbps) and a mesh ISL architecture. Link the CCSDS OCS standard to interoperability — this is a frequent “match the following” item.

Indigenous Nuclear Thermal Propulsion for Deep‑Space Missions: Reactor Design, Fuel Cycle and Test Roadmap

The Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) and ISRO have jointly initiated a Nuclear Thermal Propulsion (NTP) technology development programme aimed at enabling crewed and heavy‑cargo missions to Mars and the outer planets. The reference concept employs a solid‑core, hydrogen‑cooled reactor operating at a core outlet temperature of 2 800 K, delivering a specific impulse (Isp) of 900 s — roughly double that of the best chemical LOX/LH₂ stages. The reactor uses low‑enriched uranium (LEU) fuel in the form of uranium‑zirconium‑hydride (U‑ZrH₁.₆) fuel elements clad in a niobium‑1%zirconium alloy, a choice driven by the fuel’s inherent negative temperature coefficient and compatibility with hot hydrogen propellant.

The reactor core is a hexagonal lattice of 127 fuel pins, each 10 mm in diameter, surrounded by a beryllium reflector and a boron‑carbide (B₄C) control drum assembly for reactivity management. The hydrogen propellant flows through axial channels in the fuel pins, absorbing heat directly, and expands through a convergent‑divergent nozzle made of carbon‑carbon composite with a silicon‑carbide (SiC) coating to resist oxidation at > 2 500 K. The total engine mass, including shielding, is targeted at 3 500 kg, with a thrust of 110 kN.

Fuel cycle considerations centre on the use of LEU (≤ 19.75 % U‑235) to remain within the Non‑Proliferation Treaty (NPT) framework and the IAEA’s “peaceful use” safeguards. The fuel fabrication line at the Nuclear Fuel Complex (NFC), Hyderabad, is being qualified for U‑ZrH₁.₆ pellet production using a powder‑metallurgy route, followed by vacuum sintering at 1 600 °C. Post‑irradiation examination (PIE) facilities at the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) will assess fuel swelling, fission‑gas release and hydrogen‑induced corrosion after simulated burn‑up of 5 % FIMA (fissions per initial metal atom).

The test roadmap comprises three phases. Phase‑1 (2024‑2027) focuses on non‑nuclear “cold‑flow” testing of the nozzle and turbopump assembly at the Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre (LPSC) using gaseous hydrogen at 30 bar. Phase‑2 (2028‑2031) will conduct a series of “critical‑assembly” experiments at the Fast Reactor Critical Facility (FRCF) in Kalpakkam, employing a zero‑power mock‑up of the core to validate neutronics codes (MCNP‑6.2 and SERPENT‑2) and control‑drum worth curves. Phase‑3 (2032‑2035) aims at a full‑power, ground‑test of a 10 MWth prototype reactor at the newly constructed Nuclear Thermal Propulsion Test Facility (NTPTF) at Challakere, Karnataka, with a hydrogen flow rate of 5 kg/s and a 300‑second steady‑state run.

Regulatory clearance will require a dedicated safety case submitted to the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) covering launch‑pad abort scenarios, re‑entry breakup dispersion modelling, and radiological consequence analysis for a worst‑case core melt. The programme also coordinates with the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS) to align with the “Space Nuclear Power Sources” safety guidelines (Resolution 47/68). Successful demonstration would position India among the few nations with an operational NTP capability, reducing Mars transit time from 9 months to 4‑5 months and enabling payload mass fractions > 30 % for a 20‑tonne class launch vehicle.

Ghatak Unmanned Combat Aerial Vehicle: Flying‑Wing Design, Kaveri‑Derivative Engine and Autonomous Mission Management

The Ghatak (also referred to as the Stealth Wing Flying Testbed – SWiFT) is DRDO’s first indigenous flying‑wing unmanned combat aerial vehicle (UCAV) designed for deep‑penetration strike, intelligence‑surveillance‑reconnaissance (ISR) and electronic‑attack missions. The airframe follows a low‑observable (LO) planform with a 12 m wingspan, 5.5 m length, and a blended body‑wing contour that reduces radar cross‑section (RCS) to < 0.01 m² in the X‑band. Composite construction uses carbon‑fibre‑reinforced polymer (CFRP) skins over a honeycomb core, manufactured at the Aeronautical Development Establishment (ADE) using automated fibre‑placement (AFP) technology to ensure surface tolerance within ±0.1 mm.

Propulsion is provided by a Kaveri‑derivative turbofan, designated K9‑E, developed by the Gas Turbine Research Establishment (GTRE). The K9‑E is a 55 kN class afterburning engine derived from the Kaveri core (K9) with a redesigned low‑pressure turbine, a convergent‑divergent nozzle optimised for subsonic cruise (Mach 0.8) and a thrust‑vectoring capability of ±15° for enhanced maneuverability during terminal‑phase engagements. The engine incorporates a full‑authority digital engine control (FADEC) with health‑monitoring algorithms that enable condition‑based maintenance intervals of 1 200 hours.

The avionics suite centres on the “Mission Management Computer” (MMC) built around a radiation‑hardened quad‑core PowerPC processor running a DO‑178C Level‑A certified real‑time operating system. The MMC integrates a multi‑sensor fusion engine that correlates data from an active electronically scanned array (AESA) radar (derived from the Uttam programme), an electro‑optical/infrared (EO/IR) turret, a signals‑intelligence (SIGINT) payload and a electronic‑support‑measures (ESM) suite. Autonomous decision‑making follows a hierarchical behaviour‑tree architecture: strategic mission planning (waypoint sequencing, threat avoidance) runs at 1 Hz, tactical manoeuvre generation (terrain‑following, pop‑up attack) at 10 Hz, and low‑level flight‑control laws at 200 Hz.

Flight‑test milestones: the SWiFT demonstrator (scaled 70 % of Ghatak) completed its maiden flight on 1 July 2022 from the Chitradurga Aeronautical Test Range, validating the flying‑wing stability margins, landing‑gear retraction and data‑link integrity over a 150 km line‑of‑sight (LOS) link. Subsequent sorties in 2023 demonstrated autonomous take‑off, waypoint navigation, and a simulated weapon‑release envelope using an inert 250 kg smart‑bomb shape. The full‑scale Ghatak prototype (designated Ghatak‑1) is slated for rollout in late 2025, with first flight targeted for 2026 and initial operational clearance (IOC) by 2029.

Integration with the Indian Air Force’s (IAF) network‑centric warfare architecture is achieved via the “Air Force Network” (AFNet) using the Link‑16 compatible “Vayulink” datalink, enabling real‑time tasking from the Integrated Air Command and Control System (IACCS). The UCAV also supports the “Manned‑Unmanned Teaming” (MUM‑T) concept, where a Su‑30MKI pilot can designate targets for Ghatak via a helmet‑mounted display (HMD) and receive battle‑damage assessment (BDA) imagery over a secure beyond‑line‑of‑sight (BLOS) satellite link (GSAT‑7A).

Indigenous Long‑Range Surface‑to‑Air Missile (LRSAM) Programme: Barak‑8 Evolution, Indigenous Seeker and Naval Integration

The Long‑Range Surface‑to‑Air Missile (LRSAM), known operationally as the Barak‑8 in its joint Indo‑Israeli configuration, has been progressively indigenised to meet the Indian Navy’s requirement for a 70‑km class area‑defence missile capable of engaging anti‑ship cruise missiles, fighter aircraft and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in a saturated threat environment. The missile is a two‑stage, solid‑propellant system: a booster stage (derived from the Israeli “Booster‑8”) and a sustainer stage developed by DRDO’s Defence Research and Development Laboratory (DRDL) using a high‑energy composite propellant (HTPB/AP/Al) delivering a total impulse of 1.2 MN·s.

The key indigenous contribution is the dual‑mode seeker head, designed by the Research Centre Imarat (RCI). The seeker combines an active X‑band radar (AESA) for mid‑course guidance and terminal homing with an imaging infrared (IIR) focal‑plane array for passive terminal engagement against low‑observable targets. The seeker’s signal‑processing chain implements a track‑before‑detect (TBD) algorithm that maintains lock on targets with a radar cross‑section as low as 0.001 m² at 30 km range. The seeker is housed in a radome manufactured from a quartz‑fibre/ cyanate‑ester composite, qualified for aerodynamic heating up to 1 200 °C during the terminal dive.

Guidance and control employ a “proportional navigation with augmented bias” (PN‑AB) law, executed on a radiation‑hardened MIL‑STD‑1750A processor. The missile’s thrust‑vector control (TVC) in the sustainer stage uses a flexible‑joint nozzle actuated by electro‑mechanical actuators, providing ±12° deflection for high‑angle‑of‑attack manoeuvres. The warhead is a 60 kg directed‑energy fragmentation (DEF) type with a programmable proximity fuze, lethal radius 12 m against maneuvering targets.

Naval integration centres on the “Vertical Launch System” (VLS) cells aboard the Kolkata‑class (Project 15A) and Visakhapatnam‑class (Project 15B) destroyers, as well as the Nilgiri‑class (Project 17A) frigates. Each VLS cell accommodates a single LRSAM canister; the ship’s combat management system (CMS) — the indigenous “Sankhya” CMS on Project 15B and the “CMS‑17A” on Project 17A — conducts automatic target prioritisation, launch sequencing and mid‑course update via the ship’s MF‑STAR S‑band AESA radar. The missile receives uplink commands through a secure L‑band datalink (frequency‑hopping, 1 Mbps) that is resistant to jamming.

Operational milestones: the first successful intercept of a sea‑skimming target (simulated BrahMos‑type cruise missile) at 55 km was achieved during a joint DRDO‑Indian Navy trial off the Odisha coast in March 2022. Subsequent trials in 2023 demonstrated simultaneous engagement of two incoming targets with a single salvo of four missiles, validating the CMS’s multi‑target handling logic. The Army variant, designated MRSAM (Medium‑Range SAM), shares the same seeker and sustainer but uses a mobile launcher on a Tatra‑815 chassis; it entered service in 2022 and has been deployed along the northern borders.

Future upgrades include a “dual‑pulse” sustainer motor to extend the no‑escape zone to 90 km, integration of a gallium‑nitride (GaN) based AESA seeker for improved electronic‑counter‑counter‑measures (ECCM) performance, and a software‑defined radio (SDR) datalink compatible with the “Joint Tactical Data Link” (JTDL) standard for joint‑force interoperability.

  • Confusing SSLV’s solid‑stage heritage with PSLV’s liquid‑stage architecture — SSLV uses all‑solid first two stages, PSLV uses a solid‑first, liquid‑second configuration.
  • Assuming the GSAT‑29 laser terminal operates at 1064 nm; it operates at 1550 nm for eye‑safe, low‑atmospheric‑absorption performance.
  • Believing the NTP reactor uses highly enriched uranium (HEU); the Indian design explicitly adopts LEU (≤ 19.75 % U‑235) to comply with non‑proliferation norms.
  • Thinking the Ghatak UCAV is a direct copy of foreign flying‑wing drones; its airframe, Kaveri‑derivative engine and autonomous mission‑management software are indigenous developments.
  • Mixing up the Barak‑8’s Israeli booster with an Indian sustainer — the booster is Israeli, the sustainer, seeker and VLS integration are Indian.
  • Overlooking that the LRSAM’s dual‑mode seeker combines active X‑band AESA radar with imaging infrared, not a semi‑active radar homing only.
  • Assuming the SSLV commercial price includes insurance and launch‑site fees; the quoted US $4.5 million covers vehicle and integration only.

The sections above expand the lesson with launch‑vehicle economics, optical‑communication networking, nuclear‑thermal propulsion, autonomous combat aviation and long‑range air‑defence missile indigenisation, each grounded in verified programme milestones and technical specifications.

Indigenous High‑Power Microwave Weapon Development: KALI Series, Pulse Power Architecture and Tactical Doctrine

The KALI (Kilo‑Ampere Linear Injector) programme, managed by the Defence Research and Development Organisation’s (DRDO) Defence Electronics Research Laboratory (DLRL) and the Centre for High Energy Systems and Sciences (CHESS), represents India’s most mature effort in directed‑energy microwave weapons. The first demonstrator, KALI‑80, delivered a 0.8 GW, 80 ns pulse at 3 GHz using a Marx‑generator‑driven relativistic electron beam. Subsequent iterations — KALI‑200, KALI‑500 and the current KALI‑5000 — have scaled peak power to 5 GW, pulse width to 150 ns and repetition rate to 10 Hz, employing a water‑filled Blumlein line and a solid‑state opening switch to achieve sub‑nanosecond rise times. The microwave output is radiated through a conical horn antenna with a gain of 35 dBi, producing a far‑field power density exceeding 10 kW/m² at 1 km, sufficient to upset or permanently damage unhardened electronics.

Pulse‑power architecture centres on a modular Marx bank (12 stages, 1 MV per stage) feeding a pulse‑forming line (PFL) that shapes the voltage waveform. The PFL uses a low‑loss polyethylene dielectric and is matched to a vacuum‑diode electron gun that emits a 500 kA, 1 MeV beam. Beam‑to‑microwave conversion occurs in a virtual‑cavity oscillator (VCO) tuned to S‑band (3.2 GHz) with an efficiency of 30 %. Thermal management relies on a closed‑loop deionised‑water cooling system rated for 2 MW average dissipation, enabling the 10 Hz repetition rate without component degradation.

Tactical doctrine envisions two employment modes: (1) a “soft‑kill” role against incoming cruise missiles, UAV swarms and radar seekers by irradiating the target’s front‑end electronics at ranges of 5–10 km; (2) a “hard‑kill” adjunct where the microwave pulse is combined with a kinetic interceptor to degrade the target’s guidance before impact. The Indian Air Force’s (IAF) Air Defence Automation (ADA) network integrates KALI‑5000 as a mobile asset on a 8×8 Tatra chassis, with a deployable antenna mast and a hardened command‑and‑control shelter. Operational trials in 2022 demonstrated disruption of a simulated Brahmos‑type seeker at 7 km, and a 2023 joint DRDO‑IAF exercise validated simultaneous engagement of three UAVs using a single KALI pulse train.

Key challenges remain: (a) scaling to X‑band (10 GHz) for tighter beamwidths and reduced collateral effects; (b) hardening the platform’s own electronics against self‑generated electromagnetic interference; (c) establishing a logistics chain for the high‑voltage Marx capacitors, currently sourced from a single domestic vendor. The next development spiral, designated KALI‑10K, targets 10 GW peak power, 200 ns pulse width and a solid‑state Marx replacement using silicon‑carbide (SiC) switches to improve reliability and reduce footprint.

Nuclear Reactor Decommissioning Roadmap for India’s PHWR Fleet: Cost Modelling, Waste Categorisation and Regulatory Milestones

India operates 22 Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors (PHWRs) with a combined capacity of 6.8 GWe. The Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) issued the “Decommissioning Guidelines for Nuclear Power Plants” (Rev. 2, 2021), mandating a three‑phase approach: (i) post‑operational clean‑out (POCO) within 5 years of shutdown, (ii) safe‑store (SAFSTOR) for up to 30 years, and (iii) final dismantling and site release. The first PHWR slated for decommissioning is the 220 MWe Rajasthan Atomic Power Station (RAPS) Unit‑1, which entered commercial operation in 1973 and is scheduled for permanent shutdown in 2027.

Cost modelling follows the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) “Cost Estimation for Decommissioning” (CED) methodology, adapted to Indian labour rates and waste‑disposal tariffs. For a 220 MWe PHWR, the baseline estimate is ₹1,850 crore (≈ US $220 million) in 2024 prices, broken down as: POCO (₹320 crore), SAFSTOR surveillance (₹410 crore), dismantling (₹960 crore) and site restoration (₹160 crore). Sensitivity analysis shows a ±15 % variance driven by spent‑fuel management pathway (reprocessing vs. direct disposal) and the availability of a deep geological repository (DGR). The Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL) has provisioned a Decommissioning Fund, financed by a 0.5 % levy on gross generation revenue, which currently holds ₹4,200 crore.

Waste categorisation aligns with AERB’s “Radioactive Waste Management” (RWM) Code: (a) Very Low Level Waste (VLLW) – concrete rubble, steel, piping (< 1 Bq/g); (b) Low Level Waste (LLW) – activated reactor components, resins (1–10⁴ Bq/g); (c) Intermediate Level Waste (ILW) – reactor pressure vessel internals, control rods (10⁴–10⁶ Bq/g); (d) High Level Waste (HLW) – none generated during PHWR decommissioning because spent fuel is removed prior to POCO. VLLW and LLW are destined for the Near Surface Disposal Facility (NSDF) at Kalpakkam, while ILW will be conditioned in cementitious matrices and stored in the Interim Storage Facility (ISF) at Tarapur pending DGR availability.

Regulatory milestones include: (1) submission of the Decommissioning Plan (DP) to AERB 24 months before shutdown; (2) AERB safety review and issuance of Decommissioning Licence (DL); (3) periodic safety status reports (PSSR) every 2 years during SAFSTOR; (4) Final Safety Assessment Report (FSAR) prior to dismantling; (5) Site Release Certificate (SRC) after confirmatory surveys. The AERB has also mandated a “Decommissioning Safety Case” (DSC) that integrates probabilistic safety assessment (PSA) for external hazards (seismic, flood) and a radiological impact assessment for the public. NPCIL’s pilot decommissioning of the 100 MWe Tarapur Unit‑1 (BWR) in 2020‑2022 provided operational data that reduced the PHWR cost estimate by 8 % through lessons learned in remote cutting and waste segmentation.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “Which waste category from PHWR decommissioning requires a deep geological repository?” Options: VLLW, LLW, ILW, HLW. The correct answer is ILW, because HLW is not produced during PHWR decommissioning; ILW (activated internals) exceeds near‑surface disposal limits and must await a DGR.
The trap lies in assuming HLW is always present. In PHWRs, spent fuel is removed before decommissioning, so the highest activity waste is ILW. AERB’s RWM Code classifies ILW as requiring geological disposal, while VLLW/LLW go to NSDF. Recognising the fuel‑removal sequence eliminates the HLW distractor.
Exam‑day strategy
Memorise the three‑phase decommissioning timeline (POCO‑SAFSTOR‑Dismantling) and the four waste categories with their disposal routes. When a cost figure appears, check whether it includes spent‑fuel management — if not, the estimate is for decommissioning only. Use the 0.5 % levy figure to quickly compute fund adequacy in quantitative questions.

Space‑Based Optical Inter‑Satellite Link Network: Laser Terminal Design, Acquisition Algorithms and Integration with the Indian Data Relay Satellite System

The Indian Data Relay Satellite System (IDRSS), approved in 2022, will place two geostationary relay satellites (IDRSS‑1A and 1B) at 74° E and 83° E to provide continuous telemetry, tracking and command (TT&C) coverage for low‑earth‑orbit (LEO) missions, including Gaganyaan and future lunar landers. Each relay satellite carries a dual‑band (Ka‑band RF and 1550 nm optical) inter‑satellite link (ISL) terminal. The optical terminal, developed by the Laboratory for Electro‑Optics Systems (LEOS) under ISRO, uses a 15 cm aperture Cassegrain telescope mounted on a two‑axis fast‑steering mirror (FSM) with a bandwidth of 2 kHz and angular resolution of 0.5 µrad.

Laser source is a 1550 nm, 2 W average‑power, erbium‑doped fibre amplifier (EDFA) seeded by a narrow‑linewidth distributed‑feedback (DFB) laser.
