Modulation employs differential phase‑shift keying (DPSK) at 10 Gbps, with forward error correction (FEC) overhead of 20 %. The receiver uses a balanced coherent detector with a local‑oscillator laser phase‑locked to the incoming signal, achieving a sensitivity of –45 dBm at a bit‑error‑rate of 10⁻⁹. Link budget analysis shows a 35 dB margin for a 45,000 km GEO‑LEO slant range, assuming 0.3 dB/km atmospheric attenuation (clear sky) and 3 dB pointing loss.

Acquisition algorithm follows a three‑stage sequence: (1) coarse acquisition using RF beacon ephemeris to point the FSM within ±0.2°; (2) fine acquisition via a spiral scan of ±0.05° at 10 Hz, detecting the optical beacon (a 1550 nm, 100 mW CW laser) on the LEO satellite; (3) tracking lock using a centroiding algorithm on the received DPSK frame preamble, updating FSM commands at 2 kHz. The algorithm tolerates relative velocity up to 7 km/s and angular rate up to 0.02°/s, typical for GEO‑LEO geometry.

Integration with IDRSS ground segment occurs through the ISRO Telemetry, Tracking and Command Network (ISTRAC) at Bengaluru. The ground station hosts a 3.5 m optical telescope with adaptive optics (AO) to compensate turbulence, enabling uplink of high‑rate commands (1 Gbps) to the relay satellite. Data from LEO payloads (e.g., synthetic aperture radar, hyperspectral imager) is downlinked via the optical ISL to the relay, then relayed to ground over Ka‑band at 300 Mbps. The system demonstrated a 10 Gbps optical link in a 2023 ground‑to‑air test between LEOS and a modified Dornier‑228 aircraft, validating the acquisition sequence and FEC performance under dynamic Doppler shifts of ±200 MHz.

Future upgrades include wavelength‑division multiplexing (WDM) to carry four 25 Gbps channels on a single terminal, and integration of quantum‑key‑distribution (QKD) channels using the same aperture. The IDRSS optical ISL is also slated to support the proposed “Bharatiya Antariksh Station” (BAS) by providing high‑rate, low‑latency connectivity for crewed operations.

DRDO Technology Transfer and Commercialisation Framework: Licensing Models, Spin‑Off Companies and Private Sector Co‑Development

DRDO’s Technology Transfer (ToT) policy, revised in 2020 under the “Atmanirbhar Bharat” mandate, classifies transferable technologies into three tiers: (i) “Strategic” — systems with direct national security implications (e.g., missile guidance, nuclear instrumentation); (ii) “Dual‑Use” — technologies with both defence and civilian markets (e.g., composite materials, radar signal processing); (iii) “Commercial” — mature products ready for mass production (e.g., NBC protective suits, field rations). Each tier follows a distinct licensing model.

For Strategic tier, DRDO employs a “Government‑to‑Government” (G2G) or “Government‑to‑PSU” route, granting a non‑exclusive, royalty‑free licence to a nominated Defence Public Sector Undertaking (DPSU) such as Bharat Electronics Limited (BEL) or Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL). The licence includes a “Technology Absorption Plan” (TAP) with milestones for prototype validation, productionisation and quality certification. Dual‑Use tier adopts a “Licence‑to‑Manufacture” (LTM) model with a 5 % royalty on net sales, a 10‑year exclusivity window for the first licensee, and a mandatory “Offset‑Compliance” clause requiring 30 % of production value to be sourced from Indian MSMEs. Commercial tier uses a “Technology Licensing Agreement” (TLA) with a 2 % royalty, no exclusivity, and a fast‑track “Deemed Export” clearance for export‑oriented units.

Spin‑off creation is facilitated through the “DRDO‑Incubation Centre” (DIC) at each major laboratory. Since 2018, 27 start‑ups have been incubated, notably “Astra Microwave Products” (RF front‑ends), “Sagar Defence Engineering” (unmanned surface vessels) and “NewSpace Research & Technologies” (satellite propulsion). The DIC provides seed funding up to ₹5 crore, access to DRDO test ranges, and a “Technology Readiness Level (TRL)‑6 to TRL‑9” acceleration programme. Equity participation by DRDO is capped at 26 % to avoid conflict‑of‑interest, with a buy‑back clause after five years.

Private sector co‑development follows the “Development‑cum‑Production Partner” (DcPP) framework introduced in the Defence Acquisition Procedure (DAP) 2023. Under DcPP, a private firm (or consortium) shares 40 % of development cost and receives a 15‑year production contract with a minimum order quantity (MOQ) guarantee. The first DcPP contract was awarded in 2024 to a Tata‑DRDO consortium for the “Integrated Electronic Warfare Suite” (IEWS) for the Su‑30MKI, targeting TRL‑8 within 36 months. Intellectual property (IP) generated under DcPP is jointly owned, with DRDO retaining a “Government Purpose Licence” for unlimited internal use.

Compliance monitoring is executed through the “Technology Transfer Monitoring Cell” (TTMC) under the Department of Defence R&D. TTMC conducts quarterly audits of licensee production lines, verifies royalty payments via the “Defence Revenue Management System” (DRMS), and publishes an annual “ToT Impact Report” that tracks employment generation, export earnings and import substitution metrics. In FY 2023‑24, ToT revenues crossed ₹1,200 crore, with 68 % contributed by Dual‑Use licences, and 12,000 direct jobs created in the defence manufacturing ecosystem.

Advanced Air Independent Propulsion for Project 75I Submarines: Fuel‑Cell System Integration, Endurance Metrics and Indigenous Supply Chain

The Project 75I programme, aimed at constructing six conventional submarines with Air Independent Propulsion (AIP), selected the indigenous Phosphoric Acid Fuel Cell (PAFC) system developed by the Naval Materials Research Laboratory (NMRL) in partnership with Larsen & Toubro (L&T) and Thermax. The PAFC module delivers 300 kW continuous electrical power at 60 % electrical efficiency, using hydrogen generated on‑board from diesel reforming and stored oxygen in high‑pressure (350 bar) cylinders. Each submarine will carry two AIP modules, providing a combined 600 kW for hotel loads and low‑speed propulsion (up to 4 kn) while submerged.

System integration follows a modular “plug‑and‑play” architecture: the fuel‑cell stack (120 cells, 1.2 m² active area per cell) is housed in a pressure‑compensated enclosure rated for 30 bar external pressure. Thermal management uses a closed‑loop glycol‑water circuit with a heat‑exchanger interfacing the submarine’s seawater cooling system. The reformer unit, based on a catalytic partial oxidation (CPOX) process, converts 150 kg/h of marine diesel (NATO F‑76) into a hydrogen‑rich syngas (H₂ ≈ 45 %, CO < 1 %). A downstream preferential oxidation (PROX) reactor reduces CO to < 10 ppm to protect the platinum catalyst. Oxygen storage comprises eight 1,200 L composite cylinders (Type IV, carbon‑fiber/epoxy) providing 96 kg O₂, sufficient for 14 days of continuous AIP operation at full power.

Endurance metrics derived from sea‑trials of the technology demonstrator (TD‑AIP) on the INS Shishumar (modified) in 2022 show: (a) submerged endurance at 4 kn — 18 days (vs. 7 days on batteries alone); (b) maximum AIP‑only range — 1,200 nm; (c) acoustic signature reduction — 8 dB lower than diesel‑snorting at equivalent speed. The AIP system adds 120 tonnes to displacement, accommodated by a 1.5 m hull extension approved in the 75I design review.

Indigenous supply chain development targets 85 % local content by the third submarine. Critical components and their domestic sources: (i) PAFC membrane electrode assemblies (MEAs) — manufactured by the Centre for Fuel Cell Technology (CFCT) at ARCI, Hyderabad; (ii) CPOX reformer catalysts — supplied by Indian Oil Corporation (IOC) R&D; (iii) Type IV oxygen cylinders — produced by Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited (BHEL) using carbon‑fiber from Mitsubishi Chemical (India) joint venture; (iv) Power‑conditioning electronics (DC‑DC converters, 1 kV SiC MOSFETs) — fabricated by BEL’s Bengaluru facility. A “Supply Chain Resilience Plan” (SCRP) mandates dual‑sourcing for all Tier‑1 items and strategic stockpiling of 6 months’ worth of platinum‑group‑metal (PGM) catalyst powder.

Regulatory clearance follows the “Submarine Safety Certification” (SSC) process under the Directorate General of Naval Armament Inspection (DGNAI). The PAFC AIP received “In‑Principle Clearance” (IPC) in March 2023 after successful shock‑test (10 g, 10 ms) and fire‑test (1,200 °C for 30 min) of the hydrogen storage subsystem. Final “Type Acceptance” is scheduled after the first 75I submarine’s harbour acceptance trials (HAT) in 2027.

  • Confusing the KALI programme’s microwave output with laser‑based directed energy weapons — KALI is a high‑power microwave (HPM) source, not a laser.
  • Assuming all PHWR decommissioning waste is HLW — spent fuel is removed beforehand, so the highest category is ILW.
  • Believing the IDRSS optical ISL operates at 1064 nm — the terminal uses 1550 nm for eye‑safe, low‑atmospheric‑absorption performance.
  • Thinking DRDO’s Strategic‑tier licences carry royalties — they are royalty‑free and non‑exclusive to nominated DPSUs.
  • Mixing up the Project 75I AIP type — the selected system is a phosphoric‑acid fuel cell (PAFC), not a Stirling engine or closed‑cycle diesel.
  • Review these traps before the exam to avoid common mis‑identifications.
